1V1.2

attaching a cell

as in the book

to confirm$X \cup_\varphi e^n$ is the quotient of $X \sqcup D^n$ identifying each $u \in S^{n-1}$ with $\varphi(u)$, that is, the pushout of $X \leftarrow S^{n-1} \to D^n$.

the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §1, pp. 2–3

With $e^k$ the $k$-cell of vectors of length at most $1$ in $\mathbb R^k$, $\dot e^k$ its boundary sphere $S^{k-1}$, and $g : S^{k-1} \to Y$ continuous, the space $Y \cup_g e^k$, $Y$ with a $k$-cell attached by $g$, is obtained from the topological sum of $Y$ and $e^k$ by identifying each $x \in S^{k-1}$ with $g(x) \in Y$. For $k = 0$, $e^0$ is a point and $\dot e^0 = S^{-1}$ is empty, so that attaching a 0-cell adds a disjoint point.

Verified edition V1.2

For a topological space $X$, an integer $n \ge 0$ and a continuous map $\varphi : S^{n-1} \to X$, the space $X \cup_\varphi e^n$ is the pushout, in the category of topological spaces, of $\varphi$ and the inclusion of the unit sphere $S^{n-1}$ in the closed unit ball $D^n$ of $\mathbb R^n$: the quotient of the disjoint union $X \sqcup D^n$ by the identification of each $u \in S^{n-1}$ with $\varphi(u)$, so that a map out of it is a pair of maps on $X$ and on $D^n$ which agree along $\varphi$. For $n = 0$ the sphere is empty and $D^0$ is a point. The disk and the sphere are Mathlib's, those of its CW complexes. Book: pp. 2–3, the same definition (the topological sum of $Y$ and $e^k$ with each $x \in S^{k-1}$ identified with $g(x)$), with the same convention for $k = 0$. Hidden hypotheses: none.

2V1.3

critical points, Hessian, index and nullity in coordinates

restated

to confirmIn coordinates, a critical point is a zero of the derivative, the Hessian is the second derivative, the index is the largest dimension of a subspace on which the Hessian is negative definite, the nullity is the dimension of its null space, and non-degenerate means nullity $0$, equivalently a non-singular matrix of second partial derivatives.

index: the negative index of inertianon-degenerate: null space $0$Milnor's definitions become theorems
the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §2, pp. 4–5

A point $p$ is a critical point of a smooth $f : M \to \mathbb R$ when the induced map $f_* : TM_p \to T\mathbb R_{f(p)}$ is zero, which in local coordinates means that the first partial derivatives vanish at $p$; $f(p)$ is then a critical value. A critical point is non-degenerate when the matrix $(\partial^2 f/\partial x^i \partial x^j(p))$ is non-singular, a condition which can be checked directly not to depend on the coordinates. The index of a bilinear functional $H$ on a vector space is the maximal dimension of a subspace on which $H$ is negative definite, and its nullity is the dimension of the null space $\{v : H(v, w) = 0 \text{ for all } w\}$; a critical point is non-degenerate exactly when $f_{**}$ has nullity $0$.

The coordinate condition for a critical point is displayed in the book, but the display is lost in the scan.

Verified edition V1.3

Let $E$ be a real normed space and $f : E \to \mathbb R$. A point $p$ is a critical point of $f$ if $f$ is differentiable at $p$ with derivative $0$. The Hessian of $f$ at $p$ is the second derivative $d^2 f_p$, a continuous bilinear form on $E$, symmetric when $f$ is $C^2$ at $p$; it is defined at every point but only used at critical points. For a continuous bilinear form $H$ on $E$, the null space is $\{v : H(v, w) = 0 \text{ for all } w\}$, the nullity is its dimension, $H$ is non-degenerate if its null space is $0$, and the index of $H$ is the negative index of inertia of the quadratic form $v \mapsto H(v, v)$, which for finite-dimensional $E$ is the largest dimension of a subspace on which $H(v, v) < 0$ for all $v \ne 0$. A non-degenerate critical point is a critical point at which $d^2 f_p$ is non-degenerate. For finite-dimensional $E$, non-degenerate means nullity $0$; for $E = \mathbb R^n$ and $f$ of class $C^2$ at $p$, it means that the matrix $(\partial^2 f/\partial x^i\partial x^j(p))$ is non-singular. Book: pp. 4–5: critical points ($f_* = 0$, restated in local coordinates; the display is lost in the scan), non-degeneracy (the matrix of second partial derivatives is non-singular), the index and nullity of a bilinear functional, and the remark that a critical point is non-degenerate exactly when the nullity is $0$. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): the index is defined as Mathlib's negative index of inertia (sigNeg), and Milnor's definition as a maximum is a theorem (Morse.index_isGreatest); non-degeneracy is defined by a zero null space, and Milnor's matrix definition is a theorem.

What differs (the comparison)

  • The index is defined as Mathlib's negative index of inertia, and Milnor's definition, the maximal dimension of a negative definite subspace, is a theorem.
  • Non-degeneracy is defined by a zero null space; Milnor's definition by a non-singular matrix of second partial derivatives is a theorem, for $f$ of class $C^2$ at $p$.
  • The nullity is a dimension in Mathlib's sense, which is $0$ for an infinite-dimensional null space; the counts are meaningful in finite dimension, where they are used.
3V1.4

the same on a manifold, and Morse functions

restated

to confirmOn a manifold, with no Hausdorff hypothesis, the same notions are read in the preferred chart at $p$, critical points agree with those of the companion volume, and a Morse function is a smooth function all of whose critical points are non-degenerate.

the Hessian read in the preferred chartno vector-field extensionsno Hausdorff hypothesis
the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §2, pp. 4–5

At a critical point $p$ of $f$ on a manifold $M$, the Hessian is the symmetric bilinear functional $f_{}$ on $TM_p$ given by $f_{}(v, w) = \tilde v_p(\tilde w(f))$, where $\tilde v$ and $\tilde w$ are vector fields extending $v$ and $w$; it is symmetric because the Poisson bracket term $[\tilde v, \tilde w]_p(f)$ vanishes at a critical point, and hence independent of both extensions. In local coordinates its matrix in the basis $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$ is $(\partial^2 f/\partial x^i\partial x^j(p))$. The index of $f$ at $p$ is the index of $f_{**}$. Differentiable functions with no degenerate critical points are the subject of Theorem 3.5 (p. 20).

Verified edition V1.4

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold without boundary modelled on a real normed space $E$, with no Hausdorff or countability hypothesis, $f : M \to \mathbb R$ and $p \in M$. The point $p$ is a critical point of $f$ if the derivative $df_p : T_pM \to \mathbb R$ is $0$; equivalently, $df_p$ is not surjective, which is the companion project's definition. The Hessian $f_{}$ at $p$ is the second derivative at $\kappa(p)$ of $f\circ\kappa^{-1}$, where $\kappa$ is the preferred chart at $p$: a bilinear form on $E$, which Mathlib identifies with $T_pM$ through the same chart. The index and the nullity of $f$ at $p$ are those of $f_{}$, and $p$ is a non-degenerate critical point if it is critical and $f_{}$ is non-degenerate (V1.3). A Morse function is a $C^\infty$ function on $M$ all of whose critical points are non-degenerate. Book: pp. 4–5; the Morse functions are the differentiable functions with no degenerate critical points of Theorem 3.5 (p. 20). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): Milnor defines $f_{}(v, w) = \tilde v_p(\tilde w(f))$ for vector fields $\tilde v$, $\tilde w$ extending $v$, $w$, and checks that this is symmetric and independent of the extensions. That formula is not formalized: the formal definition is his coordinate expression (the matrix of second partial derivatives, p. 5, which is his formula for extensions with constant coefficients), and its independence of the extensions is replaced by its independence of the chart (V1.5). Mathlib's derivative is $0$ at a point where $f$ is not differentiable, so such a point counts as critical; for smooth $f$ this never matters.

independence of the coordinate system

stronger

to confirmAt a critical point of a function $C^2$ there, criticality, the Hessian (transformed as a bilinear form by the derivative of the change of coordinates), non-degeneracy, index and nullity do not depend on the coordinate system.

$f$ only $C^2$ at $p$coordinates in any normed spacecriticality used exactly once
the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §2, pp. 4–5

Milnor remarks that non-degeneracy does not depend on the coordinate system, which can be checked directly and will also follow from the intrinsic definition of the Hessian; on p. 5 he computes that the matrix $(\partial^2 f/\partial x^i\partial x^j(p))$ represents $f_{**}$ with respect to the basis $\partial/\partial x^1|_p, \dots, \partial/\partial x^n|_p$.

Verified edition V1.5

On normed spaces: if $\psi$ is $C^2$ at $q$, $f$ is $C^2$ at $\psi(q)$ and $df_{\psi(q)} = 0$, then $d^2(f\circ\psi)_q(v, w) = d^2 f_{\psi(q)}(d\psi_q v, d\psi_q w)$. On $M$ as in V1.4: a smooth coordinate system is a homeomorphism $y$ of an open subset of $M$ onto an open subset of a real normed space $E'$ which is $C^\infty$ with $C^\infty$ inverse (for $E' = E$ these are exactly the charts of the maximal atlas). Let $p$ lie in the domain of $y$. If $f$ is differentiable at $p$, then $p$ is critical if and only if $y(p)$ is a critical point of $f\circ y^{-1}$, that is, for $E' = \mathbb R^n$, if and only if all the partial derivatives $\partial f/\partial y^i(p)$ vanish. If $f$ is $C^2$ at $p$ and $p$ is critical, the Hessian of $f\circ y^{-1}$ at $y(p)$ is $f_{}$ composed in both arguments with the derivative of $y^{-1}$ at $y(p)$ (the matrix $(\partial^2 f/\partial y^i\partial y^j(p))$ represents $f_{}$ in the basis $\partial/\partial y^i|_p$); hence non-degeneracy, index and nullity are those of $f\circ y^{-1}$ at $y(p)$, and for $E' = \mathbb R^n$, $p$ is non-degenerate if and only if $\det(\partial^2 f/\partial y^i\partial y^j(p)) \ne 0$. Book: p. 4, non-degeneracy "can be checked directly" not to depend on the coordinate system; p. 5, the matrix of second partial derivatives represents $f_{*}$. *Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (stronger): $f$ need only be $C^2$ at $p$, and the coordinates may take values in any normed space. Criticality is used exactly once, to kill the first-order term $df(d^2\psi)$ of the chain rule.

  • Criticality enters exactly once, to kill the first-order term $df(d^2\psi)$ of the chain rule: away from a critical point the matrix of second partial derivatives is not a tensor.

functions on a slice submanifold

not in the book

to confirmFor $f = F|N$ on a slice submanifold $N$ of $V$, a point $q$ is critical exactly when $dF_q$ vanishes on $T_qN$ (for an inner product, when $\nabla F(q) \perp T_qN$), the Hessian, index and nullity can be computed in any slice parametrization, and for $L_p$ Milnor's criterion and Hessian formula of pp. 35–36 hold.

the setting of Chapters 2–4Hessian of $F \circ x$, not of $F$Milnor's formulas of pp. 35–36 proved
the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §6, pp. 35–36

The book has no separate setting for functions on a submanifold. §2 is written for an abstract manifold, and from §6 on Milnor computes on $M \subset \mathbb R^n$ in local coordinates $u \mapsto \vec x(u)$ without comment. For $L_{\vec p}(\vec q) = \|\vec q - \vec p\|^2$ he notes that $\vec q$ is critical iff $\vec q - \vec p$ is normal to $M$ at $\vec q$ (p. 35), and that at a critical point the second partial derivatives are $2(\partial\vec x/\partial u^i \cdot \partial\vec x/\partial u^j + \partial^2\vec x/\partial u^i\partial u^j \cdot (\vec x - \vec p))$ (p. 36).

Verified edition V1.6

This is the setting of every later statement about a submanifold of Euclidean space. $V$ is a real normed space (Milnor's $\mathbb R^K$) and $N \subseteq V$ is a slice submanifold modelled on $Z$ in the sense of the companion project: every point of $N$ lies in the domain of a slice chart, a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism $\sigma$ of an open subset of $V$ onto an open subset of $Z \times W$ which carries the points of $N$ in its domain exactly onto $Z \times \{0\}$. $N$ need not be closed; it is a smooth manifold modelled on $Z$, with the charts $q \mapsto \sigma(q)_1$ and the parametrizations $x(z) = \sigma^{-1}(z, 0)$. Let $T_qN \subseteq V$ be the range of the derivative of the inclusion $N \to V$ at $q$; it is the range of $dx$. Let $F : V \to \mathbb R$ and let $q \in N$ lie in the domain of $\sigma$. If $F$ is differentiable at $q$, then $q$ is a critical point of $F|N$ if and only if $\sigma(q)_1$ is a critical point of $F\circ x$, if and only if $dF_q$ vanishes on $T_qN$, and, when $V$ is a complete inner product space, if and only if $\nabla F(q) \perp T_qN$. If $F$ is $C^2$ at $q$ and $q$ is critical for $F|N$, the Hessian of $F\circ x$ at $\sigma(q)_1$ is $f_{*}$ composed with the derivative of the parametrization, so non-degeneracy, index and nullity of $F|N$ at $q$ are those of $F\circ x$. For $V$ an inner product space and $L_p(y) = \|y - p\|^2$: $q$ is a critical point of $L_p|N$ if and only if $q - p \perp T_qN$; for any $x$ of class $C^2$ at $u$, the second derivative of $L_p\circ x$ at $u$ is $2(\langle \partial x/\partial v, \partial x/\partial w\rangle + \langle \partial^2 x/\partial v\,\partial w, x(u) - p\rangle)$; and at a critical point $q$ the index and the nullity of $L_p|N$ are those of this form at $u = \sigma(q)_1$. *Book: §2 is written for abstract manifolds, and the reduction to a parametrization is used without comment later; the statements on $L_p$ are Milnor's criterion of p. 35 and his formula of p. 36 (§6), proved in this chapter's files. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (not in the book): the identifications themselves. The Hessian of $F\circ x$ is not the restriction of the ambient Hessian of $F$: the chain rule adds $dF_q(\partial^2 x/\partial v\,\partial w)$, which does not vanish at a critical point of $F|N$ and which, for $L_p$, is the second-fundamental-form term of Milnor's formula.

Lemma 2.1, Hadamard's lemma

stronger

to confirmA function smooth on an open convex neighbourhood $V$ of $0$ in $\mathbb R^n$ with $f(0) = 0$ is $\sum_i x_i g_i(x)$ with $g_i$ smooth on $V$ and $g_i(0) = \partial f/\partial x_i(0)$; on an open star-shaped $V$ in any normed space it is $L(x)x$ with $L$ smooth and $L(0) = df_0$, and if also $df_0 = 0$ it is $B(x)(x, x)$ with $B$ smooth and symmetric and $B(0) = \tfrac12 d^2 f_0$.

star-shaped, not convexany normed source, complete target$B(0) = \frac12 d^2f_0$ proved$V$ open
the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §2, Lemma 2.1

A $C^\infty$ function $f$ on a convex neighbourhood $V$ of $0$ in $\mathbb R^n$ with $f(0) = 0$ can be written $f(x) = \sum_i x_i g_i(x)$, the $g_i$ being $C^\infty$ on $V$ with $g_i(0) = \partial f/\partial x_i(0)$. The proof writes $f(x)$ as $\int_0^1 \frac{d}{dt} f(tx)\,dt$ and takes $g_i(x) = \int_0^1 \partial f/\partial x_i(tx)\,dt$.

Verified edition V1.7

Let $V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and convex with $0 \in V$, and $f$ smooth on $V$ with $f(0) = 0$. Then $f(x) = \sum_i x_i g_i(x)$ on $V$ for some functions $g_i$ smooth on $V$ with $g_i(0) = \partial f/\partial x_i(0)$. More generally, let $V$ be open and star-shaped about $0$ in a real normed space $E$ and $f$ smooth on $V$, with values in a complete normed space and $f(0) = 0$. Then $f(x) = L(x)\,x$ on $V$ for a family of linear maps $L$ smooth on $V$ with $L(0) = df_0$; and if moreover $df_0 = 0$, then $f(x) = B(x)(x, x)$ on $V$ for a family of bilinear maps $B$ smooth on $V$, with $B(x)$ symmetric for each $x \in V$ and $B(0) = \tfrac12 d^2 f_0$. (The proofs take $L(x) = \int_0^1 df_{tx}\,dt$ and $B(x) = \int_0^1 (1 - t)\, d^2 f_{tx}\,dt$.) Book: p. 5, Lemma 2.1, for $f$ smooth in a convex neighbourhood $V$ of $0$ in $\mathbb R^n$; on p. 7 Milnor applies it twice, symmetrizes, and asserts without proof that the coefficients at $0$ are $\tfrac12\,\partial^2 f/\partial x^i\partial x^j(0)$, which is the second-order form. Hidden hypotheses: $V$ open; and the smoothness of the $g_i$, which the book does not argue, is differentiation under the integral sign on an open set (Morse.contDiffOn_intervalIntegral: if $h$ is $C^n$ on an open $U \subseteq E \times \mathbb R$ containing $V \times [0, 1]$, $V$ open, then $x \mapsto \int_0^1 h(x, t)\,dt$ is $C^n$ on $V$). Deviation (stronger): star-shaped instead of convex, any normed source and any complete target. Proof: the second-order form is Taylor's formula with integral remainder rather than two applications of Lemma 2.1, which makes the value $B(0) = \tfrac12 d^2 f_0$ immediate.

What differs (the comparison)

  • Convexity is weakened to star-shapedness, $\mathbb R^n$ to any real normed space, and the values may lie in any complete normed space; $V$ must be open, which the book leaves implicit.
  • The smoothness of the $g_i$, which Milnor does not argue, is differentiation under the integral sign on an open set, proved here.
  • On p. 7 Milnor applies the lemma twice, symmetrizes, and asserts without proof that the coefficients at $0$ are $\frac12\,\partial^2 f/\partial x^i\partial x^j(0)$. That second-order form is proved directly, by Taylor's formula with integral remainder, with $B(x) = \int_0^1 (1 - t)\,d^2 f_{tx}\,dt$.

Lemma 2.2, the Morse lemma

stronger

to confirmNear a non-degenerate critical point $p$ of index $\lambda$ of a function smooth near $p$, on $\mathbb R^n$ or on any smooth manifold, there are coordinates with $f = f(p) - \sum_{i \le \lambda}(y^i)^2 + \sum_{i > \lambda}(y^i)^2$.

$f$ smooth only near $p$any manifold, no Hausdorff hypothesisone inverse-function step
the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §2, Lemma 2.2

Near a non-degenerate critical point $p$ of $f$ there are local coordinates $(y^1, \dots, y^n)$, all vanishing at $p$, on a neighbourhood $U$ of $p$, in which $f = f(p) - (y^1)^2 - \dots - (y^\lambda)^2 + (y^{\lambda+1})^2 + \dots + (y^n)^2$ on all of $U$, $\lambda$ being the index of $f$ at $p$. The proof writes $f = \sum x_ix_jh_{ij}$ by Lemma 2.1 and completes one square at a time by induction, after a linear change of the last $n - r + 1$ coordinates making $H_{rr}(0) \ne 0$.

Verified edition V1.8

Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, $n = \dim E$, $f$ smooth on an open set $U \ni p$, and $p$ a critical point at which $d^2 f_p$ is non-degenerate, of index $\lambda$. Then there is a homeomorphism $y$ of an open neighbourhood $U' \subseteq U$ of $p$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb R^n$, $C^\infty$ with $C^\infty$ inverse, such that $y(p) = 0$ and $f = f(p) - (y^1)^2 - \dots - (y^\lambda)^2 + (y^{\lambda+1})^2 + \dots + (y^n)^2$ throughout $U'$. In coordinate-free form, there is such a $\varphi$ onto an open subset of $E$ with $\varphi(p) = 0$, $d\varphi_p = \mathrm{id}$ and $f = f(p) + \tfrac12 d^2 f_p(\varphi, \varphi)$ on its domain. On a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary modelled on $E$, with no Hausdorff hypothesis, for $f$ smooth on an open $U \ni p$ and $p$ a non-degenerate critical point of index $\lambda$ (V1.4): there is a smooth coordinate system $y$ of $M$ (V1.5) with values in $\mathbb R^n$, domain an open neighbourhood of $p$ inside $U$, $y(p) = 0$, and the same normal form on its domain; and there is a chart $\varphi$ of the maximal atlas, with domain an open neighbourhood of $p$ inside $U$, $\varphi(p) = 0$ and $f = f(p) + \tfrac12 f_{*}(\varphi, \varphi)$ on its domain. *Book: p. 6, Lemma 2.2. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (stronger): $f$ need only be smooth near $p$. Proof: not Milnor's induction, which completes one square at a time and does not justify the linear change of the remaining coordinates making $H_{rr}(0) \ne 0$, but one application of the inverse function theorem: with $f(p + x) - f(p) = B(x)(x, x)$ and $B_0 = \tfrac12 d^2 f_p$ (V1.7), the map $T \mapsto B_0(T\cdot, T\cdot) + B_0(T\cdot, \cdot) - B_0(\cdot, T\cdot)$ on linear maps of $E$ has invertible derivative $H \mapsto 2B_0(H\cdot, \cdot)$ at the identity, which yields linear maps $C(x)$, smooth in $x$, with $C(0) = \mathrm{id}$ and $B(x)(v, v) = B_0(C(x)v, C(x)v)$ (Morse.exists_sqrt_family), so that $\varphi(p + x) = C(x)x$. Sylvester's law of inertia, from Mathlib, then diagonalizes $B_0$ with the negative squares first (Morse.exists_linearEquiv_diagForm).

What differs (the comparison)

  • The proof is not Milnor's induction, which completes one square at a time and does not justify the linear change making $H_{rr}(0) \ne 0$. One application of the inverse function theorem, to a map on linear operators whose derivative at the identity is $H \mapsto 2B_0(H\cdot, \cdot)$, gives linear maps $C(x)$, smooth in $x$, with $C(0) = \mathrm{id}$ and $f(p + x) = f(p) + \frac12 d^2 f_p(C(x)x, C(x)x)$.

Milnor §2, proof of Lemma 2.2

The proof of Lemma 2.2 begins by showing that if $f(q) = f(p) - (z^1(q))^2 - \dots - (z^\lambda(q))^2 + (z^{\lambda+1}(q))^2 + \dots + (z^n(q))^2$ in some coordinate system $z$ around $p$, then $\lambda$ must be the index of $f$ at $p$: the matrix of $f_{}$ in the basis $\partial/\partial z^i|_p$ is diagonal with $\lambda$ entries $-2$ and $n - \lambda$ entries $2$, so $f_{}$ is negative definite on a subspace of dimension $\lambda$ and positive definite on one of dimension $n - \lambda$, and no larger negative definite subspace exists.

Milnor §2, pp. 8–9

Milnor pictures five degenerate critical points: (a) $f(x) = x^3$ at the origin; (b) $e^{-1/x^2}\sin^2(1/x)$, whose origin is a degenerate and non-isolated critical point; (c) the monkey saddle $x^3 - 3xy^2$, the real part of $(x + iy)^3$, at $(0, 0)$; (d) $f(x, y) = x^2$, whose critical points, all degenerate, form the $x$ axis, a submanifold of $\mathbb R^2$; (e) $x^2y^2$, whose degenerate critical points fill the union of the $x$ and $y$ axes, not even a submanifold of $\mathbb R^2$.

Verified edition V1.12

(a) The only critical point of $x^3$ on $\mathbb R$ is $0$, where the Hessian is $0$, so it is degenerate. (c) The only critical point of $x^3 - 3xy^2$ on $\mathbb R^2$ is the origin, where the Hessian is $0$. (d) The critical points of $x^2$ on $\mathbb R^2$ are the points of the line $x = 0$, and all are degenerate. (e) The critical points of $x^2y^2$ are the points of the two coordinate axes, and all are degenerate. In (d) and (e) degeneracy is the contrapositive of V1.10: a critical point that is a limit of other critical points, of a function $C^2$ there, is degenerate. Book: pp. 8–9, examples (a), (c), (d), (e). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (stronger): in (a) and (c) the origin is also the only critical point. Deviation (value differs): in (d) the book says the critical set is the $x$ axis; since $\partial f/\partial x = 2x$ and $\partial f/\partial y = 0$, it is the $y$ axis. The formalization noticed this.

Milnor §2, pp. 9–10

Milnor's 1-parameter group of diffeomorphisms of $M$ is a $C^\infty$ map $\varphi : \mathbb R \times M \to M$ whose maps $\varphi_t$ are diffeomorphisms of $M$ with $\varphi_{t+s} = \varphi_t \circ \varphi_s$. It determines the vector field $X_q(f) = \lim_{h \to 0} (f(\varphi_h(q)) - f(q))/h$, which is said to generate $\varphi$, and each orbit $t \mapsto \varphi_t(q)$ solves $d\varphi_t(q)/dt = X_{\varphi_t(q)}$ with $\varphi_0(q) = q$.

Verified edition V1.13

On a real normed space $E$, a one-parameter group of diffeomorphisms is a map $\varphi : \mathbb R \times E \to E$, $C^\infty$ in $(t, x)$, such that each $\varphi_t$ is a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism of $E$ and $\varphi_{t+s} = \varphi_t\circ\varphi_s$ for all $t$, $s$. A vector field $X : E \to E$ generates $\varphi$ if for every $x$ the curve $h \mapsto \varphi_h(x)$ has derivative $X(x)$ at $h = 0$. Then $\varphi_0 = \mathrm{id}$, and if $\varphi$ is generated by $X$, every orbit $t \mapsto \varphi_t(x)$ is an integral curve of $X$. Book: pp. 9–10, on a manifold; the orbit computation is on p. 10. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (narrower): only for $M = E$, where a tangent vector is a vector and Milnor's $X_q(f) = \lim_{h \to 0}(f(\varphi_h(q)) - f(q))/h$ becomes the derivative of $h \mapsto \varphi_h(q)$. That $\varphi_0 = \mathrm{id}$, used implicitly on p. 10, follows from the group law because $\varphi_0$ is injective.

Milnor §2, pp. 10–11

In the proof of Lemma 2.4 Milnor quotes as well known, citing Graves, that the equation $d\varphi_t(q)/dt = X_{\varphi_t(q)}$, $\varphi_0(q) = q$, has locally a unique solution which depends smoothly on the initial conditions. Covering the compact support $K$ by finitely many such neighbourhoods gives $\epsilon_0 > 0$ and solutions for $|t| < \epsilon_0$, smooth in both variables; for larger $t$ he iterates $\varphi_{\epsilon_0/2}$, and says it is not difficult to verify that the result is well defined, smooth, and satisfies $\varphi_{t+s} = \varphi_t\circ\varphi_s$.

Verified edition V1.14

Let $E$ be a complete real normed space and $X : E \to E$ bounded and globally Lipschitz, for instance $C^1$ with compact support. Through every point there is an integral curve of $X$ defined on all of $\mathbb R$, every integral curve is a flow line, and the flow satisfies $\varphi_0 = \mathrm{id}$ and $\varphi_{s+t} = \varphi_s\circ\varphi_t$, is jointly continuous in $(t, x)$, and each $\varphi_t$ is a homeomorphism with inverse $\varphi_{-t}$. If $X$ is $C^n$, $1 \le n \le \infty$, with compact support, then $(t, x) \mapsto \varphi_t(x)$ is $C^n$ on $\mathbb R \times E$ and each $\varphi_t$ is a $C^n$ diffeomorphism. Book: p. 10, quoted as well known (citing Graves): locally the equation has a unique solution depending smoothly on the initial conditions; p. 11, "not difficult to verify" that the $\varphi_t$ obtained by iteration are well defined, smooth, and form a group. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): Milnor quotes the local theory and iterates it; the formal statements are global, for bounded Lipschitz or compactly supported fields on a vector space, and the smooth dependence, which Mathlib lacks, is proved rather than quoted. Proof: on $[0, 1]$ the flow line through $x$ solves $\Psi(\gamma) = x$ with $\Psi(\gamma) = \gamma - \int_0^{\cdot} X(\gamma)$ in the Banach space $C([0, 1], E)$; for a Lipschitz constant below $1$, $\Psi$ is a homeomorphism with everywhere invertible derivative (Neumann series) and $\gamma \mapsto X\circ\gamma$ is as smooth as $X$, so the time-one map is $C^n$ (Morse.Flow.voltHomeomorph, Morse.Flow.contDiff_voltHomeomorph_symm, Morse.Flow.contDiff_nem). General times come from $\varphi_t = (\varphi_{t/N})^N$ and joint smoothness from the flow of $(x, \tau) \mapsto (\rho(\tau)X(x), 0)$ on $E \times \mathbb R$; Milnor's iteration of $\varphi_{\epsilon_0/2}$ is replaced by Picard–Lindelöf on intervals of any length, which a bounded field allows.

Milnor §3, pp. 12–13

Throughout §3, $M^a = f^{-1}(-\infty, a] = \{p \in M : f(p) \le a\}$. Milnor uses “deformation retract” without a definition: in the proof of Theorem 3.1 he builds a 1-parameter family of maps $r_t : M^b \to M^b$ with $r_0$ the identity and $r_1$ a retraction onto $M^a$, concludes that $M^a$ is a deformation retract of $M^b$, and so that the inclusion is a homotopy equivalence.

Verified edition V2.1

For a real function $f$ on a set and $c \in \mathbb R$, $M^c = \{x : f(x) \le c\}$. A subset $A$ of a topological space $X$ is a strong deformation retract of $X$ if there are a continuous map $r : X \to X$ with values in $A$ and a homotopy $(t, x) \mapsto r_t(x)$, $0 \le t \le 1$, from $r_0 = \mathrm{id}_X$ to $r_1 = r$ with $r_t(a) = a$ for all $t$ and all $a \in A$. If $A \subseteq B$ are subsets of a space and $A$ is a strong deformation retract of $B$, the inclusion $A \to B$ is a homotopy equivalence (the proof takes $r_1$ as its homotopy inverse). Deviation (stronger): Milnor uses "deformation retract" without a definition; every deformation he constructs fixes the smaller set at all times, and every formal statement asserts this strong form, which implies the weaker ones.

For a smooth real function $f$ on a manifold $M$ and $a < b$, if the set $f^{-1}[a, b]$ of points where $a \le f \le b$ is compact and free of critical points of $f$, then $M^a$ and $M^b$ are diffeomorphic; moreover $M^a$ is a deformation retract of $M^b$, so the inclusion $M^a \to M^b$ is a homotopy equivalence. The proof chooses a Riemannian metric, takes $\rho$ equal to $1/\langle \mathrm{grad} f, \mathrm{grad} f\rangle$ on $f^{-1}[a, b]$ and vanishing outside a compact neighbourhood of it, and pushes $M^b$ down to $M^a$ along the flow $\varphi_t$ of $\rho\,\mathrm{grad} f$; then $\varphi_{b-a}$ carries $M^a$ diffeomorphically onto $M^b$.

Take a smooth $f : M \to \mathbb R$ and a non-degenerate critical point $p$ of index $\lambda$, with $c = f(p)$, and assume that for some $\epsilon > 0$ the set $f^{-1}[c - \epsilon, c + \epsilon]$ is compact with $p$ its only critical point. Then, once $\epsilon$ is small enough, $M^{c+\epsilon}$ is homotopy equivalent to $M^{c-\epsilon}$ with a $\lambda$-cell attached. In the proof a function $\mu$ modifies $f$ near $p$ to a smooth $F$ with $F^{-1}(-\infty, c - \epsilon] = M^{c-\epsilon} \cup H$, and four Assertions show that $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup e^\lambda$ is a deformation retract of $M^{c+\epsilon}$.

Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space, $f : E \to \mathbb R$ of class $C^\infty$, $p$ a critical point at which $d^2 f_p$ is non-degenerate, $\lambda$ its index (V1.3) and $c = f(p)$, and suppose that for some $\epsilon_0 > 0$ the set $f^{-1}[c - \epsilon_0, c + \epsilon_0]$ is compact and contains no critical point other than $p$. Let $A$ be a closed subset of a Hausdorff space $M$ and $\chi : \mathbb R^n \to M$ continuous and injective on $D^n$, with $\chi(z) \in A$ exactly when $|z| = 1$, for $z \in D^n$. Milnor §3, Theorem 3.5

Theorem 3.5 asserts the homotopy type of a CW-complex, for whose definition Milnor refers to J. H. C. Whitehead. In the proof (p. 23) each attaching map is replaced, by cellular approximation, by a map into the $(\lambda_j - 1)$-skeleton, so that attaching the new cells to a CW-complex gives a CW-complex again.

Verified edition V2.11

A space $K$ is an iterated adjunction space with cells $(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k)$ if it is obtained from the empty space by attaching a $\lambda_1$-cell, then a $\lambda_2$-cell, and so on, each along an arbitrary continuous map of its boundary sphere into the space built so far (V1.2). A space $X$ has the homotopy type of a finite cell complex with cells $(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k)$ if it is homotopy equivalent to such a $K$. Book: p. 20, the "CW-complex" of Theorem 3.5, for which Milnor refers to J. H. C. Whitehead. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (narrower): this is weaker than a CW-complex with these cells: the attaching maps need not be cellular, and the cells are attached in the listed order rather than by dimension. Milnor makes the attaching maps cellular by the cellular approximation theorem (p. 23), which Mathlib does not have; with it and Lemma 3.6 such a space is homotopy equivalent to a CW-complex with the same number of cells in each dimension, a step that is not formalized.

Milnor §3, Theorem 3.5

A manifold $M$ carrying a differentiable function without degenerate critical points, all of whose sublevel sets $M^a$ are compact, is homotopy equivalent to a CW-complex with one cell of dimension $\lambda$ for each critical point of index $\lambda$. The proof (pp. 23–24) lists the critical values $c_1 < c_2 < \dots$, notes that $M^a$ is vacuous for $a < c_1$, passes each critical level by Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 and Remark 3.3, and carries the cells along homotopy equivalences by Lemmas 3.6 and 3.7; the non-compact case uses a direct limit and Whitehead's theorem.

Verified edition V2.12

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, $N \subseteq V$ a compact slice submanifold modelled on a finite-dimensional $Z$, $F : V \to \mathbb R$ of class $C^\infty$, and suppose that every critical point of $f = F|N$ is non-degenerate. Then the critical points of $f$ can be listed without repetition as $p_1, \dots, p_k$, with $f(p_1) \le \dots \le f(p_k)$, so that $N$ has the homotopy type of a finite cell complex with cells $(\lambda(p_1), \dots, \lambda(p_k))$ in the sense of V2.11, $\lambda(p)$ the index of $p$. In particular $N$ has the homotopy type of such a complex whose number of cells of dimension $\lambda$ is, for every $\lambda$, the number $C_\lambda$ of critical points of index $\lambda$. If the critical values are distinct, the list is strictly increasing (Morse.theorem_3_5, Morse.theorem_3_5_count). For an attaching map $\varphi : \dot e^\lambda \to X$, every homotopy equivalence $f : X \to Y$ extends to a homotopy equivalence $F$ from $X \cup_\varphi e^\lambda$ to $Y \cup_{f\varphi} e^\lambda$. Let $M$ be a manifold modelled on a real normed space $E$ and $f : M \to \mathbb R$. A local minimum or local maximum $p$ of $f$ is a critical point (for every $f$: in the formal definition of Chapter 1 a point where $f$ is not differentiable counts as critical). In the proof of Reeb's theorem, with $f(p) = 0$ the minimum and $f(q) = 1$ the maximum, Milnor says that if $\epsilon$ is small enough the sets $M^\epsilon = f^{-1}[0, \epsilon]$ and $f^{-1}[1 - \epsilon, 1]$ are closed $n$-cells, by the lemma of Morse (2.2).

Verified edition V3.2

(i) In the setting of the second half of V3.1, if $p$ is a non-degenerate local minimum (maximum) of $f$, $f$ smooth on an open $U \ni p$, there are smooth coordinates $y$ on an open subset of $U$ containing $p$, with values in $\mathbb R^n$ with its Euclidean norm, such that $y(p) = 0$ and $f = f(p) + \|y\|^2$ (resp. $f = f(p) - \|y\|^2$) on the domain of $y$. (ii) Let $X$ be a compact topological space, $f : X \to \mathbb R$ continuous with a strict global minimum at $p$ ($f(p) < f(x)$ for all $x \ne p$), and $y$ a homeomorphism from an open neighbourhood of $p$ onto an open subset of a real normed space $F$, with $y(p) = 0$ and $f = f(p) + \|y\|^2$ on its domain. Then there is $\delta > 0$ such that for every $0 < \varepsilon < \delta$ the map $v \mapsto y^{-1}(\sqrt\varepsilon\, v)$ is continuous and injective on the closed unit ball of $F$, maps it onto $\{f \le f(p) + \varepsilon\}$, and maps the unit sphere onto the level set $\{f = f(p) + \varepsilon\}$. (i) Alexander's trick: if $g$ is a homeomorphism of the unit sphere of a real normed space $E$, the cone $x \mapsto \|x\|\, g(x/\|x\|)$, $0 \mapsto 0$, is a homeomorphism of $E$ that preserves norms and extends $g$. (ii) Let $X$ be a Hausdorff space, $n \ge 0$, $D^n$ and $S^{n-1}$ the closed unit ball and unit sphere of $\mathbb R^n$, and $h_1, h_2 : D^n \to X$ continuous and injective, with $h_1(D^n) \cup h_2(D^n) = X$, $h_1(D^n) \cap h_2(D^n) = h_1(S^{n-1})$ and $h_2(S^{n-1}) = h_1(S^{n-1})$. Book: p. 25: $M$ is the union of two closed $n$-cells matched along their common boundary, and a homeomorphism with $S^n$ is "now easy to construct"; none is constructed. Hidden hypotheses: the identification $h_2^{-1} \circ h_1$ of the boundary spheres is in general not the identity and must be extended over a ball (Alexander's trick); the inverse is continuous because a continuous bijection from a compact space onto a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism. Milnor §4, Theorem 4.1 (Reeb)

A compact manifold $M$ carrying a differentiable function with only two critical points, both non-degenerate, is homeomorphic to a sphere. The proof: the two critical points are the minimum and the maximum; small sublevel and superlevel sets are closed $n$-cells by Lemma 2.2; $M^\epsilon$ is homeomorphic to $M^{1-\epsilon}$ by Theorem 3.1; so $M$ is two closed $n$-cells matched along their boundary.

Remark 1 adds that the theorem remains true for degenerate critical points, with a more difficult proof, and Remark 2 that $M$ need not be diffeomorphic to $S^n$.

Verified edition V3.6

Let $N$ be a compact slice submanifold of a finite-dimensional real normed space $V$, modelled on a finite-dimensional space of dimension $n$, and $f = F|_N$ with $F : V \to \mathbb R$ smooth. If $f$ has exactly two critical points, both non-degenerate, then $N$ is homeomorphic to the unit sphere $S^n \subseteq \mathbb R^{n+1}$. For a compact $N \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}$ modelled on $\mathbb R^n$, $n \ge 1$, the same holds for every smooth $f : N \to \mathbb R$ (Morse.reeb_of_contMDiff; such an $f$ is the restriction of a smooth function on $\mathbb R^{K+1}$, V3.20). Milnor §5, Definition

An integer-valued function $S$, defined on certain pairs of spaces, is subadditive if $S(X, Z) \le S(X, Y) + S(Y, Z)$ for every $X \supset Y \supset Z$, and additive if equality always holds.

Verified edition V3.7

Spaces are replaced by the elements of a preordered set $\iota$, $a \le b$ standing for $X_a \subseteq X_b$. A function on pairs is an integer-valued function $S(a, b)$ of two indices, used only for $a \le b$, where $S(a, b)$ stands for Milnor's $S(X_b, X_a)$ (the smaller space is written first). $S$ is subadditive if $S(a, c) \le S(a, b) + S(b, c)$ whenever $a \le b \le c$, and additive if equality always holds. Book: p. 28: $S$ is an integer-valued function on certain pairs of spaces, subadditive if $S(X, Z) \le S(X, Y) + S(Y, Z)$ whenever $X \supset Y \supset Z$, additive if equality holds. Hidden hypotheses: the class of pairs on which $S$ is defined must be closed under the passage from $(X, Y), (Y, Z)$ to $(X, Z)$; Milnor does not say which pairs. Here every pair $a \le b$ of the index set is allowed. Deviation (restated): indices of a preorder in place of spaces, and the reversed argument order.

the homology of a filtration and its Morse numbers

to confirmA homology of a filtration is a family of finite-dimensional vector spaces $H_i(a, b)$, $a \le b$, with a long exact sequence for every triple ending in $0$; nothing else is assumed.

abstract, not singular homologyfiniteness a consequence on chains
the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §5, pp. 28–30

Milnor works with singular homology with coefficients in a field $F$: $R_\lambda(X, Y)$, the $\lambda$-th Betti number of $(X, Y)$, is the rank over $F$ of $H_\lambda(X, Y; F)$, for any pair for which this rank is finite. He uses the exact sequence of a triple $X \supset Y \supset Z$, with its final $\to 0$ (p. 29), and $C_\lambda$ counts the critical points of index $\lambda$.

Verified edition V3.9

This is the structure in which §5 is verified. Fix a field $F$ and a preordered set $\iota$. A homology of a filtration assigns to every degree $i \ge 0$ and indices $a, b$ a vector space $H_i(a, b)$ over $F$, to be read as $H_i(X_b, X_a; F)$ (only $a \le b$ is ever used), such that $H_i(a, b)$ is finite-dimensional for $a \le b$, and assigns to every triple $a \le b \le c$ a long exact sequence of $F$-linear maps $$\cdots \to H_i(a,b) \to H_i(a,c) \to H_i(b,c) \xrightarrow{\ \partial\ } H_{i-1}(a,b) \to \cdots \to H_0(a,b) \to H_0(a,c) \to H_0(b,c) \to 0,$$ exact at every term, the last condition being the surjectivity of $H_0(a, c) \to H_0(b, c)$. Nothing else is assumed: no functoriality, no compatibility between the sequences of different triples, no vanishing of $H_*(a, a)$, no excision. For a chain $X_0 \le X_1 \le \dots \le X_n$ the Betti numbers are $R_i = \dim H_i(X_0, X_n)$ (Milnor's $R_i(M)$ when $X_0 = \emptyset$, $X_n = M$), and the Morse numbers are $C_i = \sum_{k<n} \dim H_i(X_k, X_{k+1})$. The truncated alternating sum of a sequence $d$ is $S_\lambda(d) = d_\lambda - d_{\lambda - 1} + \dots \pm d_0$. On a chain indexed by $\mathbb N$, Morse.FiltrationHomology.ofSteps builds the structure from the exact sequences and the finiteness of the slabs $H_i(k, k+1)$ and of the $H_i(k, k)$ alone, so that the finiteness of $H_*(M; F)$ is a consequence rather than an assumption. Book: pp. 28–30: singular homology with coefficients in a field $F$, the exact sequence of a triple $X \supset Y \supset Z$, and $R_\lambda(X, Y) = \dim H_\lambda(X, Y; F)$ for the pairs where it is finite. Hidden hypotheses: that the sequence of a triple ends with $\to 0$ (Milnor's exact sequence "$\dots \to D \to 0$", p. 29) is the surjectivity of $H_0(X, Z) \to H_0(X, Y)$. Deviation (restated): this is an abstract structure, not singular homology. Every statement V3.10–V3.15 is a theorem about every such structure; singular homology over a field is an instance (V3.32), and the slab computation of p. 29 that applies it to a manifold is V3.33–V3.34.

Milnor's $\chi$ is the Euler characteristic $\sum (-1)^\lambda R_\lambda$ of singular homology over a field (p. 28). Verified edition V3.17

Let $N \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}$ be a compact nonempty slice submanifold modelled on $\mathbb R^{d+1}$. An integer $\chi$ is an Euler number of $N$ if for every smooth tangent vector field $v$ on $N$ whose zeros are finitely many distinct points $z_1, \dots, z_j$, $\sum_i \operatorname{index}_{z_i}(v) = \chi$, the index being that of the Milnor project (Milnor.Tub.indexN, its V6.8: the index at $z_i$ of the extension $x \mapsto v(r(x)) + (x - r(x))$ of $v$ to a tubular neighbourhood, $r$ the nearest-point retraction). For $K \ge 1$ an Euler number exists: this is the Poincaré–Hopf theorem of the Milnor project (Milnor.Tub.poincare_hopf, its V6.9), where it is the degree of the Gauss map of the boundary of a tubular neighbourhood. It is unique: by V3.20 every Euler number equals the alternating count of the critical points of any Morse function, and $N$ carries one (V4.13). Below it is written $\chi(N)$. Book: Milnor's $\chi$ is the Euler characteristic $\sum (-1)^\lambda R_\lambda$ (p. 28); in Application 2 (pp. 36–37) he uses that the index sum of a vector field is a topological invariant (citing Steenrod, §39.7). Hidden hypotheses: $N$ compact and nonempty; $K \ge 1$, i.e. ambient dimension at least $2$; the zeros indexed without repetition. Deviation (restated): $\chi(N)$ is defined through vector fields; its identification with $\sum_i (-1)^i \dim H_i(N; F)$ is V3.38.

Verified edition V3.18

Let $H$ be a symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional real inner product space and $A$ the operator with $H(v, w) = \langle Av, w\rangle$. The index of $H$ (the largest dimension of a subspace on which $H$ is negative definite) is the number of negative eigenvalues of $A$; $H$ is non-degenerate iff $A$ is bijective; and if $H$ is non-degenerate, $\operatorname{sgn}\det A = (-1)^{\operatorname{index} H}$. The right side does not involve the inner product, so the sign is the same for the operators representing $H$ with respect to any two inner products. Verified edition V3.20

Let $N \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}$, $K \ge 1$, be a compact nonempty slice submanifold of dimension $d + 1 \ge 1$. There is an integer $\chi(N)$, an Euler number of $N$ in the sense of V3.17, such that every Morse function $f$ on $N$ (smooth, with only non-degenerate critical points) satisfies $$\sum_{\lambda=0}^{d+1} (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda(f) = \sum_{q \text{ critical}} (-1)^{\operatorname{index}_q f} = \chi(N).$$ Consequently the alternating count is the same for all Morse functions on $N$, and every Euler number of $N$ equals the alternating count of any one Morse function. Every smooth $f : N \to \mathbb R$ is the restriction of a smooth function on $\mathbb R^{K+1}$ (Morse.exists_contDiff_comp_val_eq). Hidden hypotheses: "isolated" is redundant for non-degenerate critical points; $\pm C_n$ takes $n = \dim M$; distinct critical values are not needed; in Application 2, "any differentiable function" must be one with only non-degenerate critical points, and "the critical points of $X$" are the zeros of $X$; $\dim N \ge 1$ and $K \ge 1$ (the Milnor project computes the index of a non-degenerate zero only in positive dimension, and its Poincaré–Hopf theorem needs $K \ge 1$). Deviation (restated): $\chi(N)$ is the Poincaré–Hopf integer; what is verified here is the topological invariance of $\sum (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda$. Its equality with $\sum (-1)^i R_i(N)$, formula (3) as Milnor states it, is V3.35, and the identification of $\chi(N)$ with the homological Euler characteristic is V3.38. $N$ is a submanifold of Euclidean space; for an abstract compact manifold see V4.19. Proof: Application 2 run in the direction that needs no homology: the gradient field of $f$ (V3.19) has index sum $\sum (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda(f)$, and every tangent field has the index sum $\chi(N)$.

Let $f = x_1 + R + \rho$ on $T$, the height above the plane $V = \{x_1 = -(R + \rho)\}$, which touches $T$ at $p = (-(R + \rho), 0, 0)$; the axis of revolution is parallel to $V$, so the torus stands upright. to confirmRelative singular homology $H_n(X, A)$ is functorial in pairs, has the exact sequence of a pair, is homotopy invariant, and $H_n(B, A) \cong H_n(X, A)$ when $B \supseteq A$ is a strong deformation retract of $X$.

Milnor §5, pp. 28–29

Milnor quotes the homology of pairs with coefficients in a field, and its exact sequences, as standard (p. 28); on p. 29 he replaces a pair by a homotopy equivalent one without comment.

Verified edition V3.26

Coefficients are an object $R$ of an abelian category with coproducts (for instance a field, or any commutative ring); pairs $(X, A)$ are embeddings $A \hookrightarrow X$ (Mathlib's TopPair). The relative chain complex $C(X, A)$ is the cokernel of the chain map $C(A) \to C(X)$ of singular chains, which is injective, so that $0 \to C(A) \to C(X) \to C(X, A) \to 0$ is exact; $H_n(X, A)$ is its homology, and both are functorial in maps of pairs. The sequence $$\cdots \to H_{n+1}(X, A) \xrightarrow{\ \partial\ } H_n(A) \to H_n(X) \to H_n(X, A) \xrightarrow{\ \partial\ } H_{n-1}(A) \to \cdots \to H_0(X) \to H_0(X, A) \to 0$$ is exact at every place, and $\partial$ is natural in maps of pairs. $H_n(X, \emptyset) \cong H_n(X)$ naturally, and $H_n(X, X) = 0$. A map of pairs inducing isomorphisms in the homology of both spaces induces isomorphisms in relative homology (the five lemma). Maps of pairs that are homotopic through maps of pairs induce the same maps in relative homology. If $A \subseteq B \subseteq X$ are subsets of a space and $B$ is a strong deformation retract of $X$, then $H_n(B, A) \to H_n(X, A)$ is an isomorphism and $H_n(X, B) = 0$. With these data singular homology is a homotopy-invariant homology pretheory in the sense of Mathlib's formulation of the Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms. Book: p. 28: homology of pairs with coefficients in a field and its exact sequences; p. 29: pairs replaced by homotopy equivalent ones; all quoted as standard. Hidden hypotheses: the first equality of p. 29 needs homotopy equivalences of pairs, here strong deformation retracts. Deviation (not in the book): built here, since Mathlib has no relative singular homology. Proof: homotopy invariance for pairs from the absolute one, through the cylinder $(X \times I, A \times I)$ and the five lemma.

Let $E$ be a Hausdorff space, $Y \subseteq X \subseteq E$ with $Y$ closed, and $\chi_j : \mathbb R^{k_j} \to E$, $j = 1, \dots, m$, maps continuous and injective on the closed unit balls $D^{k_j}$, whose cells $e_j = \chi_j(D^{k_j})$ are pairwise disjoint, such that $\chi_j(z) \in Y$ exactly when $\|z\| = 1$, and $X = Y \cup e_1 \cup \dots \cup e_m$. Coefficients in a commutative ring $R$. For one cell of dimension $k$, the inclusion $(e_1, \chi_1(S^{k-1})) \to (X, Y)$ and the characteristic map $(D^k, S^{k-1}) \to (X, Y)$ induce isomorphisms in all degrees: $H_k(X, Y) \cong R$ and $H_i(X, Y) = 0$ for $i \ne k$ (the first statement holds for the unit ball of any finite-dimensional normed space). For several cells, $H_i(X, Y) \cong R^{c_i}$, $c_i$ the number of cells of dimension $i$, so $H_i(X, Y) = 0$ when no cell has dimension $i$, and over a field $\dim H_i(X, Y) = c_i$. Hidden hypotheses: this is not literally excision: the closure of the set to be excised is not inside the interior of $M^{a_{i-1}}$. One first deforms $X$ minus the centre of the cell onto $Y$ (pushing the punctured cell radially onto its boundary), then excises; $Y$ must be closed. With several cells on one level (Remark 3.3) the exact sequence of a triple gives only an inequality of dimensions; additivity uses the disjointness of the cells. Deviation (stronger): any number of disjoint cells, and any commutative ring of coefficients; this is the exposition's Lemma E.

The remaining items are Milnor's statements, in singular homology over a field.

For a compact $M$ and a differentiable $f$ with isolated, non-degenerate critical points, Milnor takes $a_1 < \dots < a_k$ with exactly $i$ critical points in $M^{a_i}$ and $M^{a_k} = M$, and finds $H_*(M^{a_i}, M^{a_{i-1}})$ to be the coefficient group in dimension $\lambda_i$, the index of the $i$-th critical point, and $0$ in every other dimension.

Let $N$ be a compact slice submanifold of a finite-dimensional real normed space $V$, modelled on a finite-dimensional space, and $F : V \to \mathbb R$ smooth such that every critical point of $f = F|_N$ is non-degenerate. (i) If $a' \le a$ are not critical values and all critical values in $(a', a)$ are equal, then $H_i(N^a, N^{a'}; \Bbbk)$ is finite-dimensional, of dimension the number of critical points of index $i$ in $f^{-1}(a', a)$. (ii) There are $n \ge 1$ and non-critical values $a_0 \le a_1 \le \dots$ with $N^{a_0} = \emptyset$, $N^{a_n} = N$ and at most one critical value in each $(a_k, a_{k+1})$; by (i), each step $(N^{a_{k+1}}, N^{a_k})$ has finite-dimensional homology over every field, of dimension the number of critical points of index $i$ in $f^{-1}(a_k, a_{k+1})$. (iii) Hence $H_i(N; \Bbbk)$ is finite-dimensional for every $i$. These statements are made for every space homeomorphic to $N$, homology being carried along the homeomorphism (for use in V3.39), and for $N$ itself. to confirmThe Hermitian projections of trace $1$ in $M_{n+1}(\mathbb C)$ form a compact submanifold of dimension $2n$, which is $\mathbb CP^n$, and Milnor's functions $x_j, y_j$ on $U_k$ are coordinates on it.

rank-one projections $zz^*$slice charts from Milnor's coordinates
the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §4, p. 26

$\mathbb CP_n$ is the set of equivalence classes of $(n + 1)$-tuples $(z_0, \dots, z_n)$ of complex numbers with $\sum|z_j|^2 = 1$. On the set $U_0$ where $z_0 \neq 0$, set $|z_0|\,z_j/z_0 = x_j + iy_j$; then $x_1, y_1, \dots, x_n, y_n$ "are the required coordinate functions, mapping $U_0$ diffeomorphically onto the open unit ball in $\mathbb R^{2n}$".

Verified edition V3.41

Here $\mathbb CP^n$ is the set of Hermitian projections of trace $1$ in the space $M_{n+1}(\mathbb C)$ of complex matrices (the Grassmannian of V14.16 with $m = 1$). Every point of it is $P = zz^$, that is $P_{ab} = z_a\bar z_b$, for a unit vector $z \in \mathbb C^{n+1}$. For $0 \le k \le n$ let $U_k$ be the set of $P$ with $\operatorname{Re}P_{kk} > 0$; every point of $\mathbb CP^n$ lies in some $U_k$. On $\mathbb R^{2n} = \mathbb C^n$, with coordinates $z_j = x_j + iy_j$ ($j \neq k$), put $\operatorname{param}_k(z) = vv^$, where $v_k = \sqrt{1 - |z|^2}$ and $v_j = z_j$ for $j \neq k$; and for a matrix $P$ put $\operatorname{coord}_k(P) = (P_{jk}/\sqrt{\operatorname{Re}P_{kk}})_{j \neq k}$. Then $\operatorname{coord}_k(\operatorname{param}_k(z)) = z$ for $|z| < 1$, and for $P \in \mathbb CP^n \cap U_k$, $|\operatorname{coord}_k(P)| < 1$ and $\operatorname{param}_k(\operatorname{coord}_k(P)) = P$. $\mathbb CP^n$ is a compact slice submanifold of $M_{n+1}(\mathbb C)$ of dimension $2n$, and at every $x \in \mathbb CP^n \cap U_k$ it has a slice chart whose parametrization is $z \mapsto \operatorname{param}_k(\operatorname{coord}_k(x) + z)$ near $0$. Book: p. 26: $\mathbb CP_n$ as the equivalence classes of $(n + 1)$-tuples $(z_0, \dots, z_n)$ with $\sum|z_j|^2 = 1$; on the set $U_0$ where $z_0 \neq 0$, $|z_0|\,z_j/z_0 = x_j + iy_j$, and $x_1, y_1, \dots, x_n, y_n$ "are the required coordinate functions, mapping $U_0$ diffeomorphically onto the open unit ball in $\mathbb R^{2n}$". Hidden hypotheses: "diffeomorphically" presupposes a smooth structure on $\mathbb CP_n$. Deviation (restated): $\mathbb CP^n$ is the submanifold of rank-one projections, with the smooth structure induced from the space of matrices; Milnor's coordinates are then entries of $P$, visibly independent of the representative $z$, and they are the coordinates of slice charts.

the normal bundle and the endpoint map

to confirmFor a $k$-dimensional submanifold $M \subseteq \mathbb R^n$, the normal bundle $N$ is an $n$-dimensional submanifold of $\mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^n$, and $E(q, v) = q + v$.

the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §6, p. 32

For a $k$-dimensional manifold $M$ differentiably embedded in $\mathbb R^n$, $k < n$, Milnor takes the set $N \subset M \times \mathbb R^n$ of pairs $(q, v)$ with $v$ perpendicular to $M$ at $q$, the total space of the normal vector bundle, which, he says, is not difficult to show to be an $n$-manifold differentiably embedded in $\mathbb R^{2n}$; and the endpoint map $E : N \to \mathbb R^n$, $E(q, v) = q + v$.

Verified edition V4.1

Throughout, $M \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ is a slice submanifold modelled on $\mathbb R^k$ with complement $\mathbb R^w$; if $M$ is nonempty, $k + w = n$. The normal bundle is $N = \{(q, v) \in M \times \mathbb R^n : v \perp T_qM\}$; when $k + w = n$ it is a slice submanifold of $\mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^n$ of dimension $n$ (the Milnor project's V8.11). The endpoint map is $E(q, v) = q + v$; more generally, for a map $\Gamma : \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R^n$, $E_\Gamma(q, v) = \Gamma(q) + v$, smooth over every open set on which $\Gamma$ is smooth, with $E_{\mathrm{id}} = E$. Book: p. 32: $M \subset \mathbb R^n$ a manifold of dimension $k < n$, differentiably embedded; $N$ is an $n$-dimensional manifold ("not difficult to show"); $E(q, v) = q + v$. Hidden hypotheses: "differentiably embedded" must mean a submanifold (an injectively immersed manifold need not be one, V4.14); for slice charts, $k + w = n$ needs $M \ne \emptyset$. Deviation (stronger): $k = n$ is allowed and $M$ need not be closed or compact; $E_\Gamma$ is not in the book and serves V4.20.

focal points and their multiplicity

hypotheses explicit

to confirm$e$ is a focal point of $(M, q)$ of multiplicity $\mu$ iff $(q, e - q) \in N$ and $dE$ has nullity $\mu > 0$ there; the focal points of $M$ are the critical values of $E$.

nullity read in a chart of $N$focal set = critical values of $E$
the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §6, Definition

A point $e = q + v$, $(q, v) \in N$, is a focal point of $(M, q)$, of multiplicity $\mu$, when the Jacobian of $E$ at $(q, v)$ has nullity $\mu > 0$, and a focal point of $M$ when it is one of $(M, q)$ for some $q \in M$; intuitively, focal points are where nearby normals meet. The proof of Corollary 6.2 uses that the focal points are exactly the images under $E$ of its critical points.

Verified edition V4.2

Assume $k + w = n$. The nullity of $E$ at $x \in N$ is the dimension of the kernel of $dE_x$, the tangent space of $N$ at $x$ being identified with $\mathbb R^n$ by the chart of $N$ at $x$. A point $e \in \mathbb R^n$ is a focal point of $(M, q)$ with multiplicity $\mu$ if $(q, e - q) \in N$ and the nullity of $E$ at $(q, e - q)$ is $\mu > 0$; a focal point of $(M, q)$ if this holds for some $\mu$; a focal point of $M$ if it is a focal point of $(M, q)$ for some $q \in M$. The nullity is positive exactly at the critical points of $E$ (the points where $dE$ is not onto); so $e$ is a focal point of $(M, q)$ iff $(q, e - q) \in N$ is a critical point of $E$, and the set of focal points of $M$ is the set of critical values of $E$. Book: p. 32 (the definition, with $e = q + v$ and $(q, v) \in N$); p. 33 (the proof of Corollary 6.2). Hidden hypotheses: the nullity does not depend on the chart (two charts differ by an isomorphism of $\mathbb R^n$).

Milnor §6, Theorem 6.1 (Sard)

For a $C^1$ map $f : M_1 \to M_2$ between differentiable manifolds of the same dimension, each with a countable basis, the critical points, where the Jacobian of $f$ is singular, have an image of measure $0$ in $M_2$. Milnor gives no proof, referring to de Rham.

Let $M$ be a second countable smooth manifold without boundary modelled on a finite-dimensional real normed space $E$, $F$ a finite-dimensional real normed space with a Haar measure $\mu$, $U \subseteq M$ open and $f : M \to F$ smooth on $U$. Then the image under $f$ of the points of $U$ where $df$ is not onto is $\mu$-null; in particular, for $f$ smooth on $M$, the set of critical values is null. $E$ and $F$ are required to lie in the same universe of Lean's type theory, a formality with no mathematical content (as in the Milnor project). the fundamental forms

restated

to confirmIn the slice-chart coordinates $x$ at $q$, $g = \langle dx\,\cdot, dx\,\cdot\rangle$ and $\ell_v = \langle v, d^2x(\cdot, \cdot)\rangle$ are Milnor's first and second fundamental forms.

the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §6, pp. 33–34

In local coordinates $u^1, \dots, u^k$ on $M \subset \mathbb R^n$, with $\vec x(u)$ the inclusion, the first fundamental form is the matrix $g_{ij} = \partial\vec x/\partial u^i \cdot \partial\vec x/\partial u^j$, and the second fundamental form is the symmetric matrix $(\vec\ell_{ij})$ of vector-valued functions, $\vec\ell_{ij}$ the normal component of $\partial^2\vec x/\partial u^i\partial u^j$. For a unit vector $\vec v$ normal to $M$ at $q$, the matrix $(\vec v \cdot \vec\ell_{ij})$ is the second fundamental form of $M$ at $q$ in the direction $\vec v$. Milnor gives no invariant definition and works in a fixed coordinate system.

Verified edition V4.5

For $q \in M$, Milnor's coordinates $u \mapsto x(u)$ are the inverse of the slice chart of $M$ chosen at $q$, with $x(u_q) = q$; $dx$ and $d^2x$ are its first and second derivatives at $u_q$ (Milnor's $\partial x/\partial u^i$ and $\partial^2 x/\partial u^i \partial u^j$). The first fundamental form is the bilinear form $g(\xi, \eta) = \langle dx\,\xi, dx\,\eta\rangle$ on $\mathbb R^k$; the second fundamental form in a direction $v \in \mathbb R^n$ is $\ell_v(\xi, \eta) = \langle v, d^2x(\xi, \eta)\rangle$; and for a linear map $T$ of $\mathbb R^n$ the form $(\xi, \eta) \mapsto \langle T\,dx\,\xi, dx\,\eta\rangle - \ell_v(\xi, \eta)$ is the one attached to $E_\Gamma$ with $T = d\Gamma_q$ (V4.8), equal to $g - \ell_v$ for $T = \mathrm{id}$. Book: pp. 33–34: $g_{ij} = \partial x/\partial u^i \cdot \partial x/\partial u^j$; $\ell_{ij}$ is the normal component of $\partial^2 x/\partial u^i \partial u^j$, and for a unit normal $v$ the matrix $(v \cdot \ell_{ij})$ is the second fundamental form in the direction $v$. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): $\ell_v$ is defined for every $v$ by the inner product with $d^2x$; for $v$ normal at $q$ it is Milnor's $(v \cdot \ell_{ij})$, the tangential part of $d^2x$ being orthogonal to $v$. The coordinates are those of the chosen slice chart; Milnor allows any coordinates.

Milnor §6, Lemma 6.3

Let $\vec v$ be a unit normal to $M$ at $\vec q$. On the normal line $\ell = \{\vec q + t\vec v\}$ the focal points of $(M, q)$ are exactly the points $\vec q + K_i^{-1}\vec v$ with $1 \le i \le k$ and $K_i \ne 0$; counted with their multiplicities, there are therefore at most $k$ of them on $\ell$.

Verified edition V4.7

Assume $k + w = n$, and let $\operatorname{mult}_q(e)$ be the multiplicity of $e$ as a focal point of $(M, q)$, $0$ if it is not one. For $q \in M$, $v \perp T_qM$ and $t \in \mathbb R$: $\operatorname{mult}_q(q + tv) = 0$ if $t = 0$, and otherwise it is the multiplicity of $1/t$ as an eigenvalue of $S_v$. Hence $q + tv$ is a focal point of $(M, q)$ iff $t = K^{-1}$ for a nonzero principal curvature $K$ in the direction $v$, the multiplicity of $q + K^{-1}v$ is that of $K$, and for any finitely many values of $t$ the multiplicities of the points $q + tv$ add up to at most $k$. Book: Lemma 6.3 (p. 34), for a unit normal $v$: the focal points of $(M, q)$ on the normal line $\{q + tv\}$ are exactly the points $q + K_i^{-1}v$ with $K_i \ne 0$, so there are at most $k$ of them, each counted with its multiplicity. Hidden hypotheses: $t = 0$ must be set aside in "$1/t$ is an eigenvalue" ($q$ is never a focal point of $(M, q)$, V4.9); the multiplicity of an eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix as a root of the characteristic polynomial equals the dimension of its eigenspace, which is what the proof produces. Deviation (stronger): $v$ is any normal vector, not necessarily a unit vector. In place of Milnor's normalized coordinates, for $t \ne 0$ the map $dx$ carries the null space of $g - t\ell_v$ onto the eigenspace of $S_v$ for $1/t$ (Morse.map_nullSpace_firstFF_sub_eq_eigenspace).

Milnor §6, proof of Lemma 6.3

Milnor chooses unit normal fields $\vec w_1, \dots, \vec w_{n-k}$, orthogonal to each other, coordinates $(u, t)$ on $N$ given by $(u, t) \mapsto (\vec x(u), \sum_\alpha t^\alpha\vec w_\alpha(u))$, and takes inner products of the partial derivatives of $E$ with $\partial\vec x/\partial u^1, \dots, \partial\vec x/\partial u^k, \vec w_1, \dots, \vec w_{n-k}$. This gives an $n \times n$ matrix whose rank equals that of the Jacobian of $E$, with an identity block below; he says its rank is the rank of the upper left block, which is $(g_{ij} - \sum_\alpha t^\alpha \vec w_\alpha \cdot \vec\ell_{ij})$.

Verified edition V4.8

Assume $k + w = n$ and let $(q, v) \in N$. A pair $(a, b) \in \mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^n$ is tangent to $N$ at $(q, v)$ iff $a = dx\,\xi$ for some $\xi \in \mathbb R^k$ and $\langle b, dx\,\eta \rangle + \langle v, d^2x(\xi, \eta)\rangle = 0$ for every $\eta \in \mathbb R^k$. For $\Gamma$ differentiable at $q$, the derivative of $E_\Gamma$ at $(q, v)$ is $(a, b) \mapsto d\Gamma_q(a) + b$ on this tangent space, and its nullity equals the nullity of the form $(\xi, \eta) \mapsto \langle d\Gamma_q\,dx\,\xi, dx\,\eta\rangle - \langle v, d^2x(\xi, \eta)\rangle$ on $\mathbb R^k$. For $\Gamma = \mathrm{id}$: the nullity of $E$ at $(q, v)$ is the nullity of $g - \ell_v$. Book: pp. 34–35, in the proof of Lemma 6.3: coordinates $(u, t)$ on $N$ built from orthonormal normal fields $w_\alpha$, and an $n \times n$ matrix whose upper left block is $(g_{ij} - \sum_\alpha t^\alpha w_\alpha \cdot \ell_{ij})$. Hidden hypotheses: the fields $w_\alpha$ exist only locally, and Milnor does not say why they exist; his sentence that the rank of the matrix equals the rank of the upper left block (p. 35) does not hold as written, the two ranks differing by $n - k$; what holds, and is needed, is that the nullities agree. Deviation (restated): no normal frame is used. Proof: the tangent space of $N$ is the kernel of the derivative of the local defining function of $N$ used by the Milnor project; its second condition is the derivative of Milnor's identity $w_\alpha \cdot \partial x/\partial u^j = 0$.

Milnor §6, pp. 35–36

For fixed $\vec p \in \mathbb R^n$, $f = L_{\vec p}$ satisfies $f(\vec x(u)) = \|\vec x(u) - \vec p\|^2$ and $\partial f/\partial u^i = 2\,\partial\vec x/\partial u^i \cdot (\vec x - \vec p)$, so $f$ has a critical point at $\vec q$ iff $\vec q - \vec p$ is normal to $M$ at $\vec q$. At a critical point the second partial derivatives are $2(\partial\vec x/\partial u^i \cdot \partial\vec x/\partial u^j + \partial^2\vec x/\partial u^i\partial u^j \cdot (\vec x - \vec p))$, which on setting $\vec p = \vec x + t\vec v$ becomes $2(g_{ij} - t\,\vec v \cdot \vec\ell_{ij})$.

The second display is cut off in the scan; its value is the one used on p. 38.

For $p \in \mathbb R^n$ let $L_p(q) = \|q - p\|^2$ on $M$. On a compact $M$ some vector field has index sum $\chi(M)$ over its critical points: for a differentiable $f$, $\chi(M) = \sum (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda$, and $\mathrm{grad} f$ has index $(-1)^\lambda$ where $f$ has index $\lambda$. Deviation (restated): $\chi(M)$ is the integer of V4.18, which equals the Poincaré–Hopf integer of every embedded copy and, by V3.38, the homological Euler characteristic; vector fields and their indices are defined in the Milnor project only for submanifolds of Euclidean space, so Application 2 is stated on an embedded copy; the topological invariance that Milnor quotes from Steenrod is replaced by the Poincaré–Hopf theorem and invariance under diffeomorphisms.

to confirmEvery smooth function on a submanifold of $\mathbb R^n$, bounded or not, is a uniform limit of Morse functions, with derivatives up to any order converging on compact pieces of coordinate charts.

Milnor §6, Corollary 6.8

A bounded smooth $f : M \to \mathbb R$ is a uniform limit of smooth functions $g$ without degenerate critical points, and $g$ may be chosen so that, on a given compact set $K$, its derivatives of every order $i \le k$ are uniformly close to those of $f$.

Verified edition V4.21

Let $M \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be any slice submanifold, $f : M \to \mathbb R$ smooth (bounded or not), $\varepsilon > 0$, $r \in \mathbb N$, and finitely many smooth coordinate systems $y_j$ on open subsets of $M$, with values in $\mathbb R^k$, with compact sets $K_j$ inside their ranges. There is a Morse function $g$ on $M$ with $|g - f| < \varepsilon$ on all of $M$ and $\|D^i((g - f) \circ y_j^{-1})(u)\| < \varepsilon$ for every $j$, every $i \le r$ and every $u \in K_j$. One can take $g = f + \langle a, \beta(\cdot)\rangle$ with $a$ small, where $\beta(y) = y/\sqrt{1 + \|y\|^2}$ is the diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^n$ onto its open unit ball; for compact $M$ also $g = f + \langle a, \cdot\rangle$ (Morse.exists_isMorseFunction_approx). Book: Corollary 6.8 (p. 37): any bounded smooth $f : M \to \mathbb R$ can be uniformly approximated by a smooth $g$ without degenerate critical points, and $g$ can be chosen so that its $i$-th derivatives on a given compact $K \subset M$ uniformly approximate those of $f$, for $i \le k$. Hidden hypotheses: derivatives on a manifold exist only in coordinates, so the approximation on $K$ must be read in fixed coordinate systems covering $K$ (finitely many suffice); Milnor's embedding $h$ with bounded image and first coordinate $f$ is not constructed (one can take $h = (f, \beta \circ h')$ for any embedding $h'$). Deviation (stronger): no boundedness hypothesis on $f$: the perturbation $\langle a, \beta(\cdot)\rangle$ is bounded by $\|a\|$; and $M$ need not be compact. $M$ is a submanifold of $\mathbb R^n$; abstract compact $M$ is V4.22. Proof: V4.20 applied to the slice submanifold $\beta(M)$ and $f \circ \beta^{-1}$, and the Morse property carried back along $\beta$.

Milnor §6, Lemma 6.9

At a non-degenerate critical point $\vec q$ of $L_{\vec p}$, the index is the number of focal points of $(M, \vec q)$ on the segment from $\vec q$ to $\vec p$, counted with multiplicity. The proof (p. 38): the index of $2(g_{ij} - t\,\vec v \cdot \vec\ell_{ij})$ is its number of negative eigenvalues, which, for $(g_{ij})$ the identity, is the number of eigenvalues of $(\vec v \cdot \vec\ell_{ij})$ that are $\ge 1/t$; compare Lemma 6.3.

Milnor adds that an analogous statement in Part III, the Morse index theorem, will be of fundamental importance.

Verified edition V4.23

(i) The index of $g - \ell_v$ is the number of principal curvatures in the direction $v$, counted with multiplicity, that are greater than $1$. (ii) At a critical point $q$ of $L_p$, the index of $L_p$ is the number of principal curvatures of $M$ at $q$ in the direction $p - q$ that are greater than $1$. (iii) If $k + w = n$ and $q$ is a non-degenerate critical point of $L_p$, the index of $L_p$ at $q$ is $\sum_{t \in [0, 1]} \operatorname{mult}_q(q + t(p - q))$ (all but finitely many terms vanish): the number of focal points of $(M, q)$ on the segment from $q$ to $p$, each counted with its multiplicity. Book: Lemma 6.9 (p. 37), proved on p. 38: the index of $2(g_{ij} - t\,v \cdot \ell_{ij})$ is its number of negative eigenvalues, which for $(g_{ij})$ the identity is the number of eigenvalues of $(v \cdot \ell_{ij})$ that are $\ge 1/t$; compare with Lemma 6.3. Hidden hypotheses: the eigenvalues to count are those $> 1/t$, not $\ge 1/t$: equality would make $p$ a focal point of $(M, q)$, i.e. $q$ degenerate (V4.11), and this is where non-degeneracy enters; the case $p = q$ (index $0$, and the segment $\{q\}$ holds no focal point). Deviation (restated): the direction $p - q$ is not normalized: if $p - q = tv$ with $\|v\| = 1$, the curvatures in the direction $p - q$ are $t$ times those in the direction $v$, so "greater than $1$" is Milnor's "greater than $1/t$". Proof: Sylvester's law of inertia in an orthonormal eigenbasis of $S_v$, in which $g - \ell_v$ is $\sum_i (1 - \kappa_i)c_i^2$.

Hessian, index, nullity

to confirmThe Hessian is the second derivative, defined at every point; the index of a bilinear form is the largest dimension of a subspace on which it is negative definite, and the nullity is the dimension of its null space.

the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor

No comparison row for this item; the Book note on the right gives the page.

Verified edition V5.1

For $f : E \to \mathbb R$ on a real normed space $E$ and $q \in E$, the Hessian $d^2f_q$ is the second Fréchet derivative, the bilinear form $(v, w) \mapsto d(x \mapsto df_x(w))_q(v)$; it is defined at every point (it is $0$ at a point where $x \mapsto df_x$ is not differentiable). For a bilinear form $H$, the null space is $\{v : H(v, w) = 0 \text{ for all } w\}$ and the nullity is its dimension; the index is Mathlib's negative index of inertia (sigNeg) of $v \mapsto H(v, v)$, and on a finite-dimensional space Morse.index_isGreatest proves it is the largest dimension of a subspace on which $H(v, v) < 0$ for $v \neq 0$. Book: p. 5: the index of a bilinear functional is the maximal dimension of a subspace on which it is negative definite, the nullity is the dimension of its null space; the Hessian $f_{}$ is defined at a critical point (p. 4) and is the matrix of second partial derivatives in local coordinates (p. 5). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): the formal Hessian exists at every point; at a critical point it is the matrix of $f_{}$ in the given linear coordinates. The nullity is a Mathlib finrank, which is $0$ for an infinite-dimensional null space; the statements below that compare nullities hold as stated in any dimension and are meaningful in finite dimension.

Milnor's form $Q'$ and the orthogonal map $J$

stronger

to confirm$\operatorname{Re}B$ of a complex bilinear form is Milnor's $Q'$, multiplication by $i$ is an orthogonal map with square $-1$, and it changes the sign of $\operatorname{Re}B$.

Milnor §7, p. 39

Writing $z^h = x^h + iy^h$ in a complex quadratic form $Q(z) = \sum b_{hj}z^hz^j$ of $k$ variables and taking real parts gives a real quadratic form $Q'$ in $2k$ variables. Since $Q(iz) = -Q(z)$, an orthogonal change of variables turns $Q'$ into $-Q'$.

Verified edition V5.2

For a complex vector space $V$ and a continuous complex-bilinear $B : V \times V \to \mathbb C$, $\operatorname{Re}B$ is a real bilinear form; for $B(z, z') = \sum b_{hj}z^hz'^j$ on $\mathbb C^k$ its quadratic form is Milnor's $Q'$. Multiplication by $i$ is a real-linear isomorphism $J$ with $J^2 = -1$ (inverse $-J$), and $\operatorname{Re}B(iv, iw) = -\operatorname{Re}B(v, w)$ for all $v, w$. On a complex inner product space the real inner product $\operatorname{Re}\langle v, w\rangle$ (the Euclidean inner product of $\mathbb R^{2k}$ when $V = \mathbb C^k$) satisfies $\operatorname{Re}\langle iv, iw\rangle = \operatorname{Re}\langle v, w\rangle$: $J$ is orthogonal. Book: p. 39: substituting $x^h + iy^h$ for $z^h$ in $Q(z) = \sum b_{hj}z^hz^j$ and taking real parts gives a real quadratic form $Q'$ in $2k$ variables; the identity $Q(iz) = -Q(z)$ shows that an orthogonal change of variables carries $Q'$ into $-Q'$. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (stronger): the sign change is proved for the bilinear form, not only for the quadratic form.

Milnor works on an abstract smooth manifold $M$, with tangent spaces $TM_p$, vector fields $X$, and directional derivatives $X_pf$ of real functions $f$ in the direction of a tangent vector $X_p$.

Verified edition V6.1

$T_qN \subseteq V$ is the range of the derivative at $q$ of the inclusion $N \to V$, and $P_q$ is the orthogonal projection of $V$ onto $T_qN$. For $F : N \to E$, the linear map $dN\,F\,q : V \to E$ is the derivative of $F$ at $q$ read on ambient vectors: on $v \in T_qN$ it is $dF_q(v)$ (its values off $T_qN$ depend on a chart and are never used). If $F = G$ on $N$ near $q$ for some $G : V \to E$ differentiable at $q$, then $dN\,F\,q\,v = dG_q(v)$ for $v \in T_qN$. A vector field is a map $X : N \to V$ with $X(q) \in T_qN$ for every $q$; it is smooth if it is smooth as a map $N \to V$. Milnor §8, pp. 43–44

An affine connection at $p$ is a rule giving, for a tangent vector $X_p$ and a vector field $Y$, a tangent vector $X_p \vdash Y$ at $p$, the covariant derivative of $Y$ along $X_p$; it is bilinear and satisfies $X_p \vdash (fY) = (X_pf)Y_p + f(p)\,X_p \vdash Y$. A global connection is such a rule at every point subject to the smoothness condition (1); it then satisfies (2) bilinearity, (3) $(fX) \vdash Y = f(X \vdash Y)$ and (4) $X \vdash (fY) = (Xf)Y + f(X \vdash Y)$, and (1)–(4) may serve as the definition.

A footnote identifies $X \vdash Y$ with Nomizu's $\nabla_XY$.

Verified edition V6.3

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold in Mathlib's sense (modelled on a real normed space) and $\nabla$ a Mathlib covariant derivative on its tangent bundle, $X_p \vdash Y$ being the value at $X_p$ of the linear map $\nabla Y(p) : T_pM \to T_pM$. Then Milnor's (3), $(fX) \vdash Y = f\,(X \vdash Y)$, holds at every point; (2), additivity in $Y$, holds at every point where both summands are differentiable; and (4), $X \vdash (fY) = (Xf)\,Y + f\,(X \vdash Y)$, holds at every point where $f$ and $Y$ are differentiable. Dependence on $X_p$ only, and linearity in $X_p$, are part of the definition. Book: pp. 43–44: an affine connection at $p$ assigns to $X_p$ and $Y$ a vector $X_p \vdash Y$, bilinear, with the Leibniz rule; a global one satisfies the smoothness condition (1), and conditions (1)–(4) "can be taken as the definition". Hidden hypotheses: differentiability of $f$ and $Y$ at the point, in (2) and (4). Deviation (restated): Milnor's connection is Mathlib's CovariantDerivative, his condition (1) the separate class ContMDiffCovariantDerivative; Mathlib's object is defined on all sections and is unconstrained on sections not differentiable at the point.

Milnor §8, pp. 45–46

A vector field $V$ along a parametrized curve $c$ assigns to each $t$ a tangent vector $V_t \in TM_{c(t)}$, smoothly; the velocity field is $dc/dt = c_*(d/dt)$. Given a connection, the covariant derivative $V \mapsto DV/dt$ is characterized by three axioms: (a) $D(V + W)/dt = DV/dt + DW/dt$; (b) $D(fV)/dt = (df/dt)V + f\,DV/dt$ for a smooth real function $f$ on $\mathbb R$; (c) if $V$ is induced by a vector field $Y$, $V_t = Y_{c(t)}$, then $DV/dt$ is the covariant derivative of $Y$ in the direction of the velocity vector of $c$.

Verified edition V6.5

For a curve $c : \mathbb R \to N$, a vector field along $c$ is a map $X : \mathbb R \to V$ with $X(t) \in T_{c(t)}N$ for all $t$; the velocity $c'(t)$ is tangent when $c$ is smooth; and $DX/dt\,(t) = P_{c(t)}(X'(t))$. Milnor's axioms hold: (a) $D(X + Y)/dt = DX/dt + DY/dt$ at $t$ when $X$, $Y$ are differentiable at $t$; (b) $D(fX)/dt = f'X + f\,DX/dt$ at $t$ when $f$, $X$ are differentiable at $t$ and $X(t)$ is tangent; (c) if $c$ is smooth and $Y : N \to V$ is differentiable at $c(t)$, then $D(Y \circ c)/dt\,(t) = c'(t) \vdash Y$. Book: pp. 45–46: parametrized curves, vector fields along a curve, the velocity field, and the axioms (a), (b), (c). Hidden hypotheses: differentiability at $t$ (Milnor's fields along curves are smooth by definition). Deviation (narrower): the embedded setting.

Milnor §8, proof of Lemma 8.2

The differential equations $dv^k/dt + \sum_{i,j} (du^i/dt)\Gamma^k_{ij}v^j = 0$ have solutions uniquely determined by their initial values; since the equations are linear, Milnor says, the solutions can be defined for all relevant values of $t$, citing Graves.

Verified edition V6.7

Let $A : \mathbb R \to \operatorname{End}(E)$ be continuous. (i) On a real normed space $E$, two solutions of $x' = A(t)x$ on an open interval (or on $\mathbb R$) that agree at one time agree everywhere. (ii) If $E$ is a complete real inner product space and $\langle A(t)x, x\rangle = 0$ for all $t$ and $x$, then for every $t_0$ and $x_0$ there is a solution on all of $\mathbb R$ with $x(t_0) = x_0$. Book: p. 47, proof of Lemma 8.2: the equations are linear, so the solutions are determined by their initial values and "can be defined for all relevant values of $t$" (Milnor cites Graves). Hidden hypotheses: a global existence theorem for linear equations; Mathlib has local existence (Picard–Lindelöf) and Grönwall uniqueness only. Deviation (narrower): global existence is proved only for skew-adjoint coefficients, the case needed in V6.8. Proof: solutions of the skew equation have constant norm, so the equation may be truncated outside a ball and solved by Picard–Lindelöf on any compact interval; solutions on nested intervals are glued by (i).

Along a curve $c$, every tangent vector $V_0$ at $c(0)$ extends to exactly one parallel vector field $V$, parallel meaning that $DV/dt$ vanishes identically; $V_t$ is then said to come from $V_0$ by parallel translation along $c$.

A field $X$ along $c$ is parallel if it is differentiable and $DX/dt = 0$ at every $t$. Deviation (narrower): the embedded setting. Proof: a tangent field is parallel iff $X' = P'X$, where $P(t) = P_{c(t)}$, and uniqueness is V6.7 (i) for this equation. It has no a priori bound, so existence solves instead $X' = (P'P - PP')X$, whose coefficient is skew-adjoint (V6.7 (ii)); since $PP'P = 0$, the normal part $U = X - PX$ satisfies $U' = -P'U$, so a solution that starts tangent stays tangent (V6.7 (i) again) and is then parallel. On an abstract manifold Milnor's coordinate equations would also have to be patched from chart to chart along the curve; here there is one equation in $V$.

Milnor §8, Definition 8.5

A connection is symmetric when $(X \vdash Y) - (Y \vdash X) = [X, Y]$, the bracket being the Poisson bracket $[X, Y]f = X(Yf) - Y(Xf)$. For coordinate fields this says $\Gamma^k_{ij} = \Gamma^k_{ji}$, and Milnor notes the converse.

Verified edition V6.13

Abstract: a covariant derivative is symmetric (Morse.IsSymmetric) if $X \vdash Y - Y \vdash X = [X, Y]$ at every point where $X$ and $Y$ are differentiable, $[X, Y]$ being Mathlib's Lie bracket of vector fields (which has Milnor's sign, $[X, Y]f = X(Yf) - Y(Xf)$); for a finite-dimensional model space this is "the torsion is zero". Embedded: the bracket of two maps $X, Y : N \to V$ is $[X, Y](q) = dY_q(X(q)) - dX_q(Y(q))$. For vector fields differentiable at $q$ it is tangent to $N$ at $q$; for smooth $f$ and smooth vector fields, $X(Yf) - Y(Xf) = [X, Y]f$, where $Xf = df(X)$; and the induced connection is symmetric: $X \vdash Y - Y \vdash X = [X, Y]$ at $q$ for vector fields differentiable at $q$. Book: p. 48, Definition 8.5, with $[X, Y]$ the Poisson bracket $[X, Y]f = X(Yf) - Y(Xf)$. Hidden hypotheses: differentiability at the point; in the embedded setting, that the ambient formula for the bracket is tangent and acts on functions as Milnor's bracket, neither of which is automatic. Proof: tangency of the bracket is the symmetry of $\mathrm{II}$ (V6.12): the normal part of $[X, Y]$ is $\mathrm{II}(X, Y) - \mathrm{II}(Y, X)$; the action on functions uses the symmetry of second derivatives.
