Milnor §8, Lemma 8.6

On a Riemannian manifold there is exactly one symmetric connection compatible with the metric. Uniqueness: Corollary 8.4 applied to $\partial_i$, $\partial_j$, $\partial_k$ gives three linear equations, whose solution is the first Christoffel identity, and multiplying by $(g^{k\ell})$ gives the second. Conversely, defining $\Gamma^\ell_{ij}$ by this formula, one can verify that the connection is symmetric and compatible with the metric.

Verified edition V6.14

Embedded: call an operation $D$ on maps $N \to V$ symmetric and compatible if, on smooth vector fields, $D(X, Y)$ is tangent, $D(X, Y) - D(Y, X) = [X, Y]$, and $X\langle Y, Y'\rangle = \langle D(X, Y), Y'\rangle + \langle Y, D(X, Y')\rangle$. The induced connection $P(dY(X))$ is such an operation (existence), every such operation satisfies the Koszul formula $$2\langle D(X, Y), Z\rangle = X\langle Y, Z\rangle + Y\langle X, Z\rangle - Z\langle X, Y\rangle + \langle[X, Y], Z\rangle - \langle[X, Z], Y\rangle - \langle[Y, Z], X\rangle$$ on smooth vector fields, and every such operation agrees with $P(dY(X))$ on smooth vector fields at every point (uniqueness). Abstract: for a manifold with a Riemannian metric on its tangent bundle, two covariant derivatives that are both symmetric and compatible (V6.11, V6.13) satisfy the Koszul formula and agree on every vector field differentiable at the point; with Mathlib's predicates, two torsion-free metric connections agree on such fields (finite-dimensional model space, $C^1$ metric). Book: p. 48, Lemma 8.6: a Riemannian manifold possesses one and only one symmetric connection compatible with its metric; uniqueness by the Christoffel identities (p. 49), and "one can verify" the converse. Hidden hypotheses: the existence half needs a converse of Lemma 8.3, which Milnor does not state, and a patching of the local connections. Deviation (stronger): the embedded uniqueness assumes no linearity or tensoriality of $D$, only the three properties on smooth fields. Deviation (narrower): existence is proved only in the embedded setting; on an abstract manifold only uniqueness, and only on sections differentiable at the point (a Mathlib covariant derivative is unconstrained elsewhere). Proof: the Koszul formula, the coordinate-free form of Milnor's first Christoffel identity, replaces his linear system on p. 49 (whose list of three unknowns contains $\langle\partial_i \vdash \partial_j, \partial_k\rangle$ twice, by the symmetry he quotes, a misprint); uniqueness applies it with $Z$ the field $x \mapsto P_x(D(X, Y)(q) - (X \vdash Y)(q))$ of V6.2.

to confirmA geodesic of $N$ on an open interval is a smooth curve in $N$ whose acceleration in $V$ is normal to $N$, that is, $\frac{D}{dt}\frac{d\gamma}{dt} = 0$.

the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §10, p. 55

On a connected Riemannian manifold $M$, a parametrized path $\gamma : I \to M$, $I$ any interval of the real line, is called a geodesic if its acceleration field $\frac{D}{dt}\frac{d\gamma}{dt}$ is identically zero; that is, if the velocity field $\frac{d\gamma}{dt}$ is parallel along $\gamma$. Here $D/dt$ is the covariant derivative along a curve of §8, for the Levi-Civita connection of an abstract Riemannian manifold.

Verified edition V7.1

Let $s \subseteq \mathbb R$ be open, in practice an open interval. A curve $\gamma$ is a geodesic on $s$ if it is $C^\infty$ on $s$, $\gamma(t) \in N$ for $t \in s$, and the acceleration $\gamma''(t)$ is orthogonal to $T_{\gamma(t)}N$ for every $t \in s$. The velocity at $t$ of a curve that lies in $N$ near $t$ and is differentiable at $t$ is tangent to $N$; so for a geodesic $\gamma'(t) \in T_{\gamma(t)}N$, and the condition on $\gamma''$ reads $P_{\gamma(t)}\gamma''(t) = 0$, Milnor's $\frac{D}{dt}\frac{d\gamma}{dt} = 0$ with $D/dt$ of V6.5. Formally: a smooth curve $c : \mathbb R \to N$ is a geodesic on $\mathbb R$ iff $\frac{D}{dt}\frac{dc}{dt}(t) = 0$ for all $t$ (V6.5 defines $D/dt$ for curves on all of $\mathbb R$). Constant curves at points of $N$ are geodesics. Book: p. 55: on a connected Riemannian manifold $M$, a parametrized path $\gamma : I \to M$, $I$ any interval, is a geodesic if its acceleration $\frac{D}{dt}\frac{d\gamma}{dt}$ vanishes identically, i.e. its velocity field is parallel along $\gamma$. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (narrower): the embedded setting, where a geodesic is a curve whose acceleration in $V$ is normal to $N$; geodesics live on open sets, so a geodesic on a closed interval is represented by one on a slightly larger open interval (V7.7).

What differs (the comparison)

  • Milnor's $M$ is an abstract Riemannian manifold. In Chapters 7–11 of the formalization it is a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space with the induced metric, and every row of these chapters is read in that setting; the narrowing is recorded here once rather than on every row. Every Riemannian manifold is of this kind by Nash's embedding theorem, which is quoted in the Lean files but neither proved nor used.
  • Mathlib has no Levi-Civita connection, geodesics or exponential map on an abstract manifold. In the embedded setting the connection is the tangential part of the derivative in $V$, and the Hausdorff property that Milnor uses silently is automatic.
  • Geodesics live on open sets: a geodesic on a closed interval, which Milnor allows, is represented by one on a slightly larger open interval. That the two notions give the same exponential map is proved later (V7.7).
  • Milnor's standing assumption that $M$ is connected is not made; it is assumed exactly where it is needed (finiteness of the distance, Theorem 10.9 for all pairs, Corollary 10.10, the Hopf–Rinow equivalence).

Milnor §10, pp. 55 and 57

Since $\frac{d}{dt}\langle\frac{d\gamma}{dt}, \frac{d\gamma}{dt}\rangle = 2\langle\frac{D}{dt}\frac{d\gamma}{dt}, \frac{d\gamma}{dt}\rangle = 0$, the length $\|d\gamma/dt\|$ of the velocity vector of a geodesic is constant, and the parameter $t$ is a linear function of arc length (p. 55). On p. 57 Milnor adds homogeneity: if $t \mapsto \gamma(t)$ is a geodesic, then so is $t \mapsto \gamma(ct)$ for every constant $c$.

Verified edition V7.2

For a geodesic $\gamma$ on $s$, $\frac{d}{dt}\|\gamma'\|^2 = 2\langle\gamma'', \gamma'\rangle = 0$ on $s$. If $s$ is an open interval (more generally, preconnected), the speed $\|\gamma'\|$ is constant on $s$, and the length of $\gamma$ on any $[a, b] \subseteq s$ (V7.11) is $\|\gamma'(t_0)\|\,(b - a)$ for every $t_0 \in s$. For all real $a$, $b$ the curve $t \mapsto \gamma(at + b)$ is a geodesic on $\{t : at + b \in s\}$. Book: p. 55: $\frac{d}{dt}\langle\frac{d\gamma}{dt}, \frac{d\gamma}{dt}\rangle = 2\langle\frac{D}{dt}\frac{d\gamma}{dt}, \frac{d\gamma}{dt}\rangle = 0$, so the speed is constant and the parameter is a linear function of arc length; p. 57 (homogeneity): if $t \mapsto \gamma(t)$ is a geodesic, so is $t \mapsto \gamma(ct)$ for every constant $c$. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (stronger): all affine changes of parameter $t \mapsto at + b$ ($a = 0$ gives a constant curve).

Milnor §10, p. 55

In terms of a local coordinate system $u^1, \dots, u^n$, the condition for $\gamma$ to be a geodesic becomes the system of second-order differential equations $\frac{d^2u^k}{dt^2} + \sum_{i,j}\Gamma^k_{ij}\frac{du^i}{dt}\frac{du^j}{dt} = 0$, $k = 1, \dots, n$, with the Christoffel symbols $\Gamma^k_{ij}$ of the connection. The existence of geodesics therefore rests on the existence theorem for such systems.

Verified edition V7.3

Let $\gamma$ be $C^\infty$ on an open set $s$ with $\gamma(s) \subseteq N$. Then $\gamma$ is a geodesic on $s$ iff $\gamma'' = \mathrm{II}_\gamma(\gamma', \gamma')$ on $s$, iff the lift $t \mapsto (\gamma(t), \gamma'(t))$, which then lies in $TN = \{(x, v) : x \in N,\ v \in T_xN\}$, is an integral curve on $s$ of the geodesic spray $(x, v) \mapsto (v, \mathrm{II}_x(v, v))$. In a slice chart with parametrization $x$ (V1.6) on the open set $T \subseteq Z$, put $A^+ = (A^{\mathsf T}A)^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}$ for injective $A$ and $\Gamma(u)(w, w) = (dx_u)^+\big(d^2x_u(w, w)\big)$. The field $(u, w) \mapsto (w, -\Gamma(u)(w, w))$ is smooth on $T \times Z$, and if $(u, w)$ is a $C^\infty$ solution of $u' = w$, $w' = -\Gamma(u)(w, w)$ on an open set $s$ with $u(s) \subseteq T$, then $x \circ u$ is a geodesic on $s$. Book: p. 55: in local coordinates the geodesic condition becomes the system $\frac{d^2u^k}{dt^2} + \sum_{i,j}\Gamma^k_{ij}\frac{du^i}{dt}\frac{du^j}{dt} = 0$, so the existence of geodesics rests on a system of second-order equations (the scan shows only the $\Gamma$-term of this display, a defect of the scan, not a misprint). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): $(dx_u)^+d^2x_u(w, w)$ is the coordinate vector, in the basis $\partial x/\partial u^k$, of the tangential part of $d^2x_u(w, w)$, that is $\big(\sum_{i,j}\Gamma^k_{ij}w^iw^j\big)_k$ for the Christoffel symbols of the induced metric; the Lean files define no Christoffel symbols, so this identification is a remark, not a theorem. In the chart only the direction "solutions are geodesics" is stated, which is what existence needs (V7.6); uniqueness uses the global form (V7.5).

Milnor §10, Theorem 10.1

Given a point $(u_1, v_1) \in \mathbb R^{2n}$ and $C^\infty$ functions $F = (F^1, \dots, F^n)$ defined near it, there are a neighbourhood $W$ of $(u_1, v_1)$ and a number $\varepsilon > 0$ such that for every $(u_0, v_0) \in W$ the equation $\frac{d^2u}{dt^2} = F(u, \frac{du}{dt})$ has a unique solution $t \mapsto u(t)$, defined for $|t| < \varepsilon$, with $u(0) = u_0$ and $\frac{du}{dt}(0) = v_0$; moreover the solution is $C^\infty$ as a function of $(u_0, v_0, t)$ on $W \times (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$. Milnor passes to the first-order system $du/dt = v$, $dv/dt = F(u, v)$ and quotes Graves.

Verified edition V7.4

Existence and smooth dependence. Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space (Milnor's $\mathbb R^n$), $U \subseteq E \times E$ open, $F : E \times E \to E$ smooth on $U$, and $z_1 \in U$. There are a neighbourhood $W$ of $z_1$, an $\varepsilon > 0$ and a map $(z, t) \mapsto u_z(t)$, smooth on $W \times (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$, such that for every $z = (u_0, v_0) \in W$: $u_z(0) = u_0$, $u_z'(0) = v_0$, and $(u_z(t), u_z'(t)) \in U$ and $u_z''(t) = F(u_z(t), u_z'(t))$ for $|t| < \varepsilon$. In first-order form: for $G$ smooth on an open set $U \ni x_1$ of $E$ there are a smooth $\varphi : \mathbb R \times E \to E$ and $r, \tau > 0$ such that for $\|x - x_1\| < r$ the curve $t \mapsto \varphi(t, x)$ solves $x' = G(x)$ in $U$ for $|t| < \tau$, with $\varphi(0, x) = x$. Uniqueness. Let $E$ be any real normed space and $G$ of class $C^1$ on an open set $U \subseteq E$. Two solutions of $x' = G(x)$ with values in $U$ that agree at one time agree near it, and, if both are defined on the same open interval (more generally, open preconnected set), on all of it. In particular, if $F$ is $C^1$ on $U \subseteq E \times E$, two pairs $(u_i, v_i)$ with $u_i' = v_i$, $v_i' = F(u_i, v_i)$ and $(u_i, v_i) \in U$ on an open interval $s$, with the same position and velocity at one time of $s$, have $u_1 = u_2$ on $s$. Book: p. 56, Theorem 10.1, for an $n$-tuple $F$ of $C^\infty$ functions near $(u_1, v_1) \in \mathbb R^{2n}$: a neighbourhood $W$ and an $\varepsilon > 0$ such that for $(u_0, v_0) \in W$ the equation has a unique solution for $|t| < \varepsilon$ with the given initial conditions, and $(u_0, v_0, t) \mapsto u(t)$ is $C^\infty$ on $W \times (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$; the proof passes to the first-order system $du/dt = v$, $dv/dt = F(u, v)$ and quotes Graves (the scan shows only part of the displayed equation). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (stronger): uniqueness on every common interval of definition, for $C^1$ equations on any normed space. Proof: proved, not quoted: $G$ times a bump function equal to $1$ near $x_1$ is a compactly supported smooth field whose global flow is smooth in $(t, x)$ (V1.14), and its bounded speed keeps the flow lines from points near $x_1$, for a uniform time, where the bump function is $1$; uniqueness is Grönwall's inequality (Mathlib) near each time, spread over the interval by connectedness.

For $v \in TM_q$, suppose there is a geodesic $\gamma : [0, 1] \to M$ with $\gamma(0) = q$ and $\frac{d\gamma}{dt}(0) = v$; then $\exp_q(v) = \gamma(1)$, and by homogeneity $\gamma(t) = \exp_q(tv)$ (p. 57). Verified edition V7.7

For $q, v \in V$, a geodesic from $q$ with initial velocity $v$ is a geodesic $\gamma$ on an open interval $(-\delta, 1 + \delta)$, $\delta > 0$, with $\gamma(0) = q$ and $\gamma'(0) = v$ (then $q \in N$, and $v \in T_qN$ by V7.1); a geodesic on an open interval containing $0$ and $1$ is one, from $\gamma(0)$ with initial velocity $\gamma'(0)$. The domain of $\exp$ is the set of pairs $(q, v)$ for which such a geodesic exists, and $\exp_q(v) = \gamma(1)$ (off the domain $\exp_q(v)$ is defined to be $q$, a placeholder). Two geodesics from $q$ with initial velocity $v$ agree on an open interval containing $[0, 1]$, so $\exp_q(v) = \gamma(1)$ for every such $\gamma$. For $q \in N$, $(q, 0)$ is in the domain and $\exp_q(0) = q$. If $\gamma$ is a geodesic from $q$ with initial velocity $v$, there is $\delta > 0$ such that $\gamma$ is a geodesic on $(-\delta, 1 + \delta)$ and, for each $t$ in this interval, $s \mapsto \gamma(ts)$ is a geodesic from $q$ with initial velocity $tv$ and $\exp_q(tv) = \gamma(t)$; so $t \mapsto \exp_q(tv)$ is a geodesic near $[0, 1]$, equal to $\gamma$. Milnor §10, p. 58

The tangent manifold $TM$ is given a $C^\infty$ structure by the coordinates $(u^1, \dots, u^n, t^1, \dots, t^n)$, where $t^1\partial_1 + \dots + t^n\partial_n$ is a tangent vector at a point with coordinates $u$. Lemma 10.2 says that for each $p \in M$ the map $(q, v) \mapsto \exp_q(v)$ is defined throughout a neighbourhood $V$ of $(p, 0)$ in $TM$, and is differentiable there. In the Jacobian of $F(q, v) = (q, \exp_q(v))$ at $(p, 0)$, the column $F_*(\partial/\partial t^j) = \partial/\partial u_2^j$ amounts to $d(\exp_p)_0 = \mathrm{id}$.

Verified edition V7.8

$TN = \{(q, v) \in V \times V : q \in N,\ v \in T_qN\}$ is a slice submanifold of $V \times V$ modelled on $Z \times Z$ (the companion project). (i) For every $q_0 \in N$ there are an open set $U \ni q_0$ of $V$, an $\varepsilon > 0$ and a map $F : V \times V \to V$, smooth on $U \times \{v : \|v\| < \varepsilon\}$, such that for $p \in N \cap U$ and $v \in T_pN$ with $\|v\| < \varepsilon$, $(p, v)$ is in the domain of $\exp$ and $\exp_p(v) = F(p, v)$. (ii) There is an open set $O \subseteq V \times V$ containing $(q, 0)$ for every $q \in N$ such that every point of $TN \cap O$ is in the domain of $\exp$, and $\exp$ is smooth on $TN \cap O$: near each point of $TN \cap O$ it is the restriction of a smooth map on an open set of $V \times V$, and $(q, v) \mapsto \exp_q(v)$ is smooth on the open subset $TN \cap O$ of the manifold $TN$. (iii) For each $q \in N$, $\exp_q$, as a map on the vector space $T_qN$, has derivative at $0$ the inclusion $T_qN \to V$. Book: p. 58: $TM$ is given a $C^\infty$ structure by the coordinates $(u^1, \dots, u^n, t^1, \dots, t^n)$; by Lemma 10.2, $(q, v) \mapsto \exp_q(v)$ is defined and differentiable throughout a neighbourhood of $(p, 0)$ in $TM$; in the Jacobian of $(q, v) \mapsto (q, \exp_q(v))$ at $(p, 0)$, the formula $F_*(\partial/\partial t^j) = \partial/\partial u_2^j$ amounts to $d(\exp_p)_0 = \mathrm{id}$. Hidden hypotheses: the smooth dependence in Lemma 10.2 (V7.6). Deviation (restated): Milnor's tangent manifold is the embedded $TN \subseteq V \times V$. Deviation (stronger): one open neighbourhood of the whole zero section.

Milnor §10, Lemma 10.3 (3)

Part (3) of Lemma 10.3 says that, for each $q$ in the neighbourhood $W$, $\exp_q$ maps the open $\varepsilon$-ball in $TM_q$ diffeomorphically onto an open set $U_q$. The book has no name for such an $\varepsilon$.

Verified edition V7.9

For $q \in N$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ let $B_\varepsilon(q) = \{v \in T_qN : \|v\| < \varepsilon\}$. $\varepsilon$ is a normal radius at $q$ if there are open sets $O, U \subseteq V$ and maps $F$ smooth on $O$ and $G$ smooth on $U$ such that: $B_\varepsilon(q) \subseteq O$, $B_\varepsilon(q)$ lies in the domain of $\exp_q$, and $\exp_q = F$ on $B_\varepsilon(q)$; $\exp_q$ maps $B_\varepsilon(q)$ into $U$, with $G(\exp_q v) = v$ for $v \in B_\varepsilon(q)$; and $G$ maps $U_q = N \cap U$ into $B_\varepsilon(q)$, with $\exp_q(G(y)) = y$ for $y \in U_q$. Thus $\exp_q$ is a bijection of $B_\varepsilon(q)$ onto the open subset $U_q$ of $N$, and it and its inverse are restrictions of smooth maps on open sets of $V$. A normal radius yields a diffeomorphism in Mathlib's sense: $\exp_q$, as a map from the vector space $T_qN$ to the manifold $N$, restricts to a PartialDiffeomorph of the open $\varepsilon$-ball onto $U_q$. Book: p. 59, Lemma 10.3 (3): $\exp_q$ maps the open $\varepsilon$-ball in $TM_q$ diffeomorphically onto an open set $U_q$. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): the name is the exposition's; "diffeomorphically" is made precise in Milnor's sense for subsets of Euclidean space, and Mathlib's sense follows.

Milnor §10, Lemma 10.3

For each $p \in M$ there are a neighbourhood $W$ of $p$ and a number $\varepsilon > 0$ such that: (1) any two points of $W$ are joined by a unique geodesic in $M$ of length $< \varepsilon$; (2) this geodesic depends smoothly on the two points, in that if $t \mapsto \exp_{q_1}(tv)$, $0 \le t \le 1$, is the geodesic joining $q_1$ and $q_2$, the pair $(q_1, v) \in TM$ depends differentiably on $(q_1, q_2)$; (3) for each $q \in W$, $\exp_q$ maps the open $\varepsilon$-ball in $TM_q$ diffeomorphically onto an open set $U_q \supseteq W$. Milnor §11, p. 67; used from p. 59

A piecewise smooth path is a map $\omega : [0, 1] \to M$ with a subdivision $0 = t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_k = 1$ such that each $\omega|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ is $C^\infty$ (p. 67, where the notion is first defined). From Theorem 10.4 on (p. 59) such paths on intervals $[a, b]$, and their arc lengths $\int\|d\omega/dt\|\,dt$, are used without further comment.

Verified edition V7.11

Let $c$ be a curve in a real normed space (complete, for the statements involving $\int c'$) and $a \le b$. The length of $c$ on $[a, b]$ is $L(c|[a, b]) = \int_a^b \|c'(t)\|\,dt$ ($c'$ is taken to be $0$ where $c$ is not differentiable, which for the paths below happens only on a null set). $c$ is piecewise smooth on $[a, b]$ if it is continuous on $[a, b]$ and there is a finite set $B$ of break points such that $c$ is $C^\infty$, with one-sided derivatives at the ends, on every $[s, t] \subseteq [a, b]$, $s < t$, with no point of $B$ in $(s, t)$. $c$ is admissible on $[a, b]$ if it is continuous on $[a, b]$, differentiable at all but countably many points of $(a, b)$, and $\|c'\|$ is integrable on $[a, b]$. A path in $N$ is one with $c([a, b]) \subseteq N$. Piecewise smooth paths are admissible. For admissible paths $\int_a^b c' = c(b) - c(a)$, so $\|c(b) - c(a)\| \le L(c|[a, b])$; length is additive under subdivision; a path of length $0$ is constant; a path with $\|c'\| = k$ wherever it is differentiable has length $k(b - a)$. Restriction to a subinterval, concatenation of two paths with a common endpoint, reversal $t \mapsto c(a + b - t)$ and translation of the parameter preserve piecewise smoothness; under concatenation lengths add, and under reversal and translation they are unchanged. Book: p. 67 (§11): a piecewise smooth path is a map $\omega : [0, 1] \to M$ with a subdivision $0 = t_0 < \dots < t_k = 1$ such that each $\omega|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ is $C^\infty$; from Theorem 10.4 on (p. 59) such paths on intervals $[a, b]$ and their lengths $\int\|d\omega/dt\|\,dt$ are used without comment. Hidden hypotheses: integrability of $\|d\omega/dt\|$; additivity and invariance of length under subdivision, concatenation, reversal and translation. Deviation (restated): the subdivision is given as a finite set of break points. Deviation (stronger): the lower bounds for lengths (V7.13–V7.16) are proved for admissible paths, a class that contains the piecewise smooth paths and is closed under restriction.

In $U_q$ the geodesics through $q$ are the orthogonal trajectories of the hypersurfaces $\{\exp_q(v) : \|v\| = \text{constant}\}$. $(N, \rho)$ is complete if every sequence of points $x_n \in N$ that is Cauchy for $\rho$ (for every $\varepsilon > 0$, $\rho(x_m, x_n) < \varepsilon$ for all large $m, n$) converges for $\rho$ to some $y \in N$, i.e. $\rho(x_n, y) \to 0$; for connected $N$ this is the completeness of the metric space of V7.21. (iii) If $t \mapsto \exp_y(tw)$ is a geodesic on an open interval $I \ni 0$, $s \in I$, $(y', w')$ is its position and velocity at time $s$, and $t \mapsto \exp_{y'}(tw')$ is a geodesic on an open interval $J \ni 0$, then $t \mapsto \exp_y(tw)$ is a geodesic on $I \cup (s + J)$, and its position and velocity at time $s + t$, $t \in J$, are those of $t \mapsto \exp_{y'}(tw')$ at time $t$. In particular, if $\exp_p$ is defined on all of $T_pN$, it is continuous there. Deviation (narrower): continuity of $\exp$ on its domain, not the smoothness asserted in the exposition's Lemma B; maximal geodesics are not constructed, geodesics being glued by (iii) instead. Proof: (ii) is Lemma 10.2 with smooth dependence (V7.6), rescaled by homogeneity; for (iv) the compact arc $\gamma([0, 1])$ is covered by finitely many sets $U$ of (ii) with a uniform time $2\tau_0$, and the geodesics with initial data near $(p, v)$ are continued by (iii) in steps of length $\tau_0$, their position and velocity being at each step a composition of continuous maps.

Milnor §10, p. 64

After Corollary 10.10 and its converse, Milnor no longer distinguishes geodesic from metric completeness, and calls such an $M$ simply a complete Riemannian manifold.

Verified edition V7.29

For a connected nonempty $N$ the following are equivalent: (1) $(N, \rho)$ is complete; (2) $N$ is geodesically complete; (3) $\exp_p$ is defined on all of $T_pN$ for some $p \in N$; (4) every bounded set has compact closure, contained in $N$. If $N$ is connected and $(N, \rho)$ is complete, then $N$ is geodesically complete, every geodesic on an open interval is the restriction of a geodesic on $\mathbb R$, any two points of $N$ are joined by a minimal geodesic on $[0, 1]$ whose length is their distance, and every bounded subset of $N$ that is closed in $N$ is compact (which follows from (4) alone). Milnor §11, p. 68

A variation of $\omega$ keeping the end points fixed is a map $\bar\alpha : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \to \Omega$ with $\bar\alpha(0) = \omega$ and a subdivision $0 = t_0 < \dots < t_k = 1$ such that $\alpha(u, t) = \bar\alpha(u)(t)$ is $C^\infty$ on each strip $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times [t_{i-1}, t_i]$; an $n$-parameter variation replaces $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$ by a neighbourhood of $0$ in $\mathbb R^n$. The variation vector field is $W_t = \frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(0, t)$, and "clearly" $W \in T\Omega_\omega$.

Verified edition V8.2

Let $P$ be a real normed space (Milnor's $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb R^n$) and $U \ni 0$ an open subset of $P$. A map $\alpha(u, t)$, $u \in P$, $t \in \mathbb R$, is a variation with break points $B$ (a finite set) if $\alpha(u, t) \in N$ for $u \in U$ and $t \in [0, 1]$; $\alpha(u, 0)$ and $\alpha(u, 1)$ do not depend on $u \in U$; and $\alpha$ is $C^\infty$ on every closed strip $U \times [s, t]$, $0 \le s < t \le 1$, with no point of $B$ in $(s, t)$. It is a variation of $\omega = \alpha(0, \cdot)$, and every $\alpha(u, \cdot)$, $u \in U$, lies in $\Omega(N; \omega(0), \omega(1))$; composed with a smooth map into $P$ that sends $0$ into $U$ it is again a variation (for instance a slice $u_2 \mapsto \alpha(u_1, u_2, \cdot)$). For $P = \mathbb R$ the variation field is $W_t = \frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(0, t)$; every $\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(u, t)$ is tangent to $N$ at $\alpha(u, t)$, and $W \in T\Omega_\omega$. Derivatives within a set (for instance one-sided derivatives along the edge of a strip) of maps into $N$ are tangent to $N$. Hidden hypotheses: behind "clearly": $W$ is continuous at a break point $t_i$ because both adjacent strips compute the velocity of the same curve $u \mapsto \alpha(u, t_i)$, tangent because that curve lies in $N$, and zero at the ends because they are fixed. Verified edition V8.8

For $F$ smooth on a closed strip $U \times [a, b]$, $U \subseteq \mathbb R$ open, $a < b$: the partial derivatives $\partial F/\partial u$ and $\partial F/\partial t$ computed within the strip are smooth on it, are the one-sided $t$-derivatives on the edges $t = a$, $t = b$, and the mixed partials agree on the whole closed strip, edges included. If $F$ and $F'$ are continuous on the strip and $F'$ is the $u$-derivative of $F$ at its interior points, then $u \mapsto \int_a^b F(u, t)\,dt$ has derivative $\int_a^b F'(u_0, t)\,dt$ at every $u_0 \in U$; the same holds for an integrand that on each piece of a finite subdivision agrees, inside the piece, with a function of class $C^1$ on the closed strip. If $\int_s^t g = F^-(t) - F^+(s)$ on every piece $[s, t]$ of $[a, b]$ with break points $B$, then $\int_a^b g = F^-(b) - F^+(a) - \sum_{x \in B \cap (a, b)} (F^+(x) - F^-(x))$; and properties of intervals that hold on pieces and glue at break points hold on every interval. Hidden hypotheses: smoothness on the closed strips; compactness, for the domination bound; the symmetry of second derivatives on the edges of the strips, where the $t$-derivatives are one-sided. Deviation (not in the book).

proved, not assertedany continuous coefficientsany complete normed space

Milnor §14, p. 77

The Jacobi equation, a linear second-order differential equation, has $2n$ linearly independent solutions, each of which is "defined throughout $\gamma$" and of class $C^\infty$; a Jacobi field is determined by its initial conditions $J(0)$ and $\frac{DJ}{dt}(0)$. Milnor gives no proof.

Verified edition V9.1

Let $E$ be a complete real normed space and $t \mapsto A(t)$ a continuous map from $\mathbb R$ to the continuous linear maps $E \to E$. (i) For every $t_0 \in \mathbb R$ and $x_0 \in E$ there is a solution of $x' = A(t)x$ on all of $\mathbb R$ with $x(t_0) = x_0$; the solution with value $\xi$ at $s$ depends linearly on $\xi$. (ii) If $a < b$ and $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and solves the equation on $(a, b)$, then for every $s \in [a, b]$, end points included, $f$ agrees on $[a, b]$ with the solution whose value at $s$ is $f(s)$. (iii) If $A$ is $C^\infty$ on $[a, b]$ (one-sided derivatives at the ends) and $f'(t) = A(t)f(t)$ at every $t \in [a, b]$, then $f$ is $C^\infty$ on $[a, b]$. Book: p. 77: the Jacobi equation, a linear second-order equation, has $2n$ linearly independent solutions, each "defined throughout $\gamma$", all of class $C^\infty$, and a Jacobi field is determined by $J(0)$ and $\frac{DJ}{dt}(0)$; no proof. Hidden hypotheses: a global existence theorem for linear equations; the local theorem gives solutions on intervals of length about $1/\sup\|A\|$ only. Deviation (stronger): any continuous coefficients on any complete space, extending V6.7 (ii), where they had to be skew-adjoint. Proof: the equation is truncated radially outside a ball and solved on compact intervals by Picard–Lindelöf; Grönwall's inequality, forward and backward in time, bounds the solution so that the truncation is never active (the exposition uses Picard iteration on the whole interval); (iii) is a bootstrap.

Jacobi fields and the Jacobi system

restated

to confirmA Jacobi field is a smooth tangent field with $\frac{D^2J}{dt^2} + R(V, J)V = 0$; one exists for all tangent initial values $(J(s), \frac{DJ}{dt}(s))$, and it is determined by them.

the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §14, p. 77

A vector field $J$ along a geodesic $\gamma$ is a Jacobi field if it satisfies the Jacobi differential equation $\frac{D^2J}{dt^2} + R(V, J)V = 0$, $V = d\gamma/dt$. In terms of orthonormal parallel fields $P_1, \dots, P_n$ along $\gamma$, writing $J = \sum f^iP_i$, it becomes a linear system with coefficients $\langle R(V, P_j)V, P_i\rangle$; a Jacobi field is completely determined by its initial conditions $J(0)$ and $\frac{DJ}{dt}(0)$.

Verified edition V9.2

For maps $\gamma$ and $J$ the Jacobi operator is $\frac{D^2J}{dt^2} + R(V, J)V$, $V = \gamma'$, with $D/dt$ of V8.7. $J$ is a Jacobi field along $\gamma$ if it is $C^\infty$ on $[0, 1]$ (one-sided derivatives at the ends), tangent along $\gamma$ ($J(t) \in T_{\gamma(t)}N$ for $t \in [0, 1]$), and $$\frac{D^2J}{dt^2} + R(V, J)V = 0 \quad\text{on } (0, 1).$$ Let $\gamma$ be a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$, $S = P'P - PP'$ and $K(t)v = R(V, P(t)v)V$. The Jacobi system is the first-order linear system $J' = SJ + Y$, $Y' = SY - KJ$ for $(J, Y)$ in $V \times V$; its coefficients are smooth on $[0, 1]$, and extended to $\mathbb R$ as constants they are continuous, so its solution with any value $\zeta$ at any time $s$ exists on $\mathbb R$ (V9.1). If $s \in [0, 1]$ and $\zeta = (x, y)$ with $x, y \in T_{\gamma(s)}N$, both components of this solution stay tangent on $[0, 1]$, the first is a Jacobi field and the second is its covariant derivative there. Conversely, for every Jacobi field $J$ and every $s \in [0, 1]$, $(J, \frac{DJ}{dt})$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with the solution whose value at $s$ is $(J(s), \frac{DJ}{dt}(s))$; in particular a Jacobi field with $J(s) = 0$ and $\frac{DJ}{dt}(s) = 0$ vanishes on $[0, 1]$. Book: p. 77: a vector field $J$ along a geodesic $\gamma$ is a Jacobi field if it satisfies the Jacobi equation; in orthonormal parallel fields $P_1, \dots, P_n$ along $\gamma$, $J = \sum f^iP_i$, it becomes a linear system with coefficients $\langle R(V, P_j)V, P_i\rangle$; a Jacobi field is completely determined by its initial conditions $J(0)$, $\frac{DJ}{dt}(0)$. Hidden hypotheses: the global solution theory (V9.1); parallel frames along $\gamma$ (Lemma 8.2), which V6.8 provides only for curves defined on all of $\mathbb R$. Deviation (restated): no frame: the unknown is $(J, \frac{DJ}{dt})$ in $V \times V$, and the term $S$ (the device of V6.8) keeps solutions with tangent initial values tangent, their normal parts $(1 - P)J$, $(1 - P)Y$ solving a homogeneous linear system and vanishing at $s$. Deviation (stronger): along any smooth curve in $N$, not only along a geodesic, and with initial values at any $s \in [0, 1]$.

to confirmAt a geodesic, $W_1 \in T\Omega_\gamma$ is a null vector of $E_{**}$ iff it is a Jacobi field.

the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §14, Theorem 14.1

A vector field $W_1 \in T\Omega_\gamma$ belongs to the null space of $E_{**}$ if and only if $W_1$ is a Jacobi field. Proof (pp. 78–79): a Jacobi field vanishing at the ends is null by the second variation formula; conversely, testing against $W_2 = f(t)(\frac{D^2W_1}{dt^2} + R(V, W_1)V)$, $f$ vanishing exactly at the break points, makes $W_1$ a Jacobi field on each piece, testing against a field with values $\Delta_{t_i}\frac{DW_1}{dt}$ at the break points removes the jumps, and the pieces "fit together" since a solution is determined by $W_1(t_i)$ and $\frac{DW_1}{dt}(t_i)$.

Verified edition V9.5

Let $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ be a geodesic (V8.10) and $W_1 \in T\Omega_\gamma$. Then $E_{*}(W_1, W_2) = 0$ for every $W_2 \in T\Omega_\gamma$ iff $W_1$ is a Jacobi field along $\gamma$; in particular such a $W_1$ is $C^\infty$ on all of $[0, 1]$. The steps: a Jacobi field vanishing at $0$ and $1$ lies in $T\Omega_\gamma$, and for a Jacobi field $J$ (along any curve) $\Phi(J, Y) = 0$ for every field $Y$ (V8.13); for a null vector $W_1$, the Jacobi operator of $W_1$ vanishes off its break points, and at every $t \in (0, 1)$ the jump of $W_1'$ is tangent and vanishes; for a smooth tangent field the Jacobi equation gives the second-order equation $W'' = -P(P'W') - R(V, W)V + (1 - P)(P''W + 2P'W')$ in $V$; and $W_1$ is $C^\infty$ near every point of $(0, 1)$. *Book: p. 78, Theorem 14.1 (first sentence); proof pp. 78–79: a Jacobi field vanishing at the ends lies in the null space by the second variation formula; conversely, testing against $W_2 = f(t)(\frac{D^2W_1} {dt^2} + R(V, W_1)V)$, $f$ vanishing exactly at the break points, makes $W_1$ a Jacobi field on each piece, testing against a field $W_2'$ with $W_2'(t_i) = \Delta_{t_i}\frac{DW_1}{dt}$ shows that $\frac{DW_1}{dt}$ has no jumps, and the pieces "fit together" since a solution is determined by $W_1(t_i)$ and $\frac{DW_1}{dt}(t_i)$. Hidden hypotheses: the field $W_2'$ with prescribed values at the break points has to be constructed; fitting the pieces together needs Jacobi fields along all of $\gamma$ with given initial values (V9.2), stated in the book without proof. Deviation (restated): in $V$, the absence of jumps of $\frac{DW_1}{dt} = PW_1'$ makes $W_1$ of class $C^1$ only because the normal parts of the two one-sided derivatives agree (both are $\mathrm{II}(V, W_1)$). Proof: the test fields are bump functions, supported inside one piece or centred at one break point, times $\frac{D^2W_1}{dt^2} + R(V, W_1)V$ or times the tangent projection of the jump; the pieces are joined by a local argument instead of the uniqueness of Jacobi fields: the second-order equation above holds on both sides of a former break point $x$, with a right side continuous across $x$, so $W_1'$ is differentiable at $x$, and a solution of a smooth second-order equation is $C^\infty$ (a bootstrap).

to confirmAt a geodesic, the nullity of $E_{}$ is the multiplicity of $0$ and $1$ as conjugate parameters, and $E_{}$ is degenerate iff they are conjugate.

the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §14, Theorem 14.1, pp. 77–79

The null space of $E_{}$ is the space of $W_1 \in T\Omega_\gamma$ with $E_{}(W_1, W_2) = 0$ for all $W_2$, the nullity $\nu$ is its dimension, and $E_{}$ is degenerate if $\nu > 0$ (pp. 77–78). Theorem 14.1 continues: hence $E_{}$ is degenerate if and only if the end points $p$ and $q$ are conjugate along $\gamma$, and the nullity of $E_{**}$ equals their multiplicity as conjugate points. On p. 79: the nullity is always finite.

Verified edition V9.6

For $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$, the null space of $E_{}$ is the space of the restrictions to $[0, 1]$, extended as constants, of the $W_1 \in T\Omega_\gamma$ with $E_{}(W_1, W_2) = 0$ for all $W_2 \in T\Omega_\gamma$, and the nullity $\nu$ is its dimension. If $\gamma$ is a geodesic, the null space is the space of fields of $\mathcal J(\gamma)$ vanishing at $0$ and $1$; so $\nu$ is the multiplicity of $0$ and $1$ (V9.4), in particular finite, and $\nu > 0$ ($E_{}$ is degenerate) iff $0$ and $1$ are conjugate along $\gamma$. Book: pp. 77–78: the null space of $E_{}$ is the space of the $W_1 \in T\Omega_\gamma$ with $E_{}(W_1, W_2) = 0$ for all $W_2$, the nullity $\nu$ is its dimension, and $E_{}$ is degenerate if $\nu > 0$; p. 78, Theorem 14.1: hence $E_{}$ is degenerate iff $p$ and $q$ are conjugate along $\gamma$, and the nullity is their multiplicity; p. 79: the nullity is always finite. Hidden hypotheses: finiteness needs the identification with a subspace of the $2n$-dimensional $\mathcal J(\gamma)$ (V9.3). Deviation (restated): the fields of $T\Omega_\gamma$ (V8.1) are maps on $\mathbb R$ whose values off $[0, 1]$ play no role, so the literal kernel of the formal $E_{}$ contains every field vanishing on $[0, 1]$ and is infinite-dimensional; the null space is therefore taken modulo the values off $[0, 1]$. "$p$ and $q$ conjugate" reads "$0$ and $1$ conjugate" (V9.4).

Lemmas 8.7, 9.2 on a closed strip
the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §14, Lemma 14.3

A variation of $\gamma$ through geodesics, not necessarily keeping the end points fixed, is a $C^\infty$ map $\alpha : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times [0, 1] \to M$ with $\alpha(0, t) = \gamma(t)$ and each $\bar\alpha(u)$ a geodesic (p. 79). Lemma 14.3: its variation vector field $W(t) = \frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(0, t)$ is a Jacobi field along $\gamma$. Proof: apply $\frac{D}{\partial u}$ to $\frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial t} = 0$ and use Lemmas 9.2 and 8.7.

Verified edition V9.8

Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and let $\alpha(u, t)$ be $C^\infty$ on $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times [0, 1]$ (one-sided derivatives along the edges $t = 0, 1$), with values in $N$ there, such that each $t \mapsto \alpha(u, t)$, $|u| < \varepsilon$, is a geodesic on $(0, 1)$ (V7.1). Then $W(t) = \frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(0, t)$ is a Jacobi field along $\alpha(0, \cdot)$. Being a Jacobi field along $\gamma$ depends only on $\gamma$ on $[0, 1]$. Book: p. 79: a variation of $\gamma$ through geodesics, not necessarily keeping the end points fixed, is a $C^\infty$ map $\alpha : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times [0, 1] \to M$ with $\alpha(0, t) = \gamma(t)$ and each $\bar\alpha(u)$ a geodesic; p. 80, Lemma 14.3: its variation field is a Jacobi field; proof: apply $\frac{D}{\partial u}$ to $\frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial t} = 0$ and use Lemmas 9.2 and 8.7. Hidden hypotheses: Lemmas 9.2 and 8.7 are applied to a map defined on a strip and smooth up to its edges (V8.12). Proof: Milnor's, with the identity (13.3) of V8.12 on the open strip $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times (0, 1)$; the smoothness of $W$ up to $t = 0, 1$ comes from that of $\alpha$ on the closed strip.

the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §14, Lemma 14.4

Every Jacobi field along a geodesic $\gamma : [0, 1] \to M$ may be obtained by a variation of $\gamma$ through geodesics. Proof: in a neighbourhood $U$ of $\gamma(0)$ where any two points are joined by a unique minimal geodesic depending differentiably on the end points, with $\gamma(t) \in U$ for $0 \le t \le \delta$, minimal geodesics between the points of two curves $a(u)$, $b(u)$ give Jacobi fields along $\gamma|[0, \delta]$ with arbitrary values at $0$ and $\delta$; so $J \mapsto (J(0), J(\delta))$ is onto, hence an isomorphism (both spaces have dimension $2n$); "using the compactness of $[0, 1]$", the geodesics extend over $[0, 1]$ for small $u$.

Verified edition V9.9

(i) For $x_1 \in N$ and $R > 0$ there are an open set $U \ni x_1$ of $V$, an $h > 0$ and a map $\Phi(y, w, t)$, $C^\infty$ on $U \times \{\|w\| < R\} \times (-h, h)$, such that for $y \in N \cap U$ and $w \in T_yN$ with $\|w\| < R$, $t \mapsto \exp_y(tw)$ is a geodesic on $(-h, h)$, equal to $\Phi(y, w, t)$ there. (ii) A smooth curve $\gamma$ in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ that is a geodesic on $(0, 1)$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with $t \mapsto \exp_{\gamma(0)}(tV(0))$, which is a geodesic on an open interval containing $[0, 1]$; this is the extension of a geodesic segment past its end points that V7.7 leaves unformalized. (iii) Let $c, w$ be $C^\infty$ on an open set $U_0 \ni 0$ of $\mathbb R$, with $c(u) \in N$ and $w(u) \in T_{c(u)}N$. If $t \mapsto \exp_{c(0)}(tw(0))$ is a geodesic on $(-\delta, B + \delta)$, $B \ge 0$, $\delta > 0$, there are $\varepsilon, \eta > 0$ such that every $t \mapsto \exp_{c(u)}(tw(u))$, $|u| < \varepsilon$, is a geodesic on $(-\eta, B + \eta)$ and $(u, t) \mapsto \exp_{c(u)}(tw(u))$ is $C^\infty$ on $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times (-\eta, B + \eta)$. (iv) Lemma 14.4: let $\gamma$ be a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ that is a geodesic on $(0, 1)$, and $J$ a Jacobi field along $\gamma$. There are $\varepsilon > 0$ and a map $\alpha$ satisfying the hypotheses of Lemma 14.3 (V9.8) on $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times [0, 1]$, with $\alpha(0, t) = \gamma(t)$ and $\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(0, t) = J(t)$ for $t \in [0, 1]$. Book: p. 81, Lemma 14.4: every Jacobi field along a geodesic $\gamma : [0, 1] \to M$ may be obtained by a variation of $\gamma$ through geodesics. Proof: take a neighbourhood $U$ of $\gamma(0)$ in which any two points are joined by a unique minimal geodesic depending differentiably on the end points, and $\delta$ with $\gamma(t) \in U$ for $0 \le t \le \delta$; minimal geodesics between the points of curves $a(u)$, $b(u)$ give Jacobi fields along $\gamma|[0, \delta]$ with arbitrary values at $0$ and $\delta$, so $J \mapsto (J(0), J(\delta))$ is onto, hence an isomorphism (both spaces have dimension $2n$); "using the compactness of $[0, 1]$", the geodesics extend over $[0, 1]$ for small $u$. Hidden hypotheses: the construction returns $\bar\alpha(0) = \gamma|[0, \delta]$ only if $\gamma|[0, \delta]$ is the minimal geodesic from $\gamma(0)$ to $\gamma(\delta)$, which $\gamma([0, \delta]) \subseteq U$ does not say; for Milnor's $U$ it is true, by an argument the book omits (the exposition supplies it after its Lemma 14.4, and ensures it directly by a bound on the length of $\gamma|[0, \delta]$); the compactness step is the smooth dependence of geodesics on their initial data over a compact interval, (iii), with the openness of the domain of $\exp$, neither among the statements of §10; and that the extended variation still has $J$ as variation field needs the uniqueness of Jacobi fields (V9.2). Proof: departs from Milnor's. The variation is built from initial data: $\alpha(u, t) = \exp_{c(u)}(t\, w(u))$ with $c(u) = \exp_{\gamma(0)}(uJ(0))$ and $w(u) = P_{c(u)}(V(0) + u\frac{DJ}{dt}(0))$. It is defined and smooth on $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times [0, 1]$ by (i)–(iii); its variation field is a Jacobi field (V9.8) with value $J(0)$ and covariant derivative $\frac{DJ}{dt}(0)$ at $t = 0$ (by the symmetry of the mixed partials and $PP'P = 0$), hence equals $J$ (V9.2). No minimal geodesic, restriction to $[0, \delta]$ or dimension count is used: the formal statement has no minimality hypothesis, and the minimality of $\gamma|[0, \delta]$ is neither assumed nor proved.

the index and the nullity of a bilinear form

restated

to confirmThe index of a bilinear form is the supremum of the dimensions of the finite-dimensional subspaces on which it is negative definite.

a supremum, possibly $\infty$finiteness is part of Theorem 15.1
the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §15, p. 83; §2, p. 5

The index $\lambda$ of $E_{}$ is the maximum dimension of a subspace of $T\Omega_\gamma$ on which $E_{}$ is negative definite (p. 83); for a bilinear functional on a vector space, the index and the nullity are defined in §2 (p. 5).

Verified edition V9.13

Let $B$ be a bilinear form on a real vector space $X$. $B$ is negative (positive) definite on a subspace $S$ if $B(x, x) < 0$ ($> 0$) for every $x \ne 0$ in $S$. The index of $B$ is the supremum, in $\{0, 1, 2, \dots\} \cup \{\infty\}$, of the dimensions of the finite-dimensional subspaces on which $B$ is negative definite; a finite index is the dimension of such a subspace. A linear map $L$ with $B'(Lx, Ly) = B(x, y)$ does not decrease the index (it is injective on every negative definite subspace), so a linear isomorphism carrying $B$ to $B'$ preserves it; on a finite-dimensional space the index is Mathlib's negative index of inertia (sigNeg) of $x \mapsto B(x, x)$, as in V1.3. The nullity of $B$ is the dimension of its null space $\{x : B(x, y) = 0 \text{ for all } y\}$; for $E_{}$ the null space is read on $[0, 1]$ (V9.6). Book: p. 83: the index $\lambda$ of $E_{}$ is the maximum dimension of a subspace of $T\Omega_\gamma$ on which $E_{}$ is negative definite; p. 5: the index and the nullity of a bilinear functional on a vector space. Hidden hypotheses: that the maximum exists, i.e. is finite; for $E_{}$ this is part of Theorem 15.1 (V9.19, V9.24). Deviation (restated): a supremum over finite-dimensional subspaces, possibly $\infty$; a negative definite subspace of infinite dimension contains finite-dimensional ones of every dimension, and so also gives $\infty$.

Milnor §15, pp. 85–87

The book has no such statements; on pp. 85–87 Milnor uses without proof: that the index and nullity of $E_{}$ can be computed on a summand complementary to a perpendicular subspace on which $E_{}$ is positive definite ("the proof is straightforward", Lemma 15.4); that definiteness of $H_\tau$ on a subspace persists for $H_{\tau'}$ near $H_\tau$; a positive definite subspace of dimension $ni - \lambda(\tau) - \nu$; and a compound matrix that is "certainly negative definite" for small $c$.

Verified edition V9.14

Let $B$ be a bilinear form on a real vector space $X$. (1) If $\dim X = m < \infty$, a negative definite and a positive definite subspace have dimensions adding up to at most $m$. (2) (Sylvester) If $\dim X = m < \infty$ and $B$ is symmetric, with index $\lambda$ and nullity $\nu$, then $B$ is positive definite on a subspace of dimension $m - \lambda - \nu$. (3) If $(B_\tau)$ is a family of bilinear forms on $X$ indexed by a topological space, $S \subseteq X$ is a finite-dimensional subspace, $\tau \mapsto B_\tau(x, y)$ is continuous at $\tau_0$ for all $x, y \in S$, and $B_{\tau_0}$ is negative (positive) definite on $S$, then so is $B_\tau$ for all $\tau$ near $\tau_0$. (4) (Lemma 15.B) If $X = A \oplus C$, $B(a, c) = B(c, a) = 0$ for all $a \in A$, $c \in C$, and $B$ is positive definite on $C$, then $B$ and its restriction to $A$ have the same index, and the null space of $B$ is that of its restriction to $A$. (5) (Milnor's compound matrix) If $B$ is symmetric, $U : \mathbb R^\lambda \to X$ is linear with $B(Ua, Ua) < 0$ for $a \ne 0$, and $J, Y : \mathbb R^\nu \to X$ are linear with $B(Jb, Ua) = 0$, $B(Jb, Jb') = 0$ and $B(Jb, Yb') = 2\langle b, b'\rangle$ for all $a, b, b'$, then the index of $B$ is at least $\lambda + \nu$. Book: used without proof on pp. 85–87: Lemma 15.4 ("the proof is straightforward"), the persistence of definiteness for $H_{\tau'}$ near $H_\tau$ in Assertions (3) and (4), a positive definite subspace of dimension $ni - \lambda(\tau) - \nu$, and the compound matrix, "certainly negative definite" for small $c$. Hidden hypotheses: in (5), that a negative definite Gram matrix makes the $\lambda + \nu$ fields linearly independent. Deviation (not in the book): stated and proved as lemmas. Proof: (3) by the compactness of the unit sphere of $S$; (5) by (3): for small $c \ne 0$, $B$ is negative definite on the image of $(a, b) \mapsto Ua + c^{-1}Jb - cYb$, whose Gram matrix is a perturbation of the block-diagonal one with blocks $(B(Ua_i, Ua_j))$ and $-4I$.

Milnor §15, pp. 83–84

Each $\gamma(t)$ lies in an open set $U$ in which any two points are joined by a unique minimal geodesic depending differentiably on the end points (§10), and the subdivision $0 = t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_k = 1$ is chosen "sufficiently fine" that each $\gamma|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ lies in such a $U$ and is minimal. Milnor uses two consequences: along each segment the Jacobi fields are determined by their end values, which can be prescribed (Remark 14.5); and each segment has smaller energy than any other path between its end points (p. 84).

Verified edition V9.16

Let $\gamma$ be a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$, $C \ge 0$ a bound for $\|P'(t)\|^2 + \|K(t)\|$ on $[0, 1]$ ($K$ as in V9.2), and $h_0 = 1/(C + 1) > 0$. (i) A Poincaré estimate. If $X \in T\Omega_\gamma$ and every $t \in [0, 1]$ has a zero $s \in [0, t]$ of $X$ with $t - s \le h_0$, then $$\int_0^1\|X\|^2\,dt \le \int_0^1\Big(\Big\|\frac{DX}{dt}\Big\|^2 - \langle R(V, X)V, X\rangle\Big) \,dt = \tfrac12E_{}(X, X)$$ (the equality is V8.15); so $E_{}(X, X) \le 0$ forces $X = 0$ on $[0, 1]$. (ii) If $0 \le a < b \le 1$ and $b - a \le h_0$, a field of $\mathcal J(\gamma)$ vanishing at $a$ and $b$ is $0$, and $J \mapsto (J(a), J(b))$ is a linear isomorphism $\mathcal J(\gamma) \to T_{\gamma(a)}N \times T_{\gamma(b)}N$; in particular no two parameters at distance at most $h_0$ are conjugate. (iii) For $\tau > 0$, a finite set $B \subseteq (0, \tau)$ of division points is fine for $[0, \tau]$ if consecutive points of $\{0\} \cup B \cup \{\tau\}$ are at most $h_0$ apart; for every $\tau > 0$ there is one whose last point is within $h_0/2$ of $\tau$. Book: p. 83: each $\gamma(t)$ lies in an open set $U$ in which any two points are joined by a unique minimal geodesic depending differentiably on the end points (§10), and the subdivision is chosen "sufficiently fine" that each $\gamma|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ lies in such a $U$ and is minimal. Milnor uses two consequences: along each segment the Jacobi fields are determined by their end values, which can be prescribed (Remark 14.5); and each segment has smaller energy than any other path between its end points (p. 84). Hidden hypotheses: that such subdivisions exist (a Lebesgue number of a finite cover, and a length bound for minimality, Theorem 10.4). Deviation (restated): "sufficiently fine" becomes the explicit mesh $h_0$, which depends only on bounds for $P'$ and the curvature along $\gamma$; $\gamma$ need not be a geodesic, and neither $\exp$ nor minimality enters. Proof: on a piece $[s, t]$ starting at a zero, $\|X(t)\|^2 \le L_s^t(X)^2 \le (t - s)E_s^t(X)$ (V7.11, V8.5), whence $\int_0^1\|X\|^2 \le h_0\int_0^1\|X'\|^2$; and the integrand is at least $\|X'\|^2 - C\|X\|^2$, since $\|\frac{DX}{dt}\|^2 \ge \|X'\|^2 - \|P'\|^2\|X\|^2$ for a tangent field and $\langle R(V, X)V, X\rangle \le \|K\|\,\|X\|^2$. For (ii), the field equal to $J$ on $[a, b]$ and to $0$ elsewhere has $E_{**} = 0$ by V9.15 (its only break points $a$, $b$ are zeros), so it vanishes by (i); $J$ then vanishes near the midpoint of $[a, b]$, hence everywhere (V9.2).

Milnor §15, pp. 83–84 and 86

$T\Omega_\gamma(t_0, t_1, \dots, t_k)$ is the space of vector fields $W$ along $\gamma$ vanishing at $0$ and $1$ such that each $W|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ is a Jacobi field along $\gamma|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$: a finite-dimensional space of broken Jacobi fields (p. 83). $T'$ is the space of fields with $W(t_0) = W(t_1) = \dots = W(t_k) = 0$, and "it follows from §14.5" that the broken Jacobi field with given values at the $t_i$ exists and is unique (p. 84). On p. 86, along $\gamma_\tau$, the broken Jacobi fields for $0 < t_1 < \dots < t_i < \tau$ form a space isomorphic to $TM_{\gamma(t_1)} \oplus \dots \oplus TM_{\gamma(t_i)}$.

Verified edition V9.17

Let $\gamma$ be a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$. For $\tau \in \mathbb R$, the fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ are the fields of $T\Omega_\gamma$ vanishing outside $[0, \tau]$; for $0 \le \tau \le 1$ they vanish at $\tau$. Let $0 < \tau \le 1$ and $B$ be fine for $[0, \tau]$ (V9.16). A map is a broken Jacobi field on $[0, \tau]$ for $B$ if on each piece between consecutive points of $\{0\} \cup B \cup \{\tau\}$ it agrees with a field of $\mathcal J(\gamma)$. Milnor's $T\Omega_\gamma(t_0, \dots, t_k)$ is the space of fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ that are broken Jacobi fields, and his $T'$ the space of fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ vanishing at the points of $B$. Broken Jacobi fields with arbitrary tangent values at $0$, $\tau$ and the points of $B$ exist, and one vanishing at all these points vanishes on $[0, \tau]$; so $W \mapsto (W(b))_{b \in B}$ is a linear isomorphism from the broken Jacobi fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ onto $\Sigma = \bigoplus_{b \in B}T_{\gamma(b)}N$. Book: p. 83: $T\Omega_\gamma(t_0, \dots, t_k)$, the fields $W$ along $\gamma$ vanishing at $0$ and $1$ with $W|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ a Jacobi field along $\gamma|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ for each $i$, a finite-dimensional space of broken Jacobi fields; p. 84: $T'$, the fields with $W(t_0) = W(t_1) = \dots = W(t_k) = 0$, and "it follows from §14.5" that the broken Jacobi field with given values at the $t_i$ exists and is unique; p. 86: along $\gamma_\tau$, for $0 < t_1 < \dots < t_i < \tau$, the broken Jacobi fields form a space isomorphic to $\Sigma$, since a broken Jacobi field is determined by its values at the break points. Hidden hypotheses: Remark 14.5 on each segment, and the gluing of the pieces. Deviation (restated): everything is along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ for every $\tau \in (0, 1]$, as fields on $[0, 1]$ vanishing outside $[0, \tau]$ (Milnor uses $\tau = 1$ here and $\gamma_\tau$ on p. 86); a piece is the restriction of a Jacobi field along all of $\gamma$, which is equivalent to being a Jacobi field along $\gamma|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ by V9.1–V9.2, an equivalence not stated formally. Proof: existence by induction over the division points, gluing segment by segment with V9.16 (ii); uniqueness from V9.16 (ii) on each piece.

Milnor §15, Lemma 15.3

$T\Omega_\gamma = T\Omega_\gamma(t_0, \dots, t_k) \oplus T'$, the two subspaces are mutually perpendicular with respect to $E_{}$, and $E_{}$ restricted to $T'$ is positive definite. Proof (pp. 84–85): $W = W_1 + (W - W_1)$; perpendicularity from the second variation formula; $E_{}(W, W) \ge 0$ on $T'$ because each segment is minimal, and $E_{}(W, W) = 0$ puts $W$ in the null space, so $W$ is a Jacobi field, and $T'$ contains no Jacobi field other than $0$.

Verified edition V9.18

Let $\gamma$ be a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$, $0 < \tau \le 1$ and $B$ fine for $[0, \tau]$. (i) The fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ are the direct sum of the broken Jacobi fields and $T'$ (V9.17). (ii) For a broken Jacobi field $W_1$ along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ and every field $Y$ along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$, $E_{}(W_1, Y) = -2\sum_{b \in B}\langle Y(b), \Delta_b\frac{DW_1}{dt}\rangle$; in particular $E_{}(W_1, W_2) = 0$ for $W_2 \in T'$. Milnor §15, Theorem 15.1

(Morse.) The index $\lambda$ of $E_{**}$ is equal to the number of points $\gamma(t)$, with $0 < t < 1$, such that $\gamma(t)$ is conjugate to $\gamma(0)$ along $\gamma$, each such conjugate point being counted with its multiplicity. The index $\lambda$ is always finite. On p. 87 the theorem "clearly follows" from Assertions (2), (3) and (4).

Verified edition V9.24

(i) Let $\ell, \nu : \mathbb R \to \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ and $h_0 > 0$, with $\ell$ non-decreasing on $(0, 1]$, $\ell = 0$ on $(0, h_0]$, $\ell(\tau') = \ell(\tau)$ for $\tau' < \tau$ near $\tau$ (for $0 < \tau \le 1$), and $\ell(\tau') = \ell(\tau) + \nu(\tau)$ for $\tau' > \tau$ near $\tau$ (for $0 < \tau < 1$). Then $\nu(t) \ne 0$ for only finitely many $t \in (0, 1)$, and $\ell(1) = \sum_{0 < t < 1}\nu(t)$. (ii) For every smooth curve $\gamma$ in $N$ on $[0, 1]$, $\nu(t) \ne 0$ for only finitely many $t \in (0, 1)$, and $\lambda(1) = \sum_{0 < t < 1}\nu(t)$. (iii) Theorem 15.1: let $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ be a geodesic (V8.10). The parameters $t \in (0, 1)$ conjugate to $0$ along $\gamma$ form a finite set, and the index of $E_{}$ on $T\Omega_\gamma$ (V9.13) is $$\lambda = \sum_{0 < t < 1}\nu(t),$$ the number of these parameters, each counted with its multiplicity (V9.4); in particular $\lambda$ is finite. Book: p. 83, Theorem 15.1 (Morse): the index $\lambda$ of $E_{}$ is equal to the number of points $\gamma(t)$, $0 < t < 1$, conjugate to $\gamma(0)$ along $\gamma$, each counted with its multiplicity, and is always finite; p. 87: the theorem "clearly follows" from Assertions (2), (3) and (4). Deviation (restated): parameters for points (V9.4). Milnor's metric on $\Omega$

restated

to confirmMilnor's distance $d$, the largest distance of corresponding points plus the $L^2$ distance of the speeds, is a pseudometric on paths, vanishing for paths that agree on $[0, 1]$.

a pseudometric on maps $\mathbb R \to V$Minkowski for the triangle inequality
the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §16, p. 88

The path space $\Omega$ can be topologized by the distance $d(\omega, \omega') = \max_t\rho(\omega(t), \omega'(t)) + \big[\int_0^1(\frac{ds}{dt} - \frac{ds'}{dt})^2dt\big]^{1/2}$, where $s(t)$ and $s'(t)$ are the arc lengths of $\omega$ and $\omega'$ from $0$ to $t$, and $\rho$ is the distance of §10.

Verified edition V10.1

For $\omega, \eta \in \Omega$, with speeds $\dot s_\omega(t) = \|\frac{d\omega}{dt}(t)\|$ and $\dot s_\eta(t)$, $$d(\omega, \eta) = \sup_{0 \le t \le 1}\rho(\omega(t), \eta(t)) + \Big(\int_0^1(\dot s_\omega - \dot s_\eta)^2\,dt\Big)^{1/2}.$$ This is an extended pseudometric on $\Omega$ (formally with values in $[0, \infty]$; symmetric, with the triangle inequality), and two paths that agree on $[0, 1]$ are at distance $0$. From now on $\Omega$ and its subsets carry the topology of $d$. Book: p. 88: $\Omega$ can be topologized by the distance $d(\omega, \omega') = \max_t\rho(\omega(t), \omega'(t)) + [\int_0^1(\frac{ds}{dt} - \frac{ds'}{dt})^2dt]^{1/2}$, with $s$, $s'$ the arc lengths. Hidden hypotheses: the triangle inequality for the second term is Minkowski's inequality in $L^2$; $\frac{ds}{dt}$ exists except at finitely many points. Deviation (restated): on maps $\mathbb R \to V$, $d$ is a pseudometric, not a metric; on paths $[0, 1] \to N$ it is Milnor's metric.

What differs (the comparison)

  • Paths are maps on $\mathbb R$ whose values off $[0, 1]$ play no role, and $d$ sees only $[0, 1]$, so it is a pseudometric; on paths $[0, 1] \to N$ it is Milnor's metric. Three conventions follow throughout the chapter: identities between paths hold on $[0, 1]$, homeomorphisms become homotopy equivalences up to paths at distance $0$, and geodesics are counted by their values on $[0, 1]$.

Milnor §16, Lemma 16.1

Let $M$ be complete and $c > 0$ with $\Omega^c$ non-vacuous. Then for all sufficiently fine subdivisions $(t_0, \dots, t_k)$ of $[0, 1]$, $\operatorname{Int}\Omega(t_0, \dots, t_k)^c$ can be given the structure of a smooth finite dimensional manifold "in a natural way". Proof (p. 89): for a broken geodesic $(L_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i}\omega)^2 = (t_i - t_{i-1})E_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i}\omega < \varepsilon^2$, so each segment is determined by its end points, and $\omega$ by $(\omega(t_1), \dots, \omega(t_{k-1})) \in M \times \dots \times M$; this is a homeomorphism onto an open subset of the product, whose differentiable structure is taken over.

Verified edition V10.4

Fix Milnor's data. For $y = (y_1, \dots, y_m) \in V^m$ put $x_0 = p$, $x_j = y_j$ ($1 \le j \le m$), $x_{m+1} = q$, and $$E'(y) = \sum_{i=0}^{m}\frac{\rho(x_i, x_{i+1})^2}{t_{i+1} - t_i};$$ let $U$ be the set of $y \in N^m$ with every $\rho(x_i, x_{i+1})$ finite and $E'(y) < c$. (i) $U = N^m \cap O$ for an open $O \subseteq V^m$; for every open $O \subseteq V^m$, $N^m \cap O$ is a slice submanifold of $V^m$ modelled on $Z^m$, with tangent space $T_{y_1}N \times \dots \times T_{y_m}N$ at $y$. (ii) For $y \in U$, the broken geodesic $\omega_y$, equal on $[t_i, t_{i+1}]$ to $t \mapsto \exp_{x_i}(\frac{t - t_i}{t_{i+1} - t_i}\,v(x_i, x_{i+1}))$, where $v(x, x')$ is the initial vector of the short geodesic from $x$ to $x'$ (V7.20), lies in $B$, has break points $(\omega_y(t_1), \dots, \omega_y(t_m)) = y$, and $E(\omega_y) = E'(y)$ (the exposition's formula $(\ast)$). (iii) For $\omega \in B$ and each $i$ there is $w \in T_{\omega(t_i)}N$ with $\|w\| < \delta$, $\omega(t) = \exp_{\omega(t_i)}(\frac{t - t_i}{t_{i+1} - t_i}\,w)$ for $t_i \le t \le t_{i+1}$, and $E_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}(\omega) = \|w\|^2/(t_{i+1} - t_i)$; the break points $y$ of $\omega$ lie in $U$, and $\omega_y$ agrees with $\omega$ on $[0, 1]$. Milnor §16, p. 91

The retraction $r : \operatorname{Int}\Omega^c \to B$ sends $\omega$ to the broken geodesic which on each $[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ is the geodesic of length less than $\varepsilon$ from $\omega(t_{i-1})$ to $\omega(t_i)$; "clearly" $E(r(\omega)) \le E(\omega) < c$. For $t_{i-1} \le u \le t_i$, $r_u(\omega)$ is $r(\omega)$ on $[0, t_{i-1}]$, the minimal geodesic from $\omega(t_{i-1})$ to $\omega(u)$ on $[t_{i-1}, u]$, and $\omega$ on $[u, 1]$; $r_0$ is the identity, $r_1 = r$, and "it is easily verified" that $r_u(\omega)$ is continuous as a function of both variables.

Verified edition V10.7

For Milnor's data, $\omega \in \Omega$ with $E(\omega) < c$ and $t_i \le u \le t_{i+1}$, $r_u(\omega)$ is the broken geodesic $\omega_y$ of the break points $y$ of $\omega$ on $[0, t_i]$, the short geodesic from $\omega(t_i)$ to $\omega(u)$, run at constant speed, on $[t_i, u]$, and $\omega$ on $[u, 1]$; at $u = t_{i+1}$ the formulas of the two neighbouring segments agree. On $[0, 1]$: $r_u(\omega) \in \Omega$, $E(r_u(\omega)) \le E(\omega)$, $r_0(\omega) = \omega$, $r_1(\omega) = \omega_y$, and $r_u(\omega) = \omega$ for $\omega \in B$. Completed by $\omega$ off $[0, 1]$, and set equal to $\omega$ when $u \notin [0, 1]$ or $E(\omega) \ge c$, $(u, \omega) \mapsto r_u(\omega)$ is a map $\mathbb R \times \Omega \to \Omega$, and (Lemma 16.C) it is continuous on $[0, 1] \times \operatorname{Int}\Omega^c$. Book: p. 91: the retraction $r : \operatorname{Int}\Omega^c \to B$, $r(\omega)$ being on each $[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ the geodesic of length less than $\varepsilon$ from $\omega(t_{i-1})$ to $\omega(t_i)$; "Clearly" $E(r(\omega)) \le E(\omega) < c$; for $t_{i-1} \le u \le t_i$, $r_u(\omega)$ is $r(\omega)$ on $[0, t_{i-1}]$, the minimal geodesic from $\omega(t_{i-1})$ to $\omega(u)$ on $[t_{i-1}, u]$, and $\omega$ on $[u, 1]$; $r_0$ is the identity, $r_1 = r$, and "it is easily verified" that $r_u(\omega)$ is continuous in both variables. The critical points of $E'$ are precisely the critical points of $E$ in $\operatorname{Int}\Omega^c$, namely the unbroken geodesics from $p$ to $q$ of length less than $\sqrt c$. On p. 91: every geodesic is a broken geodesic, so every critical point of $E$ in $\operatorname{Int}\Omega^c$ lies in $B$, and with the first variation formula (12.2) "it is clear" that the critical points of $E'$ are the unbroken geodesics.

Verified edition V10.9

Fix Milnor's data. (i) Every tangent vector of a slice submanifold at a point is the velocity at $0$ of a smooth curve in it. If $u \mapsto y(u)$ is a smooth curve in $U$ near $0$, then $(u, t) \mapsto \omega_{y(u)}(t)$ is, for $|u| < \varepsilon$, a variation (V8.2) through broken geodesics, smooth on each strip $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times [t_i, t_{i+1}]$, whose variation field takes the value $y'(0)_j$ at $t_j$. (ii) At $\gamma = \omega_y$, $y \in U$, the first variation (V8.7) in the direction $X$ is $-\sum_j\langle X(t_j), \Delta_{t_j}\gamma'\rangle$. (iii) Let $O \subseteq V^m$ be open with $N^m \cap O \subseteq U$, and $F$ smooth on $V^m$ with $F = E'$ on $N^m \cap O$. For $y \in N^m \cap O$ and $w \in T_{y_1}N \times \dots \times T_{y_m}N$, $dF_y(w) = -2\sum_j\langle w_j, \Delta_{t_j}\omega_y'\rangle$; and $y$ is a critical point (V1.4) of $E' = F|(N^m \cap O)$ iff $\omega_y$ is an unbroken geodesic. (iv) For every geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega$ with $E(\gamma) < c$, the break points $y$ of $\gamma$ lie in $U$, $\omega_y$ agrees with $\gamma$ on $[0, 1]$ and is an unbroken geodesic, and $E'(y) = E(\gamma)$. Book: p. 90, Theorem 16.2: the critical points of $E'$ are precisely the critical points of $E$ in $\operatorname{Int}\Omega^c$, namely the unbroken geodesics from $p$ to $q$ of length less than $\sqrt c$; p. 91: every geodesic is a broken geodesic, so every critical point of $E$ in $\operatorname{Int}\Omega^c$ lies in $B$, and with the first variation formula (§12.2) "it is clear" that the critical points of $E'$ are the unbroken geodesics. Hidden hypotheses: that every tangent vector of $B$ at $\gamma$ is the variation field of a variation through broken geodesics, smooth on the strips, which needs the smooth dependence of a geodesic segment on its end points over the whole segment (V9.9 (iii)); testing one break point at a time, with the tangent vector $\Delta_{t_j}\gamma'$; a broken geodesic without velocity jumps is unbroken (Corollary 12.3, V8.11). Fix Milnor's data and $y \in U$ with $\gamma = \omega_y$ an unbroken geodesic. (ii) For every $i$, $t_i$ and $t_{i+1}$ are not conjugate along $\gamma$ (V9.4). (iii) The broken Jacobi fields along $\gamma$ for the break points $t_1, \dots, t_m$ (V9.17, with $\tau = 1$) with arbitrary tangent values at the $t_j$ exist and are unique: $W \mapsto (W(t_1), \dots, W(t_m))$ is a linear isomorphism onto $T_{y_1}N \times \dots \times T_{y_m}N$. $\Omega^$ is the space of all continuous paths $\omega : [0, 1] \to M$ from $p$ to $q$, with the compact-open topology, which can also be described as that induced by the metric $d^(\omega, \omega') = \max_t\rho(\omega(t), \omega'(t))$. $\Omega^* = \Omega^(N; p, q)$ is the set of continuous maps $\omega : [0, 1] \to V$ with values in $N$, $\omega(0) = p$ and $\omega(1) = q$, as a subspace of the space of continuous maps $[0, 1] \to V$ with the uniform distance $d^(\omega, \eta) = \max_t\|\omega(t) - \eta(t)\|$, whose topology is the compact-open topology. The map $i : \Omega \to \Omega^$ restricts a path to $[0, 1]$; $d^(i\omega, i\eta) \le d(\omega, \eta)$, so $i$ is continuous. Milnor §17, p. 93

In the proof of Theorem 17.1, Milnor takes a continuous $f : M \to [0, \infty)$ with each $f^{-1}([0, r])$ compact, and lets $\varepsilon_1(r) \le \infty$ be the largest number such that any two points of $f^{-1}([0, r])$ at distance less than $\varepsilon_1(r)$ are joined by a unique minimal geodesic which varies differentiably with the end points.

Verified edition V10.17

For $y, z \in V$ the minimal join vector $v(y, z)$ is the unique $v \in T_yN$ with $\exp_y(v) = z$ and $\rho(y, z) = \|v\|$ for which the conclusion of Corollary 10.8 holds at some scale $\delta > \|v\|$ ($0$ if there is none), and $\sigma_{yz}(s) = \exp_y(s\,v(y, z))$. An open $O \subseteq V$ is a good ball if, for one $\delta > 0$, any two points of $N \cap O$ are at distance less than $\delta$ and joined as in Corollary 10.8 at the scale $\delta$, and $\sigma_{yz}(s) \in N \cap O$ for $y, z \in N \cap O$ and $0 \le s \le 1$ (convexity). (i) For $x \in N$, the balls $\{\|y - x\| < r\}$ of $V$ are good for all small $r > 0$. (ii) For compact $K \subseteq N$ there is $\varepsilon > 0$ such that the ball of radius $\varepsilon$ about each point of $K$ lies in a good ball. (iii) In a good ball, $\sigma_{yz}$ is the unique minimal geodesic from $y$ to $z$, its sub-arcs are minimal geodesics, and near each pair the map $(y, z, s) \mapsto \sigma_{yz}(s)$ is the restriction of a map smooth on an open set. (iv) Local smooth extensions are glued, by a partition of unity, into one map of $(y, z, s)$, smooth for $-\varepsilon < s < 1 + \varepsilon$, that agrees with $\sigma$ on a given compact set of pairs. So the balls $\{\|y - x\| < r\}$, $x \in N$, for which the concentric balls of radius up to $2r$ are good and $N \cap \{\|y - x\| \le r\}$ is compact, with the joins $\sigma$, form a join system: open good sets, convex for the joins, with $\sigma_{yz}(0) = y$, $\sigma_{yz}(1) = z$, $\sigma_{yy} = y$, one smooth map of $(y, z, s)$ on each good set, and a Lebesgue number for every compact subset of $N$. Book: p. 93: for a continuous $f : M \to [0, \infty)$ with compact sets $f^{-1}([0, r])$, $\varepsilon_1(r)$ is the largest number such that any two points of $f^{-1}([0, r])$ at distance less than $\varepsilon_1(r)$ are joined by a unique minimal geodesic which varies differentiably with the end points. Hidden hypotheses: the modified proof of Theorem 17.1 needs regions that are convex for these geodesics (J. H. C. Whitehead's convex balls), one smooth map of $(y, z, s)$ on each whole region, and a uniform scale; Milnor's construction provides none of these. Deviation (not in the book): the exposition's Lemma 17.B. Deviation (restated): good balls are balls of $V$ intersected with $N$, not metric balls of $\rho$, and their convexity is proved with the ambient distance: along a geodesic $\gamma$, $(\|\gamma - x\|^2)'' = 2\|\gamma'\|^2 + 2\langle\gamma - x, \mathrm{II}(\gamma', \gamma')\rangle > 0$ while $\gamma$ stays near $x$, so no normal coordinates or Gauss lemma are needed; smoothness in $(y, z, s)$ uses the smoothness of $\exp$ on its whole domain (V11.1).

Let $M$ be a Riemannian manifold, not necessarily complete, and $p, q \in M$. The natural map $i : \Omega \to \Omega^$ is a homotopy equivalence between $\Omega$, with the metric $d$, and the space $\Omega^$ of continuous paths. The proof (pp. 93–94) builds a continuous $A : \Omega^* \to (0, 1]$ and the broken geodesic $h(\omega)$ through $\omega(0), \omega(A), \dots, \omega(kA), \omega(1)$, asserts "Clearly $h$ is continuous", and shows $h \circ i \simeq \mathrm{id}$, $i \circ h \simeq \mathrm{id}$ by "an argument similar to that in §16".

Verified edition V10.19

(i) If $Y$ is paracompact and Hausdorff, $B_0 \subseteq B_1 \subseteq \cdots$ are subsets of $Y$ such that every point lies in the interior of some $B_n$, and $g : X \to Y$ is continuous, then $X$ is the homotopy direct limit (VA.2) of the sets $g^{-1}(B_n)$. (ii) For every join system, $i : \Omega(N; p, q) \to \Omega^(N; p, q)$ is a homotopy equivalence (VA.1). (iii) Theorem 17.1: for every slice submanifold $N$ of $V$, complete or not, and all $p, q$, the inclusion $i : \Omega \to \Omega^$, with Milnor's metric $d$ on $\Omega$ and the compact-open topology on $\Omega^$, is a homotopy equivalence. *Book: p. 93, Theorem 17.1: the natural map $i$ is a homotopy equivalence between $\Omega$ and $\Omega^$. Proof, pp. 93–94: with $f$ and $\varepsilon_1$ as in V10.17, a continuous $\varepsilon_2$ with $0 < \varepsilon_2 < \varepsilon_1$, $\varepsilon(\omega) = \varepsilon_2(\max_tf(\omega(t)))$ and $F(\omega, \alpha) = (\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\omega) + \max_{|t - t'| \le \alpha}\rho(\omega(t), \omega(t'))$, the zero $\alpha = 2A(\omega)$ of $F(\omega, \cdot)$ defines a continuous $A : \Omega^ \to (0, 1]$ such that points of $\omega$ at times less than $2A(\omega)$ apart are joined by a unique minimal geodesic; $h(\omega)$ is the path that agrees with $\omega$ at $t = 0, A(\omega), 2A(\omega), \dots, kA(\omega)$ ($k$ the largest integer in $1/A(\omega)$) and at $t = 1$, and is a geodesic in between; "Clearly $h$ is continuous"; and an argument similar to that in §16 gives $h \circ i \simeq \mathrm{id}$ and $i \circ h \simeq \mathrm{id}$. A step that does not hold as we read it: "Clearly $h$ is continuous" (p. 94) fails for the metric $d$ of $\Omega$, the topology in which Theorem 17.1 is stated ($h$ is continuous only for $d^$). When $1/A(\omega)$ crosses an integer from below, $h(\omega)$ acquires a new last segment of duration $\delta \to 0$ and length $\ell \to 0$, whose energy $\ell^2/\delta$ need not tend to $0$; for a continuous path that is not Lipschitz near $t = 1$ it can tend to infinity, and since $\sqrt E$ is $1$-Lipschitz for $d$ (V10.2), $h$ is then not continuous. The exposition's example: $M = \mathbb R$, $p = q = 0$, $f(x) = |x|$, $\varepsilon_2 \equiv 1$ and $\omega_\lambda(t) = \lambda((1 - t)^{1/3} - (1 - t))$; as $\lambda$ decreases to $\lambda_ = \sqrt3/2$, $\omega_\lambda \to \omega_{\lambda_*}$ uniformly while $E(h(\omega_\lambda)) \to \infty$. This counterexample is machine-checked (Morse.milnor_h_not_continuous, Morse.milnor_h_not_continuous'): with Milnor's $A$ and $h$ defined exactly as on p. 94 for this choice, $h$ is not continuous at $\omega_{\lambda_*}$ (it was first found by hand and numerically: Exposition/Chapter10.md, §5; Exposition/Findings.md). The theorem is true, and what is verified is the theorem itself, by the exposition's modified proof. (Also, $A$ takes its values in $(0, \frac12]$.) Hidden hypotheses (of the modified proof): good balls convex for minimal geodesics, with one smooth join on each (V10.17); the $L^2$ control of velocities by $d$ (V10.16); $\Omega$ is not Hausdorff for $d$, so Example 1 of the Appendix (paracompact Hausdorff spaces) is applied to $\Omega^$ and pulled back by $i$; Theorem A for open, not closed, pieces (VA.15). *Proof: the exposition's, not Milnor's: the open sets $Y_k$ exhaust the metric, hence paracompact, space $\Omega^*$, which is therefore the homotopy direct limit of the $Y_k$ (Example 1, VA.7), and $\Omega$ is that of the $X_k = i^{-1}(Y_k)$ by (i); $i$ carries each $X_k$ into $Y_k$ by a homotopy equivalence (V10.18); Theorem A with no closedness hypothesis (VA.15) concludes. No completeness is used.

(i) A map $\iota : A \to X$ is, up to homotopy, the inclusion of $A$ with cells $(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k)$ attached if there are a space $K$ obtained from $A$ by attaching a $\lambda_1$-cell, then a $\lambda_2$-cell, and so on (VA.18), with $j : A \to K$ the composite of the inclusions, and a homotopy equivalence $e : X \to K$ with $e \circ \iota \simeq j$. (ii) (Lemma 3.7, relative and iterated) Such an attachment $L \to K$ and a homotopy equivalence $L \to L'$ give an attachment $L' \to K'$ of the same cells and a homotopy equivalence $K \to K'$ extending $L \to L'$; and the notion in (i) is invariant under homotopy-commutative squares of homotopy equivalences. Theorem 17.3, the fundamental theorem of Morse theory

narrower

to confirmTheorem 17.3: for $N$ closed in $V$ and $q$ not conjugate to $p$ along any geodesic, $\Omega(N; p, q)$ has the homotopy type of a countable cell complex with one $\lambda$-cell for each geodesic from $p$ to $q$ of index $\lambda$.

$N$ closed in $V$, for completenessfor $\Omega$, not $\Omega^*$countable cell complex: a telescope
the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §17, Theorem 17.3

If $M$ is complete and $p, q \in M$ are not conjugate along any geodesic, then $\Omega(M; p, q)$ (or $\Omega^*(M; p, q)$) has the homotopy type of a countable CW-complex which contains one cell of dimension $\lambda$ for each geodesic from $p$ to $q$ of index $\lambda$. Proof: levels $a_0 < a_1 < \cdots$, not critical values, with "precisely one" critical value in each interval and $\Omega^{a_0}$ empty; the tower of CW-complexes; the direct limit map $\Omega \to K$ induces isomorphisms of homotopy groups, hence is a homotopy equivalence by Whitehead's theorem, $\Omega$ having the homotopy type of a CW-complex by 17.2. A different proof, not using 17.1, is referred to the Appendix.

Verified edition V10.22

Let $N$ be closed in $V$ and $p, q \in N$. (i) Suppose every geodesic in $\Omega$ has nullity $0$, and let $a_0 \le a_1 \le \cdots$ be levels tending to $\infty$, with $a_0 < 0$, none of which is the energy of a geodesic. Then there are finite lists $\mathrm{geo}_0 = \emptyset, \mathrm{geo}_1, \mathrm{geo}_2, \dots$ of geodesics in $\Omega$, $\mathrm{geo}_{n+1}$ consisting of geodesics with energy in $(a_n, a_{n+1})$, containing one geodesic that agrees on $[0, 1]$ with each geodesic of that energy and no two that agree on $[0, 1]$, ordered by energy, such that $\Omega$, with Milnor's metric, has the homotopy type of the countable cell complex (VA.18) with one cell of dimension the index of $E_{}$ at $\gamma$ for each entry $\gamma$. (ii) Theorem 17.3:* if every geodesic in $\Omega$ has nullity $0$, there are finite lists $\mathrm{geo}_0, \mathrm{geo}_1, \dots$ of geodesics from $p$ to $q$ such that every geodesic from $p$ to $q$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with exactly one entry of exactly one list, the energies increase strictly from one list to the next and weakly within a list, and $\Omega(N; p, q)$, with Milnor's metric, has the homotopy type of the countable cell complex with one cell of dimension $\lambda$ for each entry of index $\lambda$: one $\lambda$-cell for each geodesic from $p$ to $q$ of index $\lambda$, attached in order of increasing energy. (iii) The same holds if $q$ is not conjugate to $p$ along any geodesic (V11.4), which makes every nullity $0$ (Theorem 14.1, V9.6). *Book: p. 95, Theorem 17.3: if $M$ is complete and $p, q$ are not conjugate along any geodesic, then $\Omega(M; p, q)$ (or $\Omega^(M; p, q)$) has the homotopy type of a countable CW-complex containing one cell of dimension $\lambda$ for each geodesic from $p$ to $q$ of index $\lambda$. Proof, p. 95: levels $a_0 < a_1 < \cdots$, not critical values, with "precisely one" critical value in each interval and $\Omega^{a_0}$ empty; 16.2 with 3.3 and 3.7 at each step; the tower of CW-complexes (V10.20); the direct limit map $\Omega \to K$ induces isomorphisms of homotopy groups, hence is a homotopy equivalence by Whitehead's theorem, since $\Omega$ has the homotopy type of a CW-complex (17.2); and a reference to a different proof, not using 17.1, on p. 149. *Hidden hypotheses: the $a_i$ must tend to infinity, or the $\Omega^{a_i}$ do not exhaust $\Omega$; "precisely one" critical value in each interval is impossible when there are finitely many geodesics, and "at most one" suffices; the compatibility of the tower (V10.20). Deviation (narrower): completeness is replaced by the closedness of $N$ in $V$, which implies it (V7.30) and is used only through the compactness of the balls $S$ (V10.3); the statement is for $\Omega$, not for $\Omega^$; the "countable CW-complex" is the mapping telescope of a tower of cell attachments (VA.18). *Deviation (restated): geodesics are counted by their values on $[0, 1]$; an interval between consecutive levels may contain several critical values, whose cells are attached in order of energy. Proof: Milnor's second route, Theorem A of the Appendix (VA.19), through V10.20 (v) and V10.21; neither Whitehead's theorem nor Corollary 17.2 is used.

$S^n \subseteq \mathbb R^{n+1}$ is the unit sphere with the induced metric (V6.25), $n \ge 1$. (i) For unit vectors $p \perp u$ and $L \in \mathbb R$, $c(t) = \cos(Lt)\,p + \sin(Lt)\,u$ is a geodesic of $S^n$ on $\mathbb R$, with energy $L^2$ on $[0, 1]$; every geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(S^n; p, q)$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with such a $c$, with $L \ge 0$. (ii) For every $e \perp p, u$, $t \mapsto \sin(Lt)\,e$ is a Jacobi field along $c$, and so is $t \mapsto t\,c'(t)$; for $L > 0$ and $0 < t \le 1$, the multiplicity of $0$ and $t$ as conjugate parameters along $c$ (V9.4) is $n - 1$ if $Lt$ is a multiple of $\pi$, and $0$ otherwise. (iii) Let $q \ne \pm p$, $\theta \in (0, \pi)$ the angle between $p$ and $q$, and $u \perp p$ the unit vector with $q = \cos\theta\,p + \sin\theta\,u$; let $\gamma_{2j}$ be the great circle along $u$ with $L_{2j} = \theta + 2\pi j$, and $\gamma_{2j+1}$ the one along $-u$ with $L_{2j+1} = 2\pi(j + 1) - \theta$. Milnor §17, p. 96

For $n > 2$, the homology of $\Omega(S^n)$ "can be computed immediately" from the cell structure of Corollary 17.4.

Verified edition V10.25

Homology is singular homology with coefficients in a field $\Bbbk$, and $b_i = \dim_\Bbbk H_i$ (V3.33). (i) Let $A_0 \subseteq A_1 \subseteq \cdots$ be subsets of a space $X$ such that every compact subset of $X$ lies in some $A_k$ (for instance the sublevel sets of a continuous function at levels unbounded above). If $H_j(A_k, A_{k_0}) = 0$ for all $k \ge k_0$, then $H_j(X, A_{k_0}) = 0$; and if the steps $H_*(A_{k+1}, A_k)$ vanish in degrees $i$ and $i + 1$ for all $k \ge k_0$, then $b_i(X) = \dim H_i(A_{k_0})$. (ii) The homology of a slab (V3.33–V3.34) is computed in the same way for a slice submanifold that need not be compact, below a level whose sublevel set is compact. (iii) For Milnor's data and levels $a \le b < c$, neither the energy of a geodesic, with at most one energy of a geodesic in $(a, b)$ and every geodesic of energy at most $b$ of nullity $0$, $H_j(\Omega^b, \Omega^a)$ is finite-dimensional, of dimension the number of geodesics with energy in $(a, b)$ and index $j$. (iv) In the situation of V10.24 (i), with levels halfway between consecutive energies, $H_j(\Omega^{a_{k+1}}, \Omega^{a_k})$ is $\Bbbk$ for $j = d_k$ and $0$ otherwise; and if $d_k = kr$ with $r \ge 2$, then $b_i(\Omega) = 1$ when $r$ divides $i$ and $0$ otherwise.
