Milnor §18, p. 98

A critical point is defined for a smooth map between manifolds of the same dimension and applied to $\exp = \exp_p : TM_p \to M$, so $\exp_p$ is treated as smooth on all of $TM_p$. $M$ is assumed complete so that $\exp$ is everywhere defined, "although this assumption could easily be eliminated".

Verified edition V11.1

(i) Let $E$ be a real normed space, $U_0 \subseteq E$ open, $u_0 \in U_0$, and $c, w : E \to V$ of class $C^\infty$ on $U_0$ with $c(u) \in N$ and $w(u) \in T_{c(u)}N$ for $u \in U_0$. If $t \mapsto \exp_{c(u_0)}(t\,w(u_0))$ is a geodesic on $(-\delta, B + \delta)$, $B \ge 0$, $\delta > 0$, there are $\varepsilon, \eta > 0$ such that the ball of radius $\varepsilon$ about $u_0$ lies in $U_0$, every $t \mapsto \exp_{c(u)}(t\,w(u))$ with $u$ in this ball is a geodesic on $(-\eta, B + \eta)$, and $(u, t) \mapsto \exp_{c(u)}(t\,w(u))$ is $C^\infty$ on the product of the ball with $(-\eta, B + \eta)$. (ii) Every point of $N$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ in $V$ with a map $r$, $C^\infty$ on $U$, with values in $N$ and fixing the points of $N \cap U$. (iii) The domain of $\exp$ lies in $TN$; a point $(y, w)$ of $TN$ is in it as soon as $t \mapsto \exp_y(tw)$ is a geodesic on an open interval containing $[0, 1]$; and near every point $(p, v)$ of the domain there are an open set $O \subseteq V \times V$ and a map $F$, $C^\infty$ on $O$, such that every point of $TN \cap O$ is in the domain and $\exp = F$ there. Hence the domain is $TN \cap O'$ for an open $O' \subseteq V \times V$, and $(q, v) \mapsto \exp_q(v)$ is $C^\infty$ on it as a map on the manifold $TN$. Book: p. 98: a critical point is defined for a smooth map between manifolds of the same dimension and applied to $\exp = \exp_p : TM_p \to M$, so $\exp_p$ is treated as smooth on all of $TM_p$; $M$ is assumed complete so that $\exp$ is everywhere defined, "although this assumption could easily be eliminated". Deviation (stronger): the whole domain, without completeness. Proof: (i) continues the geodesics step by step with the local smooth flow (V9.9 (i)), as in V9.9 (iii), now with parameters in any normed space; (ii) from a slice chart $\sigma$, $r(y) = \sigma^{-1}(\sigma(y)_1, 0)$; (iii) is (i) with $E = V \times V$ and the data $(y, w) \mapsto (r(y), P_{r(y)}w)$, which agree with $(y, w)$ on $TN$.

Milnor §18, Theorem 18.1

The point $q = \exp v$ is conjugate to $p$ along the geodesic $\gamma_v$ from $p$ to $\exp v$ if and only if the mapping $\exp$ is critical at $v$. Proof (pp. 98–99): if $\exp_*X = 0$ with $X \ne 0$, the variation $\alpha(u, t) = \exp tv(u)$ through geodesics, for a path $v(u)$ with $v(0) = v$ and $\frac{dv}{du}(0) = X$, has a variation field $W$ with $W(0) = 0$, $W(1) = \exp_*X = 0$ and $\frac{DW}{dt}(0) \ne 0$; conversely, if $\exp_*$ is non-singular at $v$, independent $X_1, \dots, X_n$ give $n$ Jacobi fields vanishing at $p$ with independent values at $\exp v$, and "clearly" no non-trivial Jacobi field vanishes at both ends.

(i) $X \mapsto W_X$ is linear; each $W_X$ is a Jacobi field along $\gamma_v$, in $\mathcal J(\gamma_v)$ (V9.3), with $W_X(0) = 0$, $\frac{DW_X}{dt}(0) = X$ and $W_X(1) = d(\exp_q)_v(X)$. (ii) $X \mapsto W_X$ is injective, and every field of $\mathcal J(\gamma_v)$ vanishing at $0$ is a $W_X$. (iii) The fields of $\mathcal J(\gamma_v)$ vanishing at $0$ and $1$ are exactly the $W_X$ with $X \in \ker d(\exp_q)_v$; so the multiplicity of the conjugate parameters $0$ and $1$ along $\gamma_v$ (V9.4) is $\dim\ker d(\exp_q)_v$. (iv) Theorem 18.1: $0$ and $1$ are conjugate along $\gamma_v$ if and only if $\exp_q$ is critical at $v$. Hence $C(p) = \exp_p(\{v \in \mathcal D_p : \exp_p \text{ is critical at } v\})$, the set of critical values of $\exp_p$; if $N$ is geodesically complete, $\mathcal D_p = T_pN$. Book: p. 99: Corollary 18.2 "follows immediately from 18.1 together with Sard's theorem (6.1)". Hidden hypotheses: every geodesic from $p$ is a radial geodesic $t \mapsto \exp_p(tv)$ (uniqueness of geodesics, and the extension of a geodesic segment past its end points); without completeness, that the domain of $\exp_p$ is open (V11.1). Deviation (not in the book): the conjugate locus is named and identified as a set. Proof: $\gamma$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with $t \mapsto \exp_p(tv)$ (V9.9 (ii)), and Theorem 18.1 (V11.3) applies.

Milnor §18, Corollary 18.2

If $p \in M$, then for almost all $q \in M$, $p$ is not conjugate to $q$ along any geodesic. It follows "immediately from 18.1 together with Sard's theorem (6.1)".

Verified edition V11.5

Let $p \in N$, let $\sigma$ be a slice chart of $N$ (V1.6), and $\mu$ a Haar measure on $Z$. Then the image of $C(p) \cap \operatorname{dom}\sigma$ under the chart $y \mapsto \sigma(y)_1$ has $\mu$-measure $0$: $C(p)$ has measure zero in $N$. Book: p. 99, Corollary 18.2: for $p \in M$ and almost all $q \in M$, $p$ is not conjugate to $q$ along any geodesic. Hidden hypotheses: "measure zero" in a manifold is not defined in the book (Theorem 6.1, p. 33, uses the phrase for a manifold target); here it is read in charts. Proof: with $e : Z \to T_pN$ a linear isomorphism, the map $z \mapsto \sigma(\exp_p(e(z)))_1$ is $C^\infty$ on an open subset of $Z$, and the chart image of every point of $C(p) \cap \operatorname{dom}\sigma$ is a critical value of this map: a derivative that is not one-to-one stays so after composing, and a linear map of $Z$ to itself is onto iff it is one-to-one. Milnor §19, Lemma 19.1

Suppose that the sectional curvature of $M$ is everywhere $\le 0$, i.e. $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle \le 0$ for every pair of vectors $A, B$ in $TM_p$ and every $p$. Then no two points of $M$ are conjugate along any geodesic. Proof: $\langle\frac{D^2J}{dt^2}, J\rangle = -\langle R(V, J)V, J\rangle \ge 0$, so $\langle\frac{DJ}{dt}, J\rangle$ is monotonically increasing, strictly so unless $\frac{DJ}{dt} = 0$; if $J(0) = J(t_0) = 0$ it vanishes on $[0, t_0]$, so $J(0) = \frac{DJ}{dt}(0) = 0$ and $J \equiv 0$.

Verified edition V11.7

$N$ has non-positive curvature if $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle \le 0$ for all $A, B \in T_qN$ and all $q \in N$; equivalently, every sectional curvature of $N$ is $\le 0$. (i) For a smooth curve $\gamma$ in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ with velocity $V$ and a Jacobi field $J$ along it, $$\frac{d}{dt}\Big\langle\frac{DJ}{dt}, J\Big\rangle = \Big\|\frac{DJ}{dt}\Big\|^2 - \langle R(V, J)V, J\rangle \quad\text{on } (0, 1).$$ (ii) If $N$ has non-positive curvature and $\gamma$ is a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ which is a geodesic on $(0, 1)$, a Jacobi field along $\gamma$ vanishing at two parameters $a < b$ of $[0, 1]$ vanishes on $[0, 1]$; so no two parameters are conjugate along $\gamma$. Book: p. 100, Lemma 19.1: if $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle \le 0$ for every pair of vectors $A, B$ in $TM_p$ and every $p \in M$, no two points of $M$ are conjugate along any geodesic; proof: $\langle\frac{D^2J}{dt^2}, J\rangle = -\langle R(V, J)V, J\rangle \ge 0$, so $\langle\frac{DJ}{dt}, J\rangle$ is monotonically increasing, strictly so where $\frac{DJ}{dt} \ne 0$; if $J(0) = J(t_0) = 0$ it vanishes on $[0, t_0]$, so $J(0) = \frac{DJ}{dt}(0) = 0$ and $J \equiv 0$. Hidden hypotheses: $\frac{DJ}{dt}(0) = 0$ comes from $\frac{DJ}{dt} = 0$ on $(0, t_0)$ by continuity. Deviation (restated): any two parameters $a < b$ in $[0, 1]$ (Milnor: $0$ and $t_0$); conjugate parameters for points (V9.4). Deviation (stronger): (i) along any smooth curve.

the Ricci tensor and Milnor's Assertion

as in the book

to confirmThe Ricci tensor $K(U_1, U_2)$ is the trace of $W \mapsto R(U_1, W)U_2$; it is symmetric, and $K(U_n, U_n)$ is the sum of the sectional curvatures of the planes through $U_n$ and $U_i$.

the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §19, p. 104

Definition: the Ricci tensor at a point $p$ of a Riemannian manifold is the bilinear pairing $K : TM_p \times TM_p \to \mathbb R$, $K(U_1, U_2)$ the trace of the linear transformation $W \mapsto R(U_1, W)U_2$ of $TM_p$; "it follows easily from 9.3 that $K$ is symmetric". Assertion: for an orthonormal basis $U_1, \dots, U_n$ of $TM_p$, $K(U_n, U_n)$ is the sum of the sectional curvatures $\langle R(U_n, U_i)U_n, U_i\rangle$, $i = 1, \dots, n - 1$, because the $n$-th diagonal term of the matrix $(\langle R(U_n, U_i)U_n, U_j\rangle)$ is zero.

Verified edition V11.9

For $q \in N$ and $U_1, U_2 \in T_qN$, $K(U_1, U_2)$ is the trace of the linear map $W \mapsto R(U_1, W)U_2$ of $T_qN$. For an orthonormal basis $E_1, \dots, E_n$ of $T_qN$, $K(U_1, U_2) = \sum_i\langle R(U_1, E_i)U_2, E_i\rangle$, and $K(U_1, U_2) = K(U_2, U_1)$. Assertion: for an orthonormal basis $U_1, \dots, U_n$ of $T_qN$, $K(U_n, U_n) = \sum_{i \ne n}\langle R(U_n, U_i)U_n, U_i\rangle$, the sum of the sectional curvatures of the $n - 1$ planes spanned by $U_n$ and $U_i$. Book: p. 104, Definition: the Ricci tensor at $p$ is the bilinear pairing $K : TM_p \times TM_p \to \mathbb R$, $K(U_1, U_2)$ the trace of $W \mapsto R(U_1, W)U_2$; "it follows easily from 9.3 that $K$ is symmetric"; Assertion: $K(U_n, U_n)$ is the sum of the sectional curvatures $\langle R(U_n, U_i)U_n, U_i\rangle$, $i = 1, \dots, n - 1$, because the $n$-th diagonal term of the matrix $(\langle R(U_n, U_i)U_n, U_j\rangle)$ is zero. Hidden hypotheses: none. Proof: symmetry from the pair symmetry of Lemma 9.3 (4) (V6.21) in an orthonormal basis; the Assertion as Milnor's, with $R(U_n, U_n) = 0$.

In the proof of Theorem 19.4: for a geodesic $\gamma : [0, 1] \to M$ of length $L$, choose parallel vector fields $P_1, \dots, P_n$ along $\gamma$ which are orthonormal at one point, and hence everywhere, with $P_n$ pointing along $\gamma$, so that $V = \frac{d\gamma}{dt} = LP_n$ and $\frac{DP_i}{dt} = 0$.

Verified edition V11.10

Let $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ be a geodesic and $L = L(\gamma)$. (i) There are a $C^\infty$ curve $c : \mathbb R \to N$ equal to $\gamma$ on $[0, 1]$ and a $C^\infty$ field $V$ along $c$, tangent to $N$, equal to $\gamma'$ on $(0, 1)$, with $\|V(t)\| = L$ for all $t$ and $L^{-1}V$ parallel along $c$ (V6.8). (ii) If $L > 0$, there are a $C^\infty$ curve $c : \mathbb R \to N$ equal to $\gamma$ on $[0, 1]$, a $C^\infty$ field $V$ along $c$, tangent to $N$ and equal to $\gamma'$ on $(0, 1)$, and $n - 1$ parallel fields $P_1, \dots, P_{n-1}$ along $c$ with $\|P_i(t)\| = 1$, such that, for every $r$ for which $K(U, U) \ge (n - 1)/r^2$ for all unit vectors $U$ (V11.12), $\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\langle R(V, P_i)V, P_i\rangle \ge L^2(n - 1)/r^2$ at every $t$. Proof: $c$ is the radial geodesic of $\gamma'(0)$, defined near $[0, 1]$ (V9.9 (ii)), composed with a smooth map $\mathbb R \to (-\eta, 1 + \eta)$ that is the identity on $[0, 1]$; the $P_i$ are the parallel translates of an orthonormal basis of $T_{\gamma(0)}N$ containing $V(0)/L$, and the sum is $L^2K(V/L, V/L)$ by the Assertion.

the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §19, Theorem 19.4

(Myers.) Suppose that the Ricci curvature $K$ satisfies $K(U, U) \ge (n - 1)/r^2$ for every unit vector $U$ at every point of $M$, where $r$ is a positive constant. Then every geodesic on $M$ of length $> \pi r$ contains conjugate points, and hence is not minimal. On p. 105: $E_{**}(W_i, W_i) < 0$ makes the index of $\gamma$ positive, the index theorem gives conjugate points, and a variation with variation field $W_i$ decreases the energy.

Verified edition V11.12

Let $n \ge 2$, $r > 0$, and suppose $K(U, U) \ge (n - 1)/r^2$ for every unit vector $U \in T_qN$ and every $q \in N$. Then every geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ with $L(\gamma) > \pi r$ has a parameter $t \in (0, 1)$ conjugate to $0$, and is not minimal: some path of $\Omega(N; p, q)$ is shorter (V8.6). Book: p. 104, Theorem 19.4 (Myers): if $K(U, U) \ge (n - 1)/r^2$ for every unit vector $U$ at every point of $M$, $r$ a positive constant, every geodesic on $M$ of length $> \pi r$ contains conjugate points, and hence is not minimal; p. 105: $E_{}(W_i, W_i) < 0$ makes the index of $\gamma$ positive, and the index theorem gives conjugate points; a variation with field $W_i$ decreases the energy. Hidden hypotheses: $n \ge 2$: for $n = 1$ the Ricci tensor vanishes, the hypothesis holds for every $r$, and a segment of a line longer than $\pi r$ has no conjugate points and is minimal. Deviation (restated): "contains conjugate points" is "has a parameter in $(0, 1)$ conjugate to $0$"; minimality is among the paths of $\Omega(N; p, q)$ (V8.6). Proof: $E_{}$ is negative definite on the line through the $X$ of V11.11, so the index (V9.13) is positive, and the index theorem (V9.24) gives the conjugate parameter; Lemma 13.6 (V8.18) excludes minimality.

Milnor §19, proof of Theorem 19.6, p. 106

Since the space of all unit vectors $U$ on the compact $M$ is compact, the continuous function $K(U, U) > 0$ takes on a minimum, which can be denoted by $(n - 1)/r^2 > 0$. Then every geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(M; p, q)$ of length $> \pi r$ has index $\lambda \ge 1$; more generally one of length $> k\pi r$ has index $\lambda \ge k$, since $X_1, \dots, X_k$ span a $k$-dimensional subspace of $T\Omega_\gamma$ on which $E_{**}$ is negative definite.

If $L(\gamma) > k\pi r$, the index of $E_{}$ at $\gamma$ is at least $k$, and the parameters $t \in (0, 1)$ conjugate to $0$, counted with multiplicity, number at least $k$. Theorem 19.2, Cartan–Hadamard

as in the book

to confirmTheorem 19.2: a simply connected complete $N$ of curvature $\le 0$ has exactly one geodesic between any two points, and $\exp_p : T_pN \to N$ is a diffeomorphism.

the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §19, Theorem 19.2

(Cartan.) Suppose that $M$ is a simply connected, complete Riemannian manifold, and that the sectional curvature $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle$ is everywhere $\le 0$. Then any two points of $M$ are joined by a unique geodesic. Furthermore, $M$ is diffeomorphic to the Euclidean space $\mathbb R^n$. Proof (pp. 102–103): by the index theorem and 17.3, $\Omega(M; p, q)$ has the homotopy type of a $0$-dimensional complex with one vertex for each geodesic; it is connected since $M$ is simply connected, so there is precisely one geodesic from $p$ to $q$. Therefore $\exp_p : TM_p \to M$ is one-one and onto; by 18.1 it is non-critical, hence locally a diffeomorphism, hence a global diffeomorphism.

Verified edition V11.17

Let $N$ be geodesically complete (V7.22; for instance closed in $V$), simply connected (as a topological space) and of non-positive curvature (V11.7). Then any two points $p, q \in N$ are joined by a geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$, and every geodesic of $\Omega(N; p, q)$ agrees with $\gamma$ on $[0, 1]$; and $\exp_p : T_pN \to N$ is a diffeomorphism, so $N$ is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^n$, $n = \dim N$, for its manifold structure as a slice submanifold. Book: p. 102, Theorem 19.2 (Cartan): a simply connected complete $M$ with $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle \le 0$ has a unique geodesic between any two points and is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^n$; proof pp. 102–103: by 17.3 $\Omega(M; p, q)$ has the homotopy type of a connected $0$-dimensional complex, a point, so the geodesic is unique, $\exp_p$ is one-one and onto, non-critical by 18.1, hence a diffeomorphism. Hidden hypotheses: that a simply connected space is connected (needed for Hopf–Rinow); in Milnor's route, that the components of $\Omega$ are the homotopy classes of paths (Theorem 17.1). Deviation (restated): the order of the argument is reversed: $\exp_p$ is a covering (V11.19), injective because $N$ is simply connected (the image of a segment of $T_pN$ with both ends over one point is a null-homotopic loop, whose lift is closed), onto by Hopf–Rinow; uniqueness of geodesics follows. Both routes rest on Lemma 19.1.

If $M$ is complete with $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle \le 0$, then the homotopy groups $\pi_i(M)$ are zero for $i > 1$, and $\pi_1(M)$ contains no element of finite order other than the identity. If $M$ is a compact manifold, and if the Ricci tensor $K$ of $M$ is everywhere positive definite, then the path space $\Omega(M; p, q)$ has the homotopy type of a CW-complex having only finitely many cells in each dimension. Proof: by the index estimate a geodesic of length $> k\pi r$ has index $\ge k$; if $p$ and $q$ are not conjugate along any geodesic, then by 16.3 there are only finitely many geodesics of length $\le k\pi r$, hence only finitely many with index $< k$; together with 17.3 this completes the proof.

(i) If $N$ is compact, $n = \dim N \ge 2$ and the Ricci tensor is positive definite, there is $r > 0$ with $K(U, U) \ge (n - 1)/r^2$ for every unit tangent vector $U$. (ii) Under such a bound, a geodesic of index $\le d$ has energy $\le ((d + 1)\pi r)^2$. (iii) If $N$ is closed in $V$ with such a bound, or compact with positive definite Ricci tensor, and $q$ is not conjugate to $p$ along any geodesic ($q \notin C(p)$, V11.4), then $\Omega(N; p, q)$ has the homotopy type of a countable cell complex (VA.18) with only finitely many cells of each dimension. the algebraic model of a bi-invariant metric

to confirmA bi-invariant metric is modelled by a bilinear form on a Lie algebra, and its Levi-Civita connection on left-invariant fields by a bilinear $D$ with $D(X, Y) - D(Y, X) = [X, Y]$ and $B(D(X, Y), Z) + B(Y, D(X, Z)) = 0$.

Milnor §21, p. 113

Milnor works with the Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ of left-invariant vector fields on a Lie group $G$ with a left and right invariant metric, the bracket of vector fields, and the connection $X \vdash Y$ of the metric; Theorem 21.3 (a) is the identity $\langle[X, Y], Z\rangle = \langle X, [Y, Z]\rangle$.

Verified edition V12.1

$L$ is a real Lie algebra and $B : L \times L \to \mathbb R$ a bilinear form. $B$ is ad-invariant if $B([X, Y], Z) = B(X, [Y, Z])$ for all $X, Y, Z$; this is Mathlib's lieInvariant. A connection on left-invariant fields is a bilinear map $D : L \times L \to L$, $D(X, Y)$ standing for $X \vdash Y$; it is Levi-Civita for $B$ (Morse.IsLeviCivita) if $D(X, Y) - D(Y, X) = [X, Y]$ (Milnor's 8.5) and $B(D(X, Y), Z) + B(Y, D(X, Z)) = 0$ (Corollary 8.4 for fields whose inner products are constant), for all $X, Y, Z$. Book: p. 113: the Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ of left-invariant vector fields with the bracket, on a Lie group with a left and right invariant metric; 21.3 (a) is the identity $\langle[X, Y], Z\rangle = \langle X, [Y, Z]\rangle$. Hidden hypotheses: that $X \vdash Y$ is left-invariant when $X$ and $Y$ are, so that the connection restricts to a map $\mathfrak g \times \mathfrak g \to \mathfrak g$, which Milnor's computation of $R$ with (d) needs. Deviation (restated): the Lie group, its left-invariant fields and its metric are replaced by an abstract Lie algebra with a bilinear form; the geometric facts are hypotheses (V12.2, V12.3).

If the Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ of a Lie group $G$ with a bi-invariant metric has trivial centre, then $G$ is compact with finite fundamental group. Matrix groups. From here on $\mathbb K = \mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and $M_n(\mathbb K)$, the $n \times n$ matrices indexed by a finite set, carries the real inner product $\langle A, B\rangle = \operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(A^B)$ (Milnor's $\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(AB^)$ up to the order of the factors) and the Frobenius norm; $\exp$ is the matrix exponential, and $[X, Y] = XY - YX$. The groups are slice submanifolds of $M_n(\mathbb K)$ (V1.6) with the induced metric, so that geodesics (V7.1), the connection (V6.4), the curvature (V6.17) and Jacobi fields (V9.2) are those of Chapters 6–9.

Milnor §21, p. 112; §23, p. 125

A Lie group $G$ with a metric invariant under left and right translations; if $G$ is compact such a metric exists, by averaging any metric with the Haar measure (p. 112). For $U(n)$ the tangent space at $I$ is the space of skew-Hermitian matrices (p. 125, (6)).

Verified edition V12.14

Multiplication on either side by a unitary matrix is a linear isometry of $M_n(\mathbb K)$; Hermitian and skew-Hermitian matrices are orthogonal; $\exp$ is smooth and maps skew-Hermitian matrices to unitary ones. A matrix group is a pair $(G, \mathfrak g)$ of a slice submanifold $G \subseteq M_n(\mathbb K)$ and a real Lie subalgebra $\mathfrak g$ of $M_n(\mathbb K)$ such that every $g \in G$ is unitary, $G$ is closed under products and $g \mapsto g^$, every $X \in \mathfrak g$ is skew-Hermitian, $g\mathfrak gg^ \subseteq \mathfrak g$ and $\exp\mathfrak g \subseteq G$, and $\dim G = \dim\mathfrak g$. Then $T_gG = g\mathfrak g$ for every $g \in G$; left and right translations by elements of $G$ are linear isometries of $M_n(\mathbb K)$ carrying $G$ onto $G$, so the induced metric is bi-invariant; and the inner product restricted to $\mathfrak g$ is ad-invariant and positive definite, so V12.1–V12.13 apply to it. Book: p. 112: a Lie group with a metric invariant under left and right translations; for compact $G$ such a metric exists by averaging with the Haar measure; p. 125 (in §23): the tangent space of $U(n)$ at $I$ is the space of skew-Hermitian matrices. Hidden hypotheses: none at this level. Deviation (narrower): only groups given as matrices, with the induced metric; Milnor's abstract Lie groups, left-invariant fields and Haar averaging are not formalized. (Every compact Lie group is a matrix group by Peter–Weyl, which is not needed for §§23–24.) Proof: $g\mathfrak g \subseteq T_gG$ through the curves $t \mapsto g\exp(tX)$, and the dimensions agree.

Lemma 21.2 for matrix groups, and completeness

narrower

to confirmThe geodesics of a matrix group are the curves $t \mapsto g\exp(tX)$; those through $I$ are the one-parameter subgroups, and the group is complete.

matrix groupsacceleration computed, no Lemma 20.1
the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §21, Lemma 21.2

The geodesics $\gamma$ with $\gamma(0) = e$ are precisely the one-parameter subgroups of $G$. (By Corollary 20.2, p. 110, a symmetric space is complete.)

Verified edition V12.15

Let $(G, \mathfrak g)$ be a matrix group. For $g \in G$ and $X \in \mathfrak g$, $t \mapsto g\exp(tX)$ is a geodesic of $G$ on $\mathbb R$. Conversely a geodesic $\gamma$ of $G$ on a preconnected open set $s \ni t_0$ is $\gamma(t) = \gamma(t_0)\exp((t - t_0)X)$ on $s$ with $X = \gamma(t_0)^\gamma'(t_0) \in \mathfrak g$. (i) A geodesic $\gamma : \mathbb R \to G$ with $\gamma(0) = I$ satisfies $\gamma'(0) \in \mathfrak g$, $\gamma(t) = \exp(t\gamma'(0))$ and $\gamma(s + t) = \gamma(s)\gamma(t)$. (ii) A differentiable $\theta : \mathbb R \to G$ with $\theta(0) = I$ and $\theta(s + t) = \theta(s)\theta(t)$ is a geodesic. The Riemannian exponential at $g$ is $\exp_g(gX) = g\exp X$, and $G$ is geodesically complete (V7.22). *Book: p. 113, Lemma 21.2: the geodesics $\gamma$ with $\gamma(0) = e$ are precisely the one-parameter subgroups; p. 110, Corollary 20.2 (a symmetric space is complete). Hidden hypotheses: in Milnor's proof of (i), the passage from commensurable parameters to all of $\mathbb R$ "by continuity" needs the continuity of multiplication. Deviation (restated): for matrix groups; the proof does not go through Lemma 20.1. Proof: the acceleration $g\exp(tX)X^2$ is normal, $X^2$ being Hermitian; uniqueness of geodesics (V7.5) gives the converse; (ii) $\exp(-tX)\theta(t)$ has derivative $0$.

Theorem 20.5 for matrix groups: the Jacobi equation along a one-parameter subgroup

narrower

to confirmAlong $\exp(tA)$, $\exp(tA/2)U(t)\exp(tA/2)$ is a Jacobi field whenever $U'' + \tfrac14[[A, U], A] = 0$ in $\mathfrak g$.

one-parameter subgroups of matrix groupsno eigenbasismultiplicities: $SU(n)$ only (V14.18)
the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §20, Theorem 20.5

Let $\gamma$ be a geodesic in a locally symmetric manifold with $\gamma(0) = p$, $\gamma'(0) = V$, and $e_1, \dots, e_n$ the eigenvalues of $K_V(W) = R(V, W)V$. The conjugate points to $p$ along $\gamma$ are the $\gamma(\pi k/\sqrt{e_i})$, $k$ a non-zero integer, $e_i > 0$; the multiplicity of $\gamma(t)$ is the number of $e_i$ such that $t$ is a multiple of $\pi/\sqrt{e_i}$. Proof (p. 111): in a parallel orthonormal eigenframe the Jacobi equation is $w_i'' + e_iw_i = 0$.

Verified edition V12.18

Let $(G, \mathfrak g)$ be a matrix group, $A \in \mathfrak g$, $\gamma(t) = \exp(tA)$ and $h(t) = \exp(tA/2)$. For a differentiable $\mathfrak g$-valued $U$, the covariant derivative of $t \mapsto h(t)U(t)h(t)$ along $\gamma$ is $hU'h$, and $R(\gamma', hMh)\gamma' = h\,K_A(M)\,h$ for $M \in \mathfrak g$, $K_A(M) = \tfrac14[[A, M], A]$. Hence, if $U$ is a smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued curve with $U'' + K_A(U) = 0$, then $J = hUh$ is a Jacobi field along $\gamma$, with $\frac{DJ}{dt}(0) = U'(0)$. Book: p. 110, Theorem 20.5: in a locally symmetric space the conjugate points along $\gamma$ are the $\gamma(\pi k/\sqrt{e_i})$, $e_i > 0$ an eigenvalue of $K_V(W) = R(V, W)V$, with multiplicity the number of $e_i$ for which $t$ is a multiple of $\pi/\sqrt{e_i}$; proof p. 111: in a parallel eigenframe the Jacobi equation becomes $w_i'' + e_iw_i = 0$. Hidden hypotheses: that $K_V$ is self-adjoint, so that an orthonormal eigenbasis exists (Lemma 9.3). Deviation (narrower): only along one-parameter subgroups of matrix groups, and only the implication from the constant-coefficient equation to Jacobi fields; the parallel frame is $U \mapsto hUh$, so no eigenbasis is chosen. The count of conjugate points with their multiplicities is proved for $SU(n)$ only (V14.18).

to confirmTheorem 22.1: if the closed balls about $p$ are compact, every geodesic not of least energy has index $\ge \lambda_0$, and $\Omega^d$ is a retract of an open neighbourhood, then every map of a compact $P$ of dimension $< \lambda_0$ into $\Omega$ is homotopic, relative to the part already in $\Omega^d$, to a map into $\Omega^d$.

the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §22, Theorem 22.1

If the space $\Omega^d$ of minimal geodesics from $p$ to $q$ is a topological manifold, and if every non-minimal geodesic from $p$ to $q$ has index $\ge \lambda_0$, then $\pi_i(\Omega, \Omega^d) = 0$ for $0 \le i < \lambda_0$. ($M$ is complete throughout §22; proof pp. 122–123.)

Verified edition V13.2

Let $p, q \in N$, let the closed Riemannian balls about $p$ be compact, and let $\lambda_0 \ge 0$ be an integer such that every geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega$ which is not of least energy has index $\ge \lambda_0$. Suppose $\Omega^d$ is a retract of an open neighbourhood: there are an open $O \supseteq \Omega^d$ and a map $\rho : O \to \Omega^d$, continuous on $O$, equal to the identity on $\Omega^d$. Let $P$ be a compact space with a continuous injection into a real vector space of dimension $< \lambda_0$. Then every map $h : P \to \Omega$ is homotopic, relative to $h^{-1}(\Omega^d)$, to a map into $\Omega^d$; equivalently, the inclusion $\Omega^d \to \Omega$ compresses maps from $P$. Book: p. 118, Theorem 22.1: if $\Omega^d$ is a topological manifold and every non-minimal geodesic from $p$ to $q$ has index $\ge \lambda_0$, then $\pi_i(\Omega, \Omega^d) = 0$ for $0 \le i < \lambda_0$; proof pp. 122–123. Hidden hypotheses: $M$ complete (the standing assumption of §22); the meaning of $\pi_i(\Omega, \Omega^d) = 0$ for $i = 0, 1$, where these are sets. Deviation (narrower): the manifold hypothesis is replaced by the neighbourhood retraction, which is all the proof uses of it; for a manifold it follows from Hanner's theorem (in the metrizable manifold $B$ of broken geodesics, composed with Milnor's $r_1$), which is not formalized. For the sphere and for $SU(2m)$ the retraction is constructed (V13.8, V14.21). Deviation (stronger): relative to the whole part of $P$ already mapped into $\Omega^d$, at all base points, for every such $P$. Proof: Milnor's, through the finite-dimensional model (V10.4–V10.11): the energy is bounded on the compact image; Milnor's deformation $r_u$ (V10.7) moves $h$ into the broken geodesics, fixing $\Omega^d$, which consists of unbroken geodesics (V13.1); the manifold of break points carries the energy as a smooth function with compact sublevel sets, whose critical points off the minimum have index $\ge \lambda_0$ by Theorem 16.2 (V10.11); Lemma 22.5 below a level (V13.14) with the neighbourhood of V13.15 pushes the map into the minimum; the result is moved back to $\Omega$, corrected on paths at distance $0$. No reparametrization $F \circ E$ is needed, since V13.14 needs only one compact sublevel set.

Let $K$ be a compact subset of an open $U \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ and $f : U \to \mathbb R$ smooth, all of whose critical points in $K$ have index $\ge \lambda_0$. If $g : U \to \mathbb R$ is smooth and its first and second partial derivatives are within $\varepsilon$ of those of $f$ uniformly on $K$, $\varepsilon$ small, then every critical point of $g$ in $K$ has index $\ge \lambda_0$. Verified edition V13.10

Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, $U \subseteq E$ open, $K \subseteq U$ compact, $f : E \to \mathbb R$ of class $C^2$ on $U$, and suppose every critical point of $f$ in $K$ has index $\ge \lambda_0$ (critical points may be degenerate). The geometry and the topology. From here on $U(n)$, $SU(n)$ are the matrix groups of Chapter 12 (V12.14) inside $M_n(\mathbb C)$ with the Frobenius inner product, $\Omega = \Omega(SU(n); I, -I)$ is Milnor's path space with his metric (V10.1, Chapter 13), $\Omega^d$ its subset of paths of least energy (V13.1), and homotopy groups and pushing maps are as in Chapter 13. A Hermitian projection is a matrix $P$ with $P^* = P = P^2$; $G_m(\mathbb C^n)$ is the set of Hermitian projections of trace $m$ with the subspace topology (the projections onto the $m$-dimensional subspaces). A Stiefel manifold $V_k(\mathbb K^n)$ is the set of $n \times k$ matrices $F$ with $F^*F = I$ (orthonormal $k$-frames), with the subspace topology. Locally trivial maps, Serre fibrations and their exact homotopy sequences are those of Part XII of the proof-by-proof edition (Morse.Homotopy.IsLocallyTrivial, Morse.Homotopy.IsSerreFibration).

By Theorem 20.5 the conjugate points along $t \mapsto \exp tA$ are determined by the eigenvalues of $K_A(W) = \frac14[[A, W], A]$: an eigenvalue $e > 0$ gives conjugate points at the multiples of $\pi/\sqrt e$, the multiplicity counting the eigenvalues; "adding over all $j, l$".

Verified edition V14.18

Let $a \in \mathbb R^n$, $T$ unitary, $A = T\operatorname{diag}(ia_j)T^* \in \mathfrak{su}(n)$, $s_b(t) = \sin(bt)/b$ ($= t$ for $b = 0$), and $S(t) \odot W$ the matrix with entries $s_{(a_j - a_l)/2}(t)w_{jl}$. Any non-minimal geodesic from $I$ to $-I$ in $O(2m)$ has index $\ge 2m - 2$. If $J_1, \dots, J_k$ are anticommuting complex structures on $\mathbb R^n$, then for every $u$, $\langle J_\alpha u, J_\beta u\rangle = \delta_{\alpha\beta}|u|^2$ and $\langle J_\alpha u, u\rangle = 0$; so for $|u| = 1$ the $J_\alpha u$ are $k$ orthonormal vectors tangent to the unit sphere at $u$. This is written out for the eight structures of V15.9 on $\mathbb R^{16r}$ (eight fields on $S^{16r-1}$), and the general statement applies to the block-diagonal families on $\mathbb R^{4r}$ and $\mathbb R^{8r}$ built from V15.9 (three and seven fields). Book: pp. 143–144, Remark: for anticommuting $J_1, \dots, J_k$ on a space of dimension $rm_k$, the vectors $J_1u, \dots, J_ku$ are perpendicular to each other and to $u$, giving $k$ linearly independent vector fields on the $(rm_k - 1)$-sphere: $3$ on $S^{4r-1}$, $7$ on $S^{8r-1}$, $8$ on $S^{16r-1}$ (Hurwitz–Radon; Adams showed these are best possible). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (narrower): the identities only (the fields are linear in $u$, hence continuous); the general Hurwitz–Radon count and Adams's theorem are not formalized.

to confirmIf $x\exp A \in N$ and $A \in T_{x\exp A}$ for $A \in T_x$, with $\dim T_x = \dim N$, then the geodesics of $N$ are exactly the curves $t \mapsto x\exp(tA)$, $A \in T_x$, and $N$ is complete.

the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor §24, footnote, p. 136; p. 137

A submanifold of a Riemannian manifold is called totally geodesic if each geodesic in the submanifold is also a geodesic in the larger manifold. The description of $\Omega_k(n)$ near $J$ as the points $J\exp A$, $A$ in a linear subspace, "clearly implies" that $\Omega_k(n)$ is a totally geodesic submanifold of $O(n)$.

Verified edition V15.21

Let $N \subseteq M_n(\mathbb R)$ be a slice submanifold consisting of orthogonal matrices, and for each $x \in N$ let $T_x$ be a space of skew matrices with $\dim T_x = \dim N$, such that $x\exp A \in N$ and $A \in T_{x\exp A}$ whenever $A \in T_x$. Then: (i) the tangent space of $N$ at $x$ is $x\,T_x$; (ii) for $A \in T_x$ the curve $t \mapsto x\exp(tA)$ is a geodesic of $N$ on all of $\mathbb R$; (iii) every unbroken geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with $s \mapsto p\exp(sV)$ for some $V \in T_p$; (iv) the Riemannian exponential of $N$ is $\exp_x(xA) = x\exp A$ for $A \in T_x$, and $N$ is geodesically complete. Also, as a tool for V15.23: let $S$ be a subset of a real normed space $V$ such that near each $x \in S$ there is a smooth $\Phi : Z \times W \to V$ ($Z$, $W$ finite-dimensional) with $\Phi(0) = x$ and invertible derivative at $0$, for which, near $0$, the points $\Phi(z, 0)$ lie in $S$ and every point $\Phi(q) \in S$ equals $\Phi(g(q), 0)$ with $g(q) \to 0$ as $q \to 0$; then $S$ is a slice submanifold modelled on $Z$. Book: p. 136, footnote: a submanifold is totally geodesic if each of its geodesics is a geodesic of the larger manifold; p. 137: the description of $\Omega_k(n)$ near $J$ "clearly implies" that it is a totally geodesic submanifold of $O(n)$. Hidden hypotheses: "clearly" needs an argument (the exposition's Lemma 2.2). Deviation (restated): "totally geodesic" is not used as a definition, and the geodesics of $N$ are not compared with those of $O(n)$; what Milnor draws from it, the list (ii)–(iii) of the geodesics of $N$, is proved directly. Proof: the acceleration of $t \mapsto x\exp(tA)$ is $yA^2$, $y = x\exp(tA)$; $A^2$ is symmetric, hence $yA^2$ is orthogonal to the tangent space $y\,T_y$, which consists of $y$ times skew matrices; so the curve is a geodesic of the submanifold $N$, and (iii) follows by the uniqueness of geodesics.

For small skew $A$: $J\exp A$ is a complex structure if and only if $A$ anticommutes with $J$; $J\exp A$ anticommutes with $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}$ if and only if $A$ commutes with them. For a matrix $x$ let $\mathcal T_x$ be the space of skew matrices $A$ with $Ax = -xA$ and $AJ_\alpha = J_\alpha A$ for $1 \le \alpha \le k - 1$; for $k = 0$ the first condition is dropped, so that $\mathcal T_x$ is the space $\mathfrak o(n)$ of all skew matrices, the same for every $x$. The stratum of $\Omega_k(n)$ through a matrix $p$ is the set of $x \in \Omega_k(n)$ with $\dim\mathcal T_x = \dim\mathcal T_p$. (ii) The stratum is open in $\Omega_k(n)$ (each of its points has a neighbourhood in $M_n(\mathbb R)$ whose points in $\Omega_k(n)$ belong to it), closed in $M_n(\mathbb R)$, and compact. (iii) It is a slice submanifold of $M_n(\mathbb R)$ modelled on $\mathcal T_p$, and it satisfies the hypotheses of V15.21 with $T_x = \mathcal T_x$. Consequently its tangent space at $x$ is $x\mathcal T_x$, its geodesics are the curves $t \mapsto x\exp(tA)$ with $A \in \mathcal T_x$, and it is geodesically complete. Book: p. 136, Lemma 24.4: each $\Omega_k(n)$ is a smooth, totally geodesic submanifold of $O(n)$; p. 139: $\Omega_3(16r)$ "contains components of varying dimension" (and p. 141 for $\Omega_7(16r)$). Hidden hypotheses: as the components of $\Omega_k(n)$ may have different dimensions, the lemma must be read on each component separately. Deviation (restated): on the stratum through $p$, which is open and closed in $\Omega_k(n)$, hence a union of components, among them that of $p$ when $p \in \Omega_k(n)$; as a submanifold of $M_n(\mathbb R)$ rather than of $O(n)$; and with "totally geodesic" in the sense of V15.21. Proof: near a point $x$ of the stratum, $(a, w) \mapsto x(\exp a + w)$, $a \in \mathcal T_x$, $w \in \mathcal T_x^\perp$, is a parametrization as in V15.21, by V15.22 (iii) and (i).

In the block normal form with $a_1, \dots, a_m \ge 0$: $\exp(\pi A) = -I$ if and only if $a_1, \dots, a_m$ are odd integers; $\langle A, A\rangle = 2(a_1^2 + \dots + a_m^2)$; therefore the geodesic $\exp(\pi tA)$ from $I$ to $-I$ is minimal if and only if $a_1 = \dots = a_m = 1$, and then $A^2 = -I$.

Let $V$ be a skew matrix with $\exp V = -I$. If $E \neq 0$ is a matrix and $V^2E = -\lambda E$ for a real $\lambda$, then $\lambda \ge \pi^2$. Hence $\|V\|^2 \ge \pi^2n$, and if $\|V\|^2 \le \pi^2n$ then $V^2 = -\pi^2I$. That this bound describes the minimal geodesics is V15.25.

Since $\Omega_k(n)$ is a totally geodesic submanifold of $O(n)$, $K_A$ can be computed by $K_AB = -\tfrac14[A, [A, B]]$ on $T$. Each eigenvalue $e^2$ of $K_A$ gives rise to conjugate points for $t = e^{-1}, 2e^{-1}, 3e^{-1}, \dots$ by 20.5; then apply the index theorem.

Let $J_1, \dots, J_k$ be an anticommuting family, $p \in \Omega_k(n)$, $N$ the stratum through $p$, and $V \in \mathcal T_p$. The isotropy algebra of $p$ is the space of skew matrices commuting with $p$ and with $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}$. (i) For $X$ in the isotropy algebra, $K(t) = X\gamma(t) - \gamma(t)X$ is a Jacobi field along $\gamma(t) = p\exp(tV)$ in $N$. (ii) Let $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ be an unbroken geodesic equal to $t \mapsto p\exp(tV)$ on $[0, 1]$, let $\tau \in [0, 1]$, and let $\mathcal X$ be a subspace of the isotropy algebra whose elements commute with $\exp(\tau V)$ and none of whose non-zero elements commutes with $V$. Then $\gamma(\tau)$ is conjugate to $\gamma(0)$ along $\gamma$ with multiplicity (V9.4) at least $\dim\mathcal X$. (iii) For a finite set $T \subset (0, 1)$ and such subspaces $\mathcal X_\tau$, $\tau \in T$, the index of $\gamma$ is at least $\sum_{\tau \in T}\dim\mathcal X_\tau$. Hidden hypotheses: that the curvature of a totally geodesic submanifold is that of the ambient manifold, and Theorem 20.5 for the components of $\Omega_k(n)$. Deviation (restated): neither is formalized, and neither is needed for a lower bound, which only asks for Jacobi fields vanishing at $0$ and at $\tau$. These come from the isometries $y \mapsto gyg^{-1}$, $g = \exp(uX)$, of $N$, which fix $p$: $K$ is the variation field of the geodesics $t \mapsto g\,p\exp(tV)\,g^{-1}$ (Lemma 14.3, V9.8), and it vanishes at $\tau$ when $X$ commutes with $\exp(\tau V)$. (iii) is the Index Theorem (V9.24).

$\mathbb R^n = M_1 \oplus \dots \oplus M_s$, mutually orthogonal subspaces closed and minimal under the action of $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}$, $J$ and $A$. The eigenvalues of $A$ on $M_h$ "must be all equal, except for sign": $\pm ia_h$, with $a_h$ odd and positive. $J' = a_h^{-1}JA|M_h$ makes $M_h$ a minimal $(J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}, J, J')$-space, so $\dim M_h = m_{k+1}$ and $s = n/m_{k+1}$. Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and $\mathcal G$ a set of operators on $E$, each self-adjoint or skew-adjoint. A subspace is minimal invariant if it is non-zero, invariant under $\mathcal G$, and contains no invariant subspace other than $0$ and itself. (i) Every invariant subspace $U$ is spanned by a list of pairwise orthogonal minimal invariant subspaces of $U$ whose dimensions add up to $\dim U$; and a self-adjoint operator that commutes with $\mathcal G$ and preserves a minimal invariant $M$ is a scalar on $M$. (ii) Let $A$ be skew-adjoint, let $J, J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}$ be skew-adjoint operators with square $-1$, anticommuting with one another, and let $A$ anticommute with $J$ and commute with the $J_\alpha$ (for $k = 0$: $J = 1$ and there are no $J_\alpha$); put $\mathcal G = \{A, J, J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}\}$. On each minimal invariant $M$, $A^2 = -c$ for a real $c$; and for real $s$ with $s^2c = 1$ the restrictions of $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}, J, sJA$ to $M$ satisfy the Clifford relations (V15.10) and make $M$ a minimal space for $k + 1$ structures (V15.13). For matrices: if $A$ is skew, $\exp(\pi A) = -I$, and $A^2 = -c$ on a non-zero subspace of $\mathbb R^n$, then $c \ge 1$. (iii) If $k \le 7$, $k \not\equiv 2 \pmod 4$, and $M_0$, $M_1$ are minimal invariant with $A^2 = -a_0^2$ on $M_0$ and $A^2 = -b^2$ on $M_1$, $a_0, b > 0$, there is a linear isomorphism $T : M_0 \to M_1$ that commutes with $J$ and the $J_\alpha$ and carries $a_0^{-1}JA$ to $-b^{-1}JA$. (iv) If moreover $c \ge 1$ on every minimal invariant subspace and $A^2 \neq -1$, then in a splitting (i) of $E$ some piece $M_0$ has $c > 1$; and there are an integer $s$ with $(s + 1)m_{k+1} = \dim E$, reals $a_0 > 1$ and $b_1, \dots, b_s \ge 1$, and operators $D_1, \dots, D_s$ on $E$ (each the projection onto $M_0$ followed by an isomorphism (iii) onto another piece) which commute with $J$ and the $J_\alpha$, satisfy $b_jD_jA = -a_0AD_j$, $A^2D_j = -b_j^2D_j$ and $D_jA^2 = -a_0^2D_j$, and for which the $AD_j$ are separated by projections (for $k = 0$ there are two for each $j$, $D_j$ and $D_jA$). Deviation (restated): $a_h = \sqrt c$; that the $a_h$ are odd integers is not used, only $c \ge 1$. Milnor §24, pp. 147–148

$f$ maps the geodesic into a closed loop on $S^1$ "which is completely determined by the trace of $A$. It follows that this trace is invariant under homotopy of the geodesic within the path space". Then: "restrict attention to some fixed component of $\Omega\Omega_k(n)$".

Verified edition V15.33

Let $F$ be a complex-valued function on a finite-dimensional real inner product space $V$ and $\omega : \mathbb R \to V$. An angle of $F \circ \omega$ is a continuous $\theta : [0, 1] \to \mathbb R$ with $\theta(0) = 0$ and $F(\omega(t)) = e^{i\theta(t)}$ for $t \in [0, 1]$. An angle is unique, and it exists whenever $t \mapsto F(\omega(t))$ is continuous on $[0, 1]$, of modulus $1$, with $F(\omega(0)) = 1$. For $N \subseteq V$, points $p$, $q$ and a real $w$, let $\Omega_w \subseteq \Omega(N; p, q)$ be the set of paths $\omega$ for which $F \circ \omega$ has an angle with $\theta(1) = w$. If $F$ is continuous and $|F| = 1$ on a compact set containing $N$, every $\Omega_w$ is open and closed in $\Omega(N; p, q)$; and $\Omega_w$, $\Omega_{w'}$ are disjoint for $w \neq w'$. Book: p. 147: $f$ maps the geodesic into a closed loop on $S^1$ "which is completely determined by the trace of $A$", and "this trace is invariant under homotopy of the geodesic within the path space"; p. 148: "restrict attention to some fixed component of $\Omega\Omega_k(n)$". Hidden hypotheses: Theorem 22.1 is applied to one class of paths, which must then be open and closed in the path space (V13.16). Deviation (restated): the classes $\Omega_w$ in place of components. Proof: paths that are close in Milnor's metric are uniformly close on $[0, 1]$; then $|F \circ \omega' - F \circ \omega| < 1$, the quotient $F \circ \omega'/F \circ \omega$ has positive real part, and adding its argument to the angle of $\omega$ gives the angle of $\omega'$, with the same end value.

(i) A $16 \times 16$ matrix that commutes with $J'_1, \dots, J'_7$ is $b\,I + c\,W$ for real $b$, $c$, where $W = 1 \otimes 1 \otimes 1 \otimes \tau$ in the notation of V15.9. (ii) With $P_\pm = \tfrac12(1 \pm W)$ and $q(U, V) = P_+ \otimes U + P_- \otimes V$ for $r \times r$ matrices $U$, $V$: every matrix on $\mathbb R^{16r}$ that commutes with $J_1, \dots, J_7$ (V15.41) is $q(U, V)$ for some $U$, $V$. (iii) $\Omega_8(16r)$, for the structures of V15.41, is homeomorphic to $O(r)$: $J$ corresponds to the $U$ with $-J_8J = q(U, U^{\mathsf T})$, and $U$ to $J_8\,q(U, U^{\mathsf T})$; the base point $J_8$ corresponds to $I$. Book: pp. 141–142, Lemma 24.6 (8): $\Omega_8(16r)$ can be identified with the set of all real isometries from $X_1$ to $X_2$, through $J_7J_8$; "Thus we see that $\Omega_8(16r)$ is diffeomorphic to the orthogonal group $O(r)$". Deviation (restated): Milnor's $X_1$, $X_2$ are replaced by the commutant of $J_1, \dots, J_7$: for $J \in \Omega_8(16r)$, $-J_8J$ commutes with $J_1, \dots, J_7$, and the conditions on $q(U, V)$ are that $U$ be orthogonal and $V = U^{\mathsf T}$. Deviation (narrower): a homeomorphism, not a diffeomorphism, and for the explicit structures. The other parts of Lemma 24.6 remain as in V15.11–V15.12. Proof of (i): the $256$ Kronecker words in $1, \sigma, \tau, \kappa$ form a basis of the $16 \times 16$ matrices, each word commutes or anticommutes with each $J'_\alpha$, and a finite check shows that only $1$ and $W$ commute with all seven.

Appendix (Milnor pp. 149–153)

378VA.1

homotopy equivalences

to confirmA homotopy equivalence is a map with a two-sided homotopy inverse; a map with a left and a right homotopy inverse is one.

the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor

No comparison row for this item; the Book note on the right gives the page.

Verified edition VA.1

A map $f : X \to Y$ is a homotopy equivalence if there is a map $g : Y \to X$ with $gf \simeq \mathrm{id}_X$ and $fg \simeq \mathrm{id}_Y$. A composite of homotopy equivalences is one; a map homotopic to a homotopy equivalence is one; a homotopy inverse is one; and a map with a left homotopy inverse and a right homotopy inverse is a homotopy equivalence. If $f$ carries $A \subseteq X$ into $B \subseteq Y$, $f|A : A \to B$ is its restriction. Book: p. 22, Assertion: if a map $F$ has a left homotopy inverse $L$ and a right homotopy inverse $R$, then $F$ is a homotopy equivalence; p. 153 refers to it ("compare page 22"). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (not in the book): the closure properties, used throughout without comment.

the telescope and homotopy direct limits

hypotheses explicit

to confirmThe telescope is $X_\Sigma = \bigcup_nX_n \times [n, n + 1] \subseteq X \times \mathbb R$, and $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of $\{X_i\}$ when $(x, \tau) \mapsto x$ is a homotopy equivalence; raising $\tau$ stays in $X_\Sigma$.

Milnor's definition verbatim(T1), used without comment
the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor Appendix, p. 149

For a topological space $X$ and a sequence $X_0 \subset X_1 \subset X_2 \subset \cdots$ of subspaces, it is convenient to consider the infinite union $X_\Sigma = X_0 \times [0, 1] \cup X_1 \times [1, 2] \cup X_2 \times [2, 3] \cup \cdots$, "to be topologized as a subset of $X \times \mathbb R$". Definition: $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of the sequence $\{X_i\}$ if the projection map $p : X_\Sigma \to X$, $p(x, \tau) = x$, is a homotopy equivalence.

Verified edition VA.2

For subsets $X_0, X_1, \dots$ of $X$, the telescope is $X_\Sigma = \bigcup_n X_n \times [n, n + 1] \subseteq X \times \mathbb R$, with the subspace topology; the $n$-th strip is the map $X_n \times [0, 1] \to X_\Sigma$, $(x, t) \mapsto (x, n + t)$; $p : X_\Sigma \to X$ is $p(x, \tau) = x$; and $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of $\{X_i\}$ if $p$ is a homotopy equivalence. (T1) For a monotone sequence, $(x, \tau) \in X_\Sigma$ iff $x \in X_n$ for some integer $n \ge 0$ with $n \le \tau$; so $(x, \tau) \in X_\Sigma$ and $\tau' \ge \tau$ give $(x, \tau') \in X_\Sigma$. Book: p. 149: for subspaces $X_0 \subset X_1 \subset \cdots$, the infinite union $X_\Sigma = X_0 \times [0, 1] \cup X_1 \times [1, 2] \cup \cdots$, "to be topologized as a subset of $X \times \mathbb R$"; Definition: $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of $\{X_i\}$ if $p : X_\Sigma \to X$, $p(x, \tau) = x$, is a homotopy equivalence. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (not in the book): (T1), used without comment.

(T3) pasting along the strips

not in the book

to confirmIf the $X_n$ are closed, a map on $X_\Sigma$ (or $P \times X_\Sigma$) continuous on each strip is continuous.

the hidden closedness hypothesisstrips closed, locally finite
the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor Appendix, pp. 151–153

The book has no such statement. Every map and homotopy on a telescope in the proof of Theorem A (pp. 151–153) is given strip by strip, by formulas in $(x, n + t)$, $0 \le t \le 1$, and its continuity is taken for granted.

Verified edition VA.3

If every $X_n$ is closed in $X$, then for every space $P$ a function $F$ on $P \times X_\Sigma$ is continuous as soon as each $(p, x, t) \mapsto F(p, (x, n + t))$ is continuous on $P \times X_n \times [0, 1]$. Hence, for a monotone sequence of closed sets, maps $\Phi_n : P \times X_n \times [0, 1] \to Z$ with $\Phi_{n+1}(p, x, 0) = \Phi_n(p, x, 1)$ define a continuous map $P \times X_\Sigma \to Z$, $(p, (x, n + t)) \mapsto \Phi_n(p, x, t)$; in particular maps $X_\Sigma \to Z$, and homotopies between them, may be given strip by strip. Book: every map and homotopy on a telescope in the proof of Theorem A (pp. 151–153) is given strip by strip, by formulas in $(x, n + t)$, $0 \le t \le 1$. Hidden hypotheses: closedness of the $X_n$, which Milnor never states; then the strips are closed in $X_\Sigma$ and form a locally finite family. Deviation (not in the book): stated and proved as a lemma.

Example 1, and sublevel sets

to confirmExample 1 holds for paracompact Hausdorff $X$; sublevel sets $\{E \le a_i\}$ of a continuous $E$ with $a_i \to \infty$ need no paracompactness.

sublevel sets: no paracompactnessHausdorff, for partitions of unity
the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor Appendix, Example 1

Suppose that each point of $X$ lies in the interior of some $X_i$, and that $X$ is paracompact. Then using a partition of unity one can construct a map $f : X \to \mathbb R$ so that $f(x) \ge i + 1$ for $x \notin X_i$ and $f(x) \ge 0$ for all $x$; and $X$ is a homotopy direct limit.

Verified edition VA.7

(i) Let $X$ be paracompact and Hausdorff, and $X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \cdots$ with every point of $X$ in the interior of some $X_i$. Then $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of $\{X_i\}$. (ii) Let $E : X \to \mathbb R$ be continuous, on any space $X$, and $a_0 \le a_1 \le \cdots$ with $a_i \to \infty$. Then $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of the sublevel sets $\{x : E(x) \le a_i\}$. Book: p. 149, Example 1: if each point of $X$ lies in the interior of some $X_i$ and $X$ is paracompact, a partition of unity gives $f : X \to \mathbb R$ with $f(x) \ge i + 1$ for $x \notin X_i$ and $f \ge 0$, and $X$ is a homotopy direct limit. Hidden hypotheses: Hausdorff: Mathlib's partitions of unity need a normal space, and Milnor's "paracompact" is read with the Hausdorff axiom. Deviation (stronger): (ii) needs no paracompactness; it covers the sublevel sets of the energy in Theorem 17.3, where Milnor uses Example 1 and the paracompactness of a metric space. Proof: (i) $f = \sum_ii\,\varphi_i$ for a partition of unity $\{\varphi_i\}$ subordinate to $\{\operatorname{int}X_i\}$, then VA.6 (i); (ii) $f = \sum_j\min(1, \max(0, E - a_j + 1))$, locally a finite sum.

Verified edition VA.9

Let $X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \cdots$ be closed in $X$. (i) For a map $\rho : I \to I$ with $\rho(0) = 0$ and $\rho(1) = 1$, $(x, n + t) \mapsto (x, n + \rho(t))$ is homotopic to the identity of $X_\Sigma$; in particular so is $R_c(x, n + t) = (x, n + \min(ct, 1))$, $c \ge 1$. (ii) Let $\psi : X_\Sigma \to X_\Sigma$ be a map with $\psi(x, n + t) = (x, n + 2t)$ for $t \le \frac12$ and $\psi(x, n + t)$ at level $n + 1$ for $t \ge \frac12$. Then $\psi$ fixes the points at integer levels, and it is a homotopy equivalence, with homotopy inverse Milnor's $g$: $g(x, n + t) = (x, n + 2t)$ for $t \le \frac12$ and $\psi(x, n + \frac32 - t)$ for $t \ge \frac12$. Hidden hypotheses: the $X_n$ closed (VA.3); the formula for $h_1g$ uses that $h_1$ fixes the integer levels. the mapping telescope

not in the book

to confirmThe mapping telescope of $K_0 \to K_1 \to \cdots$ is the homotopy direct limit of its closed truncations, each homotopy equivalent to the corresponding $K_n$.

pasting with no closednessstands for a union of complexes
the full statement, Milnor beside Lean

Milnor Appendix, pp. 149–153

The book has no such construction. The Appendix works with the telescope $X_\Sigma$ of a sequence of subspaces of one space $X$, and the application to Theorem 17.3 with a union $K = \bigcup K_i$ of complexes $K_0 \subset K_1 \subset \cdots$.

Verified edition VA.13

For a sequence of spaces and maps $K_0 \xrightarrow{c_0} K_1 \xrightarrow{c_1} \cdots$, the mapping telescope $T$ is the quotient of the disjoint union of the blocks $K_n \times [0, 1]$ by $(k, 1)_n \sim (c_n(k), 0)_{n+1}$, with the quotient topology; $(k, t)_n$ is at level $n + t$, a continuous function on $T$. Maps out of $T$, and out of $P \times T$ for a locally compact $P$ (for homotopies, $P = I$), may be given block by block, compatibly with the gluing, with no closedness condition. The truncations $T_n = \{\text{level} \le n\}$ are closed and increasing, and $T$ is the homotopy direct limit of $\{T_n\}$; $k \mapsto (k, 0)_n$ is an embedding $K_n \to T$ and a homotopy equivalence $K_n \to T_n$. Book: not in the book; the exposition's proof of the Corollary uses it. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (not in the book): the device that removes the closedness hypotheses (VA.15) and replaces a union of complexes that are not subspaces of one space (VA.16, VA.17). Proof: the product of a quotient map with a locally compact space is a quotient map; the homotopy inverse of $K_n \to T_n$ reads off the point reached by pushing each point of $T_n$ up to level $n$ along the maps $c_m$, and is continuous because $K_n \to T$ is an embedding; $T$ is a homotopy direct limit by VA.6 (i) with $f = \text{level} + 1$.

Let $X$ be the homotopy direct limit of $X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \cdots$ and $Y$ that of $Y_0 \subseteq Y_1 \subseteq \cdots$, arbitrary subsets, and let $f : X \to Y$ carry each $X_i$ into $Y_i$ by a homotopy equivalence $f_i = f|X_i : X_i \to Y_i$. Book: p. 150, Theorem A: suppose that $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of $\{X_i\}$ and $Y$ the homotopy direct limit of $\{Y_i\}$, and let $f : X \to Y$ be a map which carries each $X_i$ into $Y_i$ by a homotopy equivalence; then $f$ itself is a homotopy equivalence. Hidden hypotheses: none. Proof: departs from Milnor's in the space on which his proof is run. The map $(x, t)_n \mapsto (f(x), t)_n$ of the mapping telescopes of the inclusions carries the $m$-th truncation into the $m$-th by a map homotopic to the composite of homotopy equivalences $T_m \to X_m \xrightarrow{f_m} Y_m \to T_m$ (VA.13), and the truncations are closed, so VA.12 (Milnor's proof, Cases 1 and 2) makes it a homotopy equivalence; the mapping telescopes are homotopy equivalent to $X$ and $Y$ by maps commuting with $f$ (VA.14).

Assuming Theorem A, the alternative proof of Theorem 17.3: the constructed homotopy equivalences $\Omega^{a_i} \to K_i$ form a commutative diagram with $K_0 \subset K_1 \subset \cdots$; since $\Omega = \bigcup\Omega^{a_i}$ and $K = \bigcup K_i$ are homotopy direct limits (Examples 1 and 2), the limit mapping $\Omega \to K$ is also a homotopy equivalence.

Verified edition VA.16

(i) If $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of $X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \cdots$, the $Y_i \subseteq Y$ are closed and increasing, and $f : X \to Y$ carries each $X_i$ into $Y_i$ by a homotopy equivalence, then $X$ is homotopy equivalent to the telescope $Y_\Sigma$. (ii) If $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of $X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \cdots$ (closed or not), $K_0 \xrightarrow{c_0} K_1 \xrightarrow{c_1} \cdots$ is a sequence of spaces and maps, and $g_n : X_n \to K_n$ are homotopy equivalences with $c_ng_n \simeq g_{n+1}$ on $X_n$, then $X$ is homotopy equivalent to the mapping telescope of the $K_n$. Book: p. 150: in the proof of Theorem 17.3 homotopy equivalences $\Omega^{a_i} \to K_i$ form a commutative diagram with $K_0 \subset K_1 \subset \cdots$; since $\Omega = \bigcup\Omega^{a_i}$ and $K = \bigcup K_i$ are homotopy direct limits (Examples 1 and 2), the limit mapping $\Omega \to K$ is a homotopy equivalence. Hidden hypotheses: the limit mapping exists only because each map extends the previous one; $K$ is the homotopy direct limit of $\{K_i\}$ by Example 2, which is not verified. Deviation (restated): the conclusion is a homotopy equivalence with $Y_\Sigma$, or with the mapping telescope of the $K_n$, which stands for the union $K$ with the weak topology; the two are homotopy equivalent by Example 2 (Whitehead's theorem). Deviation (stronger): in (ii) the squares need only commute up to homotopy, and the $K_n$ need not be subspaces of one space. Proof: (ii) Milnor's map $G$ of Case 2, built from homotopy inverses of the $g_n$ and defined from the mapping telescope of the $K_n$ to $X_\Sigma$, where it is continuous block by block, is a homotopy equivalence by VA.12 for the closed truncations.

A space $K$ is obtained from $L$ by attaching cells of dimensions $(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k)$ if it is obtained by attaching a $\lambda_1$-cell to $L$, then a $\lambda_2$-cell, and so on, each along an arbitrary map of its boundary sphere into the space built so far (V1.2); the map $L \to K$ is the composite of the inclusions. A cell tower with cells $\mathrm{cells}_0, \mathrm{cells}_1, \dots$ (finite lists of dimensions) is a sequence $K_0 \to K_1 \to \cdots$ in which $K_0$ is an iterated adjunction space with cells $\mathrm{cells}_0$ (V2.11) and $K_{n+1}$ is obtained from $K_n$ by attaching the cells $\mathrm{cells}_{n+1}$, the map $K_n \to K_{n+1}$ being the inclusion; each $K_n$ is then an iterated adjunction space with the cells $\mathrm{cells}_0, \dots, \mathrm{cells}_n$. A space $X$ has the homotopy type of a countable cell complex with cells $\mathrm{cells}_0, \mathrm{cells}_1, \dots$ if it is homotopy equivalent to the mapping telescope (VA.13) of such a tower; this is invariant under homotopy equivalence. Book: p. 149: each $\Omega^{a_i}$ has the homotopy type of "a certain CW-complex", and so should the union; p. 150: $K = \bigcup K_i$. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (narrower): weaker than a CW-complex: the attaching maps need not be cellular (V2.11), and the mapping telescope of the tower stands for the union of the $K_n$ with the weak topology, to which it is homotopy equivalent by Example 2, not verified.

The alternative final step of Theorem 17.3: a commutative diagram of homotopy equivalences $\Omega^{a_i} \to K_i$, Examples 1 and 2, and Theorem A make the limit mapping $\Omega \to K$ a homotopy equivalence.

Verified edition VA.19

(i) If $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of $X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \cdots$ and $g_n : X_n \to K_n$ are homotopy equivalences to the stages of a cell tower with $c_ng_n \simeq g_{n+1}$ on $X_n$, then $X$ has the homotopy type of the countable cell complex. (ii) Let $E : X \to \mathbb R$ be continuous, $a_0 \le a_1 \le \cdots$ with $a_n \to \infty$, and $g_n : \{E \le a_n\} \to K_n$ homotopy equivalences to the stages of a cell tower (given as a tower, or by its stages $K_n$ and the inclusions $c_n : K_n \to K_{n+1}$ attaching the cells $\mathrm{cells}_{n+1}$) with $c_ng_n = g_{n+1}$ on $\{E \le a_n\}$. Then $X$ has the homotopy type of the countable cell complex with cells $\mathrm{cells}_0, \mathrm{cells}_1, \dots$. Book: p. 150, the alternative final step of Theorem 17.3 (VA.16). Hidden hypotheses: $a_i \to \infty$, so that the sublevel sets exhaust $X$; each $g_{n+1}$ extends $g_n$, for the limit map. Deviation (stronger): no paracompactness (VA.7 (ii)). Deviation (restated): "CW-complex" in the sense of VA.18. Proof: VA.16 (ii), with VA.7 (ii) in (ii).

What differs (the comparison)

  • No paracompactness: the sublevel sets of a continuous function with levels tending to infinity always form a homotopy direct limit (VA.7 (ii)). The levels must tend to infinity, so that the sublevel sets exhaust $X$, which the book leaves implicit.
  • "CW-complex" is read in the sense of VA.18; the application to the path space is Chapter 10 (V10.20–V10.22).
